                                      Answers in 03_Answer_Key.md. Mark honestly — a wrong answer you understand is worth more than a right answer you guessed.

                                      Document 03

                                      Answer Key — Grammar Practice Workbook

                                      💡 = an explanation worth reading even if you got it right.

                                      SECTION A — Nouns

                                      1. leaves
                                      2. thieves
                                      3. potatoes
                                      4. pianos 💡 Musical instruments ending in -o take just -s.
                                      5. mice
                                      6. sheep 💡 No change in the plural.
                                      7. women
                                      8. babies
                                      9. roofs 💡 An exception — not "rooves".
                                      10. teeth
                                      11. swarm
                                      12. school (also accept: shoal)
                                      13. advice 💡 Uncountable — never "advices".
                                      14. boys' 💡 Plural already ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.
                                      15. children's 💡 Irregular plural takes 's.

                                      SECTION B — Pronouns

                                      1. me 💡 Test: "Aunt Mary gave the tickets to me." ✓
                                      2. Jia Wei and I 💡 Test: "I went cycling." ✓
                                      3. its
                                      4. It's 💡 = It is.
                                      5. his or her 💡 "Everyone" is singular. "Their" is common in speech but avoid it in the exam.
                                      6. her 💡 "Neither" is singular.
                                      7. themselves 💡 "Theirselves" is not a word.
                                      8. mine
                                      9. him 💡 Object of "by".
                                      10. I 💡 Never use "myself" as a subject.
                                      11. me 💡 Object of the preposition "between".
                                      12. who
                                      13. whose
                                      14. his / her (accept: his or her)
                                      15. ourselves

                                      SECTION C — Articles and Determiners

                                      1. an 💡 "Honest" begins with a vowel SOUND — the h is silent.
                                      2. an 💡 Silent h again.
                                      3. a 💡 "University" begins with a "yoo" sound.
                                      4. The 💡 Unique object.
                                      5. X (no article before meals)
                                      6. a few 💡 "A few" = some, positive. The sharing shows there were enough.
                                      7. little 💡 "Little" = almost none, negative — matches "always shouting".
                                      8. fewer 💡 Cars are countable.
                                      9. less 💡 Homework is uncountable.
                                      10. Much 💡 Furniture is uncountable.
                                      11. a large amount of 💡 Money is uncountable.
                                      12. X 💡 "Go to school" as a pupil takes no article.

                                      SECTION D — Subject–Verb Agreement

                                      1. is 💡 Subject = box, not chocolates.
                                      2. were 💡 Subject = pupils.
                                      3. are 💡 Nearer subject = students.
                                      4. is 💡 Nearer subject = teacher.
                                      5. has 💡 "Each" is singular.
                                      6. is 💡 Subjects ending in -ics are singular.
                                      7. was 💡 "News" is singular.
                                      8. were 💡 "A number of" = many → plural.
                                      9. has 💡 "The number" is one single thing → singular.
                                      10. are 💡 Trousers is plural-only.
                                      11. is 💡 "A pair" is one item.
                                      12. are 💡 Verb agrees with "reasons".
                                      13. is 💡 A sum of money is treated as one amount.
                                      14. is 💡 One combined dish.
                                      15. is 💡 The team acts as one unit.
                                      16. wants
                                      17. was 💡 "Together with…" does not change the subject.
                                      18. was 💡 Cake is uncountable here.
                                      19. were 💡 Pupils is plural.
                                      20. play 💡 "Who" refers to "the boys".

                                      SECTION E — Tenses

                                      1. goes
                                      2. is crying
                                      3. visited
                                      4. was watching … rang 💡 Long action interrupted by a short one.
                                      5. had left 💡 The earlier of two past actions.
                                      6. has lived (accept: has been living)
                                      7. have finished
                                      8. did not see 💡 "Yesterday" is a finished past time → simple past, not present perfect.
                                      9. boils 💡 General truth.
                                      10. reach 💡 Never "will reach" after "when" in a future sense.
                                      11. is going to rain 💡 Prediction based on present evidence.
                                      12. broke
                                      13. has written 💡 "So far this week" — the week is unfinished.
                                      14. was cooking … was washing
                                      15. have known 💡 "For ten years" and still true.
                                      16. left … had locked
                                      17. leaves 💡 Timetable → simple present.
                                      18. have never eaten
                                      19. is doing
                                      20. had taught (accept: had been teaching)
                                      21. rains 💡 First conditional — no "will" in the if-clause.
                                      22. was lying 💡 "Lie" (recline) → lying, not laying.
                                      23. laid 💡 "Lay" (put down) → past tense "laid".
                                      24. rises
                                      25. will have completed

                                      SECTION F — Adjectives and Adverbs

                                      1. taller 💡 Only two things → comparative.
                                      2. worst
                                      3. more quickly 💡 "Quickly" has three syllables → use "more".
                                      4. good 💡 "Taste" is a linking verb here → adjective.
                                      5. well 💡 Describes how she sings → adverb.
                                      6. hard
                                      7. hardly 💡 "Hardly works" = barely works at all.
                                      8. boring … bored 💡 -ing = the cause, -ed = the feeling.
                                      9. exciting
                                      10. a beautiful old Chinese vase 💡 Opinion → Age → Origin.
                                      11. better
                                      12. fluently
                                      13. most careful
                                      14. peacefully
                                      15. sad 💡 "Look" as a linking verb → adjective.

                                      SECTION G — Prepositions

                                      1. at
                                      2. on
                                      3. in
                                      4. since 💡 A point in time.
                                      5. for 💡 A length of time.
                                      6. by 💡 = not later than.
                                      7. under
                                      8. over (accept: across)
                                      9. between 💡 Two people.
                                      10. among 💡 More than two.
                                      11. on
                                      12. at
                                      13. to … for 💡 Apologise TO a person FOR a thing.
                                      14. of
                                      15. after 💡 "Look after" = take care of.
                                      16. from
                                      17. on
                                      18. We discussed the problem. 💡 "Discuss" takes no preposition.
                                      19. in 💡 Arrive IN a country/city; arrive AT a small place.
                                      20. X 💡 "Reach home" — no preposition.

                                      SECTION H — Conjunctions and Connectors

                                      1. Although he was tired, he continued working. (or: He was tired, but he continued working.) 💡 Do not use "although" and "but" together.
                                      2. Because it rained, we stayed at home. (or: It rained, so we stayed at home.)
                                      3. because of 💡 + noun phrase.
                                      4. because 💡 + clause.
                                      5. Although 💡 + clause.
                                      6. Despite 💡 + noun.
                                      7. nor
                                      8. but
                                      9. or 💡 = otherwise.
                                      10. however 💡 Contrast — you would expect the match to stop.
                                      11. therefore 💡 Result.
                                      12. Unless 💡 "Unless" = if not.

                                      SECTION I — Modal Verbs

                                      1. swim 💡 A modal is always followed by the base form.
                                      2. must not 💡 Prohibition.
                                      3. need not 💡 No obligation.
                                      4. May
                                      5. should 💡 "Should have" = it ought to have happened but didn't.
                                      6. will be able to 💡 Two modals cannot be used together.
                                      7. could
                                      8. should

                                      SECTION J — Punctuation

                                      1. "Where are you going?" asked Mother.
                                      2. "I am going to the library," said Siti.
                                      3. "Stop!" shouted the policeman.
                                      4. We bought apples, oranges, pears and bananas at the market.
                                      5. My brother, who lives in Perth, is a chef. 💡 Non-defining clause → commas.
                                      6. "Don't forget your umbrella," she reminded me.
                                      7. "If you finish early," Mother said, "you may play outside." 💡 The second part starts with a small letter — same sentence continuing.
                                      8. Mr Tan, the principal, will speak on Monday, 5 May.

                                      SECTION K — Active and Passive Voice

                                      1. The mouse was chased by the cat.
                                      2. My bicycle has been stolen. 💡 "By someone" is dropped — the doer is unknown.
                                      3. The papers are being marked by the teacher.
                                      4. The results will be announced tomorrow.
                                      5. The window had been broken by the boy.
                                      6. A delicious cake was baked by Mother.
                                      7. The form must be completed (by you). 💡 Modal → must be + past participle.
                                      8. I was given a present by her. (also accept: A present was given to me by her.)
                                      9. He was bitten by the dog. 💡 "Him" → "He" as the new subject.
                                      10. English is spoken all over the world.
                                      11. Ravi wrote the letter.
                                      12. The pupils planted the trees.

                                      SECTION L — Reported Speech

                                      1. Ali said (that) he was hungry.
                                      2. She said (that) she would help me the next day. 💡 will → would; tomorrow → the next day.
                                      3. He asked where I lived. 💡 Statement word order — not "where did I live".
                                      4. She asked whether/if I was coming.
                                      5. The teacher told us to sit down.
                                      6. He told us not to run in the corridor. 💡 Negative command → "not to".
                                      7. Mei Ling said (that) she had finished her homework the day before.
                                      8. She asked me to pass her the salt.
                                      9. He suggested going swimming. (also accept: He suggested that we should go swimming.)
                                      10. She exclaimed that it was a beautiful garden.
                                      11. The teacher said (that) the earth is round. 💡 No tense shift for a general truth.
                                      12. The boy said (that) he could swim.

                                      SECTION M — Relative Clauses

                                      1. The boy who is wearing a red cap is my cousin.
                                      2. I lost the pen which/that my father gave me.
                                      3. That is the girl whose mother is a nurse.
                                      4. This is the house where I was born.
                                      5. Mr Lim, who lives next door, is a kind man. 💡 Commas, and never "that" in a non-defining clause.
                                      6. The film which/that we watched last night was boring.
                                      7. I remember the day when we first met.
                                      8. The man whom the police were looking for was arrested. (also accept: The man for whom the police were looking was arrested.)
                                      9. She has a brother who works in a bank.
                                      10. The cake which/that my aunt baked was delicious.

                                      SECTION N — Question Tags

                                      1. isn't she
                                      2. have they
                                      3. didn't you
                                      4. shall we
                                      5. aren't I

                                      23. The man warned us not to touch the wet paint.
                                      24. The dog was too fierce for anybody to approach. (also: … for anyone to dare to approach it.)
                                      25. No other boy in the class is as hardworking as he is. (also: … is more hardworking than he is.)

                                      Scoring Guide

                                      Section score What it means
                                      90–100% Solid. Move on to the next section.
                                      70–89% Log every error, then redo the section in one week.
                                      Below 70% Re-read the matching reference section before redoing. Don't move on.

                                      Track which sections keep falling below 70% — those are the two or three topics worth 80% of your revision time.

                                      Document 04

                                      Vocabulary Bank — P3 to P6

                                      How to learn vocabulary so it actually sticks: Do not memorise word lists in isolation. Use the 3-step method:

                                      1. Read the word in its example sentence here.
                                      2. Write your own sentence using it — about your own life, not a made-up one.
                                      3. Use it once in your next composition. A word is only yours after you have used it.

                                      Target: 10 words + 3 idioms per week. That is ~500 words a year, which is more than enough.

                                      PART 1 — Words by Theme

                                      PART 6 — "Show, Don't Tell" Bank

                                      Instead of naming an emotion, describe the body. This is the single fastest way to raise a composition's language mark.

                                      Instead of… Write something like…
                                      I was scared. My throat tightened. My legs felt like jelly and refused to move.
                                      I was angry. My fists clenched at my sides and I felt heat rising up my neck.
                                      I was sad. A lump rose in my throat and the words would not come out.
                                      I was nervous. My palms grew clammy and I kept rubbing them on my shorts.
                                      I was happy. I could not stop the grin spreading across my face.
                                      I was surprised. My jaw dropped and I stood rooted to the spot.
                                      I was embarrassed. My cheeks burned and I stared hard at my shoes.
                                      I was tired. My eyelids felt weighted with lead.
                                      I was relieved. The knot in my stomach finally loosened.
                                      I was guilty. I could not meet her eyes.
                                      It was hot. My shirt clung to my back and sweat trickled down my temple.
                                      It was noisy. I could barely hear my own voice above the din.

                                      PART 7 — The Five Senses Checklist

                                      A strong descriptive paragraph uses at least three senses.

                                      Sense Ask yourself
                                      Sight What colours, shapes, movements?
                                      Sound What can be heard in the background?
                                      Smell Is there an aroma, a stench, something faint?
                                      Touch Temperature, texture, weight, pain?
                                      Taste Only if relevant — food, blood, salt, dryness of the mouth

                                      The market was a riot of colour (sight). Hawkers called out their prices over the clatter of woks (sound), and the smoky aroma of grilled satay drifted through the humid air (smell + touch).

                                      PART 8 — Useful Words for Comprehension Answers

                                      Comprehension open-ended answers score higher when you use precise inference verbs:

                                      • The author implies / suggests / indicates that…
                                      • This shows that the character was reluctant / determined / remorseful…
                                      • The word "___" suggests that…
                                      • This is because…
                                      • As a result…
                                      • In contrast…

                                      For "How do you know…?" questions: always quote or refer to the evidence in the passage. For "Why…?" questions: the answer must start in a way that answers why — usually "Because…" or "This is because…" For inference questions: never lift a sentence wholesale; adapt the words to fit your answer.

                                      Document 05

                                      Composition Guide — Continuous Writing (Paper 1 Part 2)

                                      40 marks: Content 20 + Language 20. Recommended time: 50 minutes. Minimum 150 words.

                                      PART 1 — Understanding the Question

                                      The PSLE Continuous Writing question gives you:

                                      • A theme (one or two words, e.g. Honesty, A Difficult Decision, Helping Someone)
                                      • Three pictures related to the theme
                                      • The instruction that you may use one, two, three, or none of the pictures, but your story must be relevant to the theme

                                      The single most important rule

                                      The theme is compulsory. The pictures are optional.

                                      Most content marks are lost because the story drifts away from the theme, not because the writing is weak. Before you write a single word, finish this sentence in your head:

                                      "By the end of my story, the reader will clearly see that this story is about __."

                                      If you cannot finish that sentence, do not start writing.

                                      Using the pictures well

                                      Approach Risk Recommendation
                                      Use all three Story becomes rushed and shallow Avoid unless they connect naturally
                                      Use one or two Clean, focused plot ✅ Best choice
                                      Use none Allowed, but examiners look extra hard at theme relevance Only if you have a strong, clearly on-theme story

                                      Do not describe the picture. Use it as an object or event inside your story. If the picture shows a wallet, your story is not "a wallet"; it is what happened when I found a wallet on the way home.

                                      PART 2 — The Marking Criteria in Plain Words

                                      Content (20 marks) — the examiner asks:

                                      1. Is the story clearly relevant to the theme?
                                      2. Is the plot believable and complete (a real beginning, middle and end)?
                                      3. Are the details developed, especially at the climax?
                                      4. Is there insight — do we understand what the character felt and learnt?

                                      Language (20 marks) — the examiner asks:

                                      1. Is the grammar accurate (tense, subject–verb agreement, sentence structure)?
                                      2. Is the vocabulary varied and used correctly?
                                      3. Is there sentence variety (not all short, not all long)?
                                      4. Is the paragraphing logical?
                                      5. Is the spelling and punctuation accurate?

                                      The trade secret: a simple plot told with excellent language and one well-developed climax scores far higher than an ambitious, complicated plot told badly. Do not write about kidnappings, murders or superheroes. Write about one small, real event and go deep.

                                      PART 3 — Planning (5–7 minutes, always)

                                      Never skip this. Unplanned compositions run out of steam in paragraph 3.

                                      The 6-Box Plan

                                      Draw six boxes on your question paper and fill them with notes, not sentences:

                                      Box What goes in it
                                      1. Theme One sentence: what the story proves
                                      2. Setting Where and when
                                      3. Characters Who (keep it to 2–3 people, use real-sounding names)
                                      4. Problem What goes wrong
                                      5. Climax The single most tense moment — this gets the most words
                                      6. Resolution + Lesson How it ends and what was learnt

                                      Worked example

                                      Theme given: Perseverance

                                      1. Theme: Giving up is easy; trying again is what counts.
                                      2. Setting: School field, Sports Day, late afternoon
                                      3. Characters: Me (Rachel), Coach Lim, my rival Priya
                                      4. Problem: I sprained my ankle two weeks before the 800 m final
                                      5. Climax: The last lap — ankle throbbing, Priya pulling ahead, deciding whether to stop
                                      6. Resolution: I finish third, not first — but I finish. Coach Lim says finishing mattered more.

                                      Notice the resolution: she does not win. Realistic endings score better than fairy-tale ones.

                                      PART 4 — Structure: The Five-Paragraph Shape

                                      Para Purpose Approx. words
                                      1. Opening Hook the reader; establish setting and mood 40–60
                                      2. Rising action Introduce the problem; build tension 60–80
                                      3. Climax ⭐ The critical moment — slow it down, expand it 90–120
                                      4. Falling action Immediate aftermath 50–70
                                      5. Resolution & reflection Outcome + what was learnt 50–70

                                      Target: 280–380 words for P6. The minimum is 150, but 150-word compositions almost never develop the climax enough for high content marks. For P4–P5, aim for 180–280.

                                      The Climax Rule ⭐

                                      The climax should take up roughly a third of your composition. Beginners rush it in two sentences; strong writers stretch it.

                                      How to stretch a climax — the slow-motion technique:

                                      1. Physical sensation — what the body feels
                                      2. A single sensory detail — one sound, one smell
                                      3. A thought — what is going through the character's head
                                      4. Dialogue or a shout — a line of speech
                                      5. The action itself — short, punchy sentences
                                      6. The immediate result

                                      Rushed version (weak):

                                      I ran to the road and pulled the boy back. A car sped past. He was safe.

                                      Expanded version (strong):

                                      My legs moved before my brain caught up. The screech of tyres tore through the afternoon air, sharp and terrible. Three metres. Two. I lunged forward, my fingers closing around the collar of the boy's T-shirt, and yanked with everything I had. We crashed onto the pavement in a tangle of limbs. A rush of hot air swept over us as the lorry thundered past, so close that I felt the grit sting my cheek. For a moment neither of us moved. Then the boy began to wail, and I realised my own hands were shaking uncontrollably.

                                      Same event. One is 20 words; the other is 100. The second one earns the content mark.

                                      PART 5 — Openings

                                      Never open with: One fine day… / It was a sunny Saturday morning… / Hi, my name is… / I will never forget the day when… (overused)

                                      Six opening types that work

                                      ① Action opening — start in the middle of something happening

                                      The glass shattered before I could even shout a warning.

                                      ② Dialogue opening — a line of speech

                                      "You promised you wouldn't tell anyone," Wei Jie whispered, his voice cracking.

                                      ③ Sound opening

                                      A single, piercing scream cut through the stillness of the void deck.

                                      ④ Feeling / thought opening

                                      I had told exactly one lie in my life, and it was about to catch up with me.

                                      ⑤ Setting-with-mood opening — description that carries an emotion

                                      The classroom felt unusually cold that morning, as though the walls themselves knew something was wrong.

                                      ⑥ Flashback opening

                                      Even now, three years later, I cannot walk past that bakery without my stomach tightening.

                                      Tip: whichever opening you choose, your first sentence should be short. Short openings pull the reader in; long ones lose them.

                                      PART 6 — Endings

                                      A good ending does two things: it closes the event and it shows what changed inside the character.

                                      Four endings that work

                                      ① Reflection

                                      I have kept that crumpled ten-dollar note in my drawer ever since. It is worth nothing now, but it reminds me of the day I nearly became someone I would not have liked.

                                      ② Changed behaviour

                                      These days, I check on Mrs Rahim every Saturday. She always pretends she does not need the help, and I always pretend I have nothing better to do.

                                      ③ Full-circle — echo the opening image

                                      (Opening: the classroom felt cold.) → The classroom was still cold when the bell rang, but somehow I no longer minded.

                                      ④ Dialogue ending

                                      "You came back," she said quietly. I nodded. "I always would have."

                                      Endings to avoid

                                      ❌ …and then I woke up. It was all a dream. ❌ …we all lived happily ever after. ❌ …it was the best day of my life. (too vague) ❌ A moral tacked on that has nothing to do with the story: …this shows that we must always be filial.

                                      The lesson should be shown through the story, then briefly named — never announced out of nowhere.

                                      PART 7 — Paragraphing and Sentence Variety

                                      Start a new paragraph when:

                                      • Time changes
                                      • Place changes
                                      • A new speaker speaks
                                      • The focus shifts to a new event or idea

                                      Vary your sentence openings

                                      If four sentences in a row start with I or The, the language mark drops. Rotate through these:

                                      Opening type Example
                                      Adverb Suddenly, the lights went out.
                                      Prepositional phrase In the corner of the room, something moved.
                                      -ing phrase Gripping the railing tightly, I peered over the edge.
                                      -ed phrase Startled by the noise, the cat bolted.
                                      Subordinate clause Before I could react, he had already left.
                                      Dialogue "Wait!" I called after her.
                                      Short dramatic sentence Silence.

                                      Vary sentence length

                                      A short sentence after two long ones creates impact:

                                      I had spent three weeks preparing for the audition, rehearsing every night until my parents begged me to stop, and I had been certain — absolutely certain — that I was ready. Then I forgot the first line.**

                                      PART 8 — Writing Dialogue

                                      Dialogue makes a composition come alive, but only if it is purposeful. Two to four exchanges per composition is enough.

                                      Rules recap:

                                      "I'm not going in there," Mei whispered, tugging at my sleeve.
"We have to," I replied. "There's no other way out."
                                      • New speaker → new paragraph
                                      • Comma inside the inverted commas before said/whispered/replied
                                      • Add an action beat instead of always writing he said: He looked away. "It wasn't me."

                                      Cut dialogue that does nothing: ❌ "Hello." "Hi." "How are you?" "I am fine, thank you. And you?" This wastes 20 words and adds nothing.

                                      PART 9 — Phrase Banks

                                      Building tension

                                      • My heart hammered against my ribs.
                                      • Time seemed to slow to a crawl.
                                      • A cold knot formed in the pit of my stomach.
                                      • Every second stretched into an eternity.
                                      • The silence was so complete that I could hear my own breathing.
                                      • I did not dare to look.

                                      Describing a place

                                      • The void deck was deserted, save for a stray cat curled in one corner.
                                      • Sunlight filtered through the leaves, dappling the pavement with gold.
                                      • The corridor smelt faintly of disinfectant and old paper.
                                      • Rain drummed steadily on the zinc roof above us.

                                      Showing regret

                                      • The words left my mouth before I could stop them.
                                      • I would have given anything to take it back.
                                      • Her expression was the kind I would remember for years.
                                      • Something in me shrank when I saw her face.

                                      Showing determination

                                      • I gritted my teeth and pressed on.
                                      • Giving up now was not an option.
                                      • I forced my trembling legs to move.
                                      • One more step. Then another.

                                      Transitions (use sparingly, and vary them)

                                      Moments later · Before long · By the time · No sooner had I… than · As the minutes crawled past · The next thing I knew · Little did I know · It was only later that I realised

                                      PART 10 — Model Composition 1 (Annotated)

                                      Theme: Honesty · Pictures: a wallet, a school gate, a police post

                                      The Wallet

                                      The brown leather wallet was lying in the drain grating outside the school gate, half hidden by a soggy flyer. ⟵ ① Action/object opening. Specific detail: "soggy flyer".

                                      I glanced around. The afternoon crowd had thinned, and nobody seemed to be looking for anything. I picked it up. Inside were three fifty-dollar notes, crisp and new, and a photograph of a man holding a toddler on his shoulders. ⟵ ② Problem established. The photograph is a deliberate choice — it makes the owner a person, not just a wallet.

                                      One hundred and fifty dollars. I thought of the bicycle I had been saving for since March, the one I was still eighty dollars short of. My fingers tightened around the notes. Nobody had seen me. Nobody would ever know.

                                      But the toddler in the photograph was still grinning up at me. ⟵ ③ Climax begins — internal conflict, not external drama.

                                      I stood there for what felt like an hour, the wallet growing heavier in my hand. A bus rumbled past. Somewhere behind me, a child laughed. My mother's voice surfaced in my head, unbidden: "Rachel, the things you do when nobody is watching are the things that tell you who you are." My throat tightened. Slowly, I closed the wallet.

                                      The police post was a ten-minute walk in the wrong direction. I walked it anyway. ⟵ ④ Decision shown through action. Two short sentences for impact.

                                      Three days later, a man appeared at our door with a bag of oranges and the same toddler on his hip. He had wanted to thank me in person, he said. He was a delivery driver, and the money had been that week's earnings. ⟵ ⑤ Falling action — realistic reward, not a cash prize.

                                      I never did get the bicycle that year. I saved for two more months and bought it in August instead. But every time I ride past that drain grating, I remember that I very nearly became someone else that afternoon — and that being honest cost me eight weeks and nothing more. ⟵ ⑥ Reflective ending. The lesson is shown, not announced.

                                      Word count: ~330 · Why it scores well: one simple event, a fully developed internal climax, no melodrama, realistic outcome, varied sentence length, strong final line.

                                      PART 11 — Model Composition 2 (Annotated)

                                      Theme: A Difficult Decision · Pictures: a friend crying, a mobile phone, a teacher

                                      What I Owed Her

                                      "You can't tell anyone. Promise me." ⟵ Dialogue opening — instant tension.

                                      Nadia's voice was barely a whisper, but it filled the empty stairwell between the third and fourth floors. Her eyes were red-rimmed, and she kept twisting the strap of her bag around her fingers.

                                      She had just told me that Suri and two other girls had been sending her messages for the past three weeks. Not the loud, obvious kind of bullying that teachers notice — the quiet kind, the kind that arrives at eleven at night and is deleted by morning. ⟵ Problem established with a precise, believable detail.

                                      "Promise," she repeated.

                                      I promised.

                                      For four days I kept that promise, and for four days I watched my best friend grow smaller. She stopped putting up her hand in class. She stopped eating during recess. On Thursday, she did not come to school at all. ⟵ Rising action — the escalation is shown through small changes, not stated.

                                      That evening I sat on my bed with my phone in my hand for a very long time. ⟵ Climax begins.

                                      Mrs Devi's number was saved in my contacts from our class group chat. All I had to do was press call. But Nadia had trusted me — had chosen me, out of everyone — and I could still hear her voice in that stairwell. If I told, she might never forgive me. If I stayed silent, I would keep watching her disappear.

                                      My thumb hovered over the screen. The room was so quiet I could hear the fan clicking. I thought about Thursday, about her empty chair. Then I pressed call. ⟵ Slow-motion climax: sensory detail, thought, decision, short final sentence.

                                      Nadia did not speak to me for two weeks. They were the longest two weeks of my life. ⟵ Falling action — realistic consequence.

                                      On the fifteenth day, she sat down beside me at recess and pushed half her sandwich towards me without a word. It was not an apology, and it was not forgiveness. It was something better than both. ⟵ Understated, memorable ending.

                                      I have learnt that keeping a promise is not always the same as keeping a friend safe. ⟵ One clear line of reflection.

                                      Word count: ~350

                                      PART 12 — Ten Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them

                                      Mistake Fix
                                      Story drifts off-theme Write the theme at the top of your plan and check it after every paragraph
                                      Too many events One problem, one climax. Cut everything else
                                      The climax is two sentences long Apply the slow-motion technique (Part 4)
                                      Tense keeps switching Choose simple past and stay there
                                      Every sentence starts with "I" or "Then" Use the sentence-opening table (Part 7)
                                      Telling emotions: "I was very sad" Use the Show-Don't-Tell bank in 04_Vocabulary_Bank.md
                                      Dialogue punctuated wrongly Revise Section 12.1 of 01_Grammar_Reference.md
                                      Fantasy or violent plots Examiners reward believability. Keep it grounded
                                      Moral bolted on at the end The lesson must grow out of the story
                                      No time left to check Reserve the last 5 minutes for editing

                                      PART 13 — Time Management (50 minutes)

                                      Minutes Task
                                      0–6 Read the theme and pictures. Complete the 6-Box Plan.
                                      6–10 Write the opening paragraph carefully — it sets your language level.
                                      10–40 Write paragraphs 2–5, giving the climax the most space.
                                      40–45 Write the ending.
                                      45–50 Edit using the checklist below.

                                      PART 14 — Five-Minute Self-Editing Checklist

                                      Read your composition backwards, sentence by sentence — it forces you to see the words rather than the story.

                                      • ☐ Does every sentence have a subject and a verb?
                                      • ☐ Is the tense consistent throughout?
                                      • ☐ Subject–verb agreement: check every sentence with a plural subject
                                      • ☐ Are all plurals correct? (no missing -s)
                                      • ☐ Are capital letters used for every sentence start and proper noun?
                                      • ☐ Is every piece of dialogue punctuated correctly and on a new paragraph?
                                      • ☐ Any spelling you are unsure of? Swap in a word you can spell.
                                      • ☐ Did you repeat any word too often? (especially said, went, nice, very, then)
                                      • ☐ Is the theme unmistakable to someone who has not read the question?
                                      • ☐ Is your final sentence strong?

                                      PART 15 — Theme-to-Plot Bank (Practice Prompts)

                                      Use one a week. Plan it in 6 minutes, write it in 44.

                                      Theme Simple plot ideas
                                      Honesty Finding money · owning up to breaking something · admitting you cheated on a test
                                      Perseverance An injury before a competition · failing a test repeatedly · learning a difficult skill
                                      Kindness Helping an elderly neighbour · including a new classmate · giving up something for someone
                                      A Difficult Decision Reporting a friend · choosing between two commitments · returning something valuable
                                      Regret Words said in anger · a promise broken · not visiting someone in time
                                      Courage Standing up to a bully · admitting fear · speaking in front of a crowd
                                      Teamwork A group project that goes wrong · a relay race · organising a school event
                                      A Misunderstanding Being wrongly accused · misreading a message · assuming the worst about someone
                                      An Unexpected Discovery An old letter · a hidden talent · learning something about a family member
                                      Gratitude Realising what a parent gave up · thanking a teacher years later
                                      A Lesson Learnt Carelessness causing a loss · procrastination before an exam
                                      Helping Others A neighbourhood clean-up · assisting at an accident · volunteering
                                      Facing a Fear Water, heights, dogs, public speaking
                                      Friendship A quarrel and reconciliation · a friend moving away · standing up for a friend
                                      Responsibility Caring for a pet · looking after a younger sibling · a task you neglected

                                      Document 06

                                      Situational Writing (Paper 1 Part 1) and Oral (Paper 4)

                                      PART A — SITUATIONAL WRITING (15 marks, ~20 minutes)

                                      1. What You Are Marked On

                                      Component Marks What it means
                                      Task Fulfilment 9 Did you cover every bullet point in the question, with enough detail?
                                      Language and Organisation 6 Correct tone for the audience, accurate grammar, clear paragraphs, correct format

                                      Task fulfilment is worth more than language here. A beautifully written response that misses one bullet point loses more marks than a plain response that covers everything. Tick off the bullet points as you write.

                                      2. PAC — Do This Before Writing (2 minutes)

                                      Every situational writing question contains three clues. Underline them on the question paper.

                                      Question to ask Why it matters
                                      P — Purpose Why am I writing? (to inform / invite / request / thank / apologise / complain / suggest / report) Determines your opening line
                                      A — Audience Who am I writing to? (friend / teacher / principal / stranger / shop manager) Determines formal or informal tone
                                      C — Context What is the situation? What details am I given? Prevents you from inventing wrong facts

                                      The tone test

                                      Audience Tone Greeting Sign-off
                                      Close friend, cousin, sibling Informal Hi Aisha, / Dear Aisha, Love, / Your friend, / Bye for now,
                                      Teacher you know well Semi-formal Dear Mrs Tan, Yours sincerely,
                                      Principal, a company, a stranger Formal Dear Mr Lim, / Dear Sir or Madam, Yours sincerely, (named) / Yours faithfully, (unnamed)

                                      Informal features allowed: contractions (I'm, don't), exclamation marks, chatty phrases (Guess what!, Can't wait!), questions to the reader. Formal features required: no contractions, no slang, no exclamation marks, complete sentences, polite requests (I would be grateful if…, Could you kindly…).

                                      ⚠️ Never mix tones. "Dear Sir or Madam, Hey, I'm writing about…" loses language marks immediately.

                                      3. Formats

                                      3.1 Informal Email

                                      To: aisha@email.com
Subject: Our trip to the Science Centre this Saturday

Hi Aisha,

[Opening: greeting + reason for writing]

[Body paragraph(s): cover every bullet point]

[Closing: what you want them to do, or a warm sign-off line]

Your friend,
Rachel

                                      3.2 Formal Email or Letter

                                      To: enquiries@library.gov.sg
Subject: Enquiry about the Junior Reading Programme

Dear Sir or Madam,

[Opening: state who you are and why you are writing, in one sentence]

[Body: cover the bullet points, one idea per paragraph]

[Closing: state what response you would like, and thank them]

Yours faithfully,
Rachel Tan
Primary 6 Resilience
Sengkang Primary School

                                      Yours sincerely when you know the person's name (Dear Mrs Tan). Yours faithfully when you do not (Dear Sir or Madam).

                                      3.3 Report (to a teacher or committee)

                                      Report on the Primary 6 Recycling Drive
By: Rachel Tan, Primary 6 Resilience
Date: 14 August 2026

Purpose
[One or two lines on why the report was written]

Details of the event
[What happened, when, where, who was involved]

Feedback / Findings
[What went well, what did not]

Recommendations
[What should be done differently next time]

                                      Reports use headings, factual language, and no personal chatter.

                                      3.4 Short Message or Note

                                      Keep it brief and cover all points. Still start with a greeting and end with your name.

                                      4. Worked Example

                                      Question: Your school library is starting a Book Buddy Programme. You would like your friend Daniel, who has moved to another school, to know about it and to join a joint online session. Write an email to Daniel.

                                      You should include: - what the programme is about - when and where it takes place - why you think he would enjoy it - how he can join the online session

                                      Planning (1 minute)

                                      • P: to inform + invite
                                      • A: a friend → informal
                                      • C: four bullet points, all must be covered

                                      Model answer

                                      To: daniel.ong@email.com
Subject: You have to join our Book Buddy Programme!

Hi Daniel,

How have you been settling in at your new school? I have some news that I think
you will love.

Our library has just started a Book Buddy Programme. Each of us is paired with a
reading partner, and every week we read the same book and then discuss our
favourite parts. There are also small challenges, such as designing a new cover
for the book we have read.

The sessions are held every Wednesday from 2 p.m. to 3 p.m. in the school
library. Since you are no longer here, the good news is that there is an online
session on the last Wednesday of each month, and pupils from other schools are
welcome to join.

I really think you would enjoy this. You were always the one recommending
mystery novels to me, and this month's book is a detective story set in
Singapore. It would be just like our old recess conversations.

To join the online session, simply fill in the form on the school library
website and pick "Guest Reader" when it asks for your role. Let me know once
you have signed up so that I can request to be your buddy.

Hope to see you online soon!

Your friend,
Rachel

                                      Why this scores well: all four bullet points covered with a detail each · consistent informal tone · logical paragraphing · a clear call to action at the end.

                                      5. Situational Writing Checklist

                                      • ☐ Did I identify Purpose, Audience and Context?
                                      • ☐ Have I covered every bullet point? (Tick them off on the question paper.)
                                      • ☐ Did I add one supporting detail to each point, not just repeat the bullet?
                                      • ☐ Is the tone consistent from greeting to sign-off?
                                      • ☐ Correct format (To / Subject / greeting / paragraphs / sign-off / name)?
                                      • ☐ Did I invent any information that contradicts the question?
                                      • ☐ Grammar, spelling, punctuation checked?

                                      6. Practice Prompts

                                      1. Write to your form teacher explaining why you were absent from the class outing, apologising, and asking what work you missed.
                                      2. Write to the manager of a bookshop about a damaged book you bought, describing the problem, when you bought it, and what you would like done.
                                      3. Write to your cousin overseas inviting her to your school's Racial Harmony Day performance, including what you will perform, when it is, and how she can watch it online.
                                      4. Write a report to your principal on the Primary 5 camp, covering the activities, what pupils enjoyed, one problem faced, and one recommendation.
                                      5. Write to your neighbour thanking her for looking after your rabbit while your family was away, mentioning something she did well and offering to return the favour.
                                      6. Write to the community centre asking about their holiday coding workshop: the dates, the fee, whether beginners are welcome, and how to register.

                                      PART B — ORAL COMMUNICATION (Paper 4, 30 marks)

                                      1. Reading Aloud (10 marks)

                                      You are given a short passage and about five minutes to prepare.

                                      What examiners listen for
                                      Pronunciation Clear consonants, especially final sounds (-s, -ed, -t, -k)
                                      Fluency Smooth, no stumbling, no long pauses in the middle of a phrase
                                      Expression Voice matches the meaning — rising for questions, warmth for happy content
                                      Pace Not too fast. Slower than you think is right.

                                      Preparation routine (use every second of the five minutes)

                                      1. Read the whole passage silently once to understand what it is about. You cannot read expressively if you do not know the meaning.
                                      2. Mark your pauses with a pencil slash: / at commas, // at full stops.
                                      3. Circle difficult words and say them quietly to yourself twice.
                                      4. Underline words to stress — usually the key noun or verb in each sentence.
                                      5. Note any question marks and exclamation marks — your voice must change there.

                                      Common Singapore-specific pronunciation points to watch

                                      • Final consonants: say "wanted", "asked", "both", not "wan", "ask", "bof"
                                      • -s endings: "the boys run", "he walks"
                                      • th sounds: three (not tree), this (not dis)
                                      • v vs w: very (not wery)
                                      • Word stress: com-FOR-ta-ble, in-TER-es-ting, VEG-e-ta-ble

                                      During the reading

                                      • Look up briefly at the examiner once or twice — but do not lose your place
                                      • If you make a mistake, repeat only that word and carry on calmly. Do not restart the sentence.
                                      • Breathe at the full stops. Rushing is the most common cause of lost marks.

                                      2. Stimulus-Based Conversation (20 marks)

                                      You are shown a video clip, then asked three questions by the examiner.

                                      The three questions usually follow this pattern

                                      Question Type What to do
                                      Q1 About the video Give your view on what you saw, and explain why
                                      Q2 About your personal experience Tell a short, specific story from your own life
                                      Q3 A broader opinion question Give an opinion, reasons, and a suggestion

                                      The golden rule: never give a one-sentence answer

                                      Aim for 4–6 sentences per answer. Use the PEEL structure:
                                      P — Point State your answer clearly
                                      E — Elaborate Explain what you mean
                                      E — Example Give a personal example or a specific instance
                                      L — Link Round off with a conclusion or a suggestion

                                      Worked example

                                      Examiner: Do you think students should be encouraged to take part in community projects?

                                      Weak answer: "Yes, because it is good."

                                      Strong answer (PEEL): P — "Yes, I strongly believe students should take part in community projects. E — This is because such projects teach us responsibility and help us understand people whose lives are different from our own, which we cannot learn from textbooks alone. E — Last year, my class helped to pack and deliver food parcels to elderly residents in our neighbourhood. I spoke to one gentleman who lived alone, and I realised how much a short conversation meant to him. L — Because of that experience, I think every school should organise at least one community project a year, so that more students get the chance to see this for themselves."

                                      Useful phrases

                                      Giving an opinion: In my opinion… · I strongly believe that… · From my point of view… · I feel that… Explaining: This is because… · The reason for this is… · What I mean by this is… Giving examples: For instance… · Let me give you an example… · This reminds me of a time when… Agreeing partly: I agree to a certain extent, however… · While that is true, I also think… Concluding: All things considered… · That is why I believe… · Overall…

                                      Buying thinking time (better than "erm"): That is an interesting question… · Let me think about that for a moment…

                                      Preparation that actually works

                                      • Talk about the news at dinner. Pick one everyday topic a week — recycling, screen time, road safety, kindness to seniors, food waste, exercise, saving money — and discuss it for five minutes.
                                      • Build a personal-story bank. Have 5–6 real experiences ready that can be adapted to many questions: a time you helped someone, a time you failed, a school event, a family trip, a time you learnt something, a time you were disappointed. Most oral questions can be answered using one of these.
                                      • Practise out loud, not in your head. Record yourself on a phone and listen back once.

                                      Delivery

                                      • Eye contact with the examiner
                                      • Sit up straight, hands still
                                      • Speak at a moderate pace and finish your sentences
                                      • Smile — examiners mark on engagement as well as content

                                      3. Listening Comprehension (Paper 3, 20 marks) — Quick Tips

                                      • The passage is read twice. Use the first reading to understand and the second to confirm.
                                      • Read the questions and all the options before the recording starts.
                                      • Underline key words in each question so you know what to listen for.
                                      • Distractors are common: the recording often mentions all four options — listen for which one actually answers the question.
                                      • Do not leave any question blank. Make your best choice and move on.

                                      You now have the complete set. Start with 00_START_HERE_Study_Plan.md for the weekly routine.

                                      Document 07

                                      Comprehension Guide — Paper 2 Open-Ended (20 marks)

                                      Comprehension is the largest single component of Paper 2 Booklet B, and the one where marks are most often lost to technique rather than understanding. Most children understand the passage perfectly well and still lose six or seven marks, because they answer the question they expected instead of the question that was asked.

                                      This guide has two parts: the eight question types and how each one must be answered, then four full passages with model answers.

                                      Part 1 — The Eight Question Types

                                      1. "Why…?" questions · 1–2m

                                      Your answer must be a reason, and it must start in a way that answers 'why'. Begin with 'Because…' or 'This is because…'. If the question says 'Why do you think…', the reason is not stated in the passage — you must infer it and support it with something that is.

                                      Question: Why did Meilin hide the letter under her mattress?

                                      ❌ Weak: She put it under her mattress.

                                      ✅ Strong: Because she did not want her mother to find out that she had failed the test.

                                      The weak answer repeats the question. The strong answer supplies the reason the question asked for.

                                      2. "How do you know…?" questions · 1–2m

                                      This asks for evidence. Point to something specific in the passage — an action, a word, a detail. Do not answer with an opinion or a feeling.

                                      Question: How do you know that the old man was poor?

                                      ❌ Weak: Because he looked very poor and sad.

                                      ✅ Strong: His shoes were held together with tape and he counted out his coins before buying a single bun.

                                      Evidence means details you can point at, not restating the conclusion.

                                      3. "How did X feel?" questions · 1–2m

                                      Name a precise emotion, then justify it. Avoid 'sad', 'happy', 'bad' — reach for relieved, humiliated, resentful, apprehensive, remorseful, indignant. Two marks usually means one mark for the emotion and one for the reason.

                                      Question: How did Devi feel when the results were read out? (2m)

                                      ❌ Weak: She felt bad.

                                      ✅ Strong: She felt humiliated, because her name was called out last in front of the whole class.

                                      One precise word plus a 'because' clause earns both marks.

                                      4. Vocabulary-in-context questions · 1m

                                      Replace the word with your own, and make sure your replacement fits the sentence grammatically. Read the sentence back with your word in it. If the word is a verb in the past tense, your answer must be a verb in the past tense.

                                      Question: What does the word 'trudged' tell us about how the boy walked?

                                      ❌ Weak: It means he walked.

                                      ✅ Strong: He walked slowly and heavily, as if he was tired or unwilling.

                                      Explain the extra meaning the writer chose that word for, not just the basic action.

                                      5. "What does 'it' / 'this' refer to?" · 1m

                                      Look at the sentence before. Write out the thing in full — never answer with another pronoun. Check by substituting your answer back into the original sentence.

                                      Question: In line 14, what does 'this' refer to?

                                      ❌ Weak: It refers to what he did.

                                      ✅ Strong: The fact that Kumar had returned the wallet without taking any money from it.

                                      'What he did' is still vague. Name the thing.

                                      6. Questions that say "in your own words" · 2m

                                      You will lose the mark if you lift the phrase from the passage. Change the key words, not just the small ones. Keep the meaning identical.

                                      Question: In your own words, explain why the villagers were reluctant to leave.

                                      ❌ Weak: They were reluctant to leave because they had lived there all their lives.

                                      ✅ Strong: They did not want to go because the village had been their home since they were born.

                                      'Reluctant' and 'all their lives' were both lifted in the weak version.

                                      7. True / False with evidence · 2m

                                      One mark for the tick, one for the evidence. The evidence must be the specific line that proves it — not a general summary. Always fill in the evidence box even when you are unsure of the tick.

                                      Question: The narrator's father approved of her decision. True or false? Give evidence.

                                      ❌ Weak: False, he did not approve.

                                      ✅ Strong: False — 'He said nothing for a long moment, then folded the form in half and set it aside.'

                                      The evidence must do work. Repeating the statement is not evidence.

                                      8. The 3-mark 'explain' question · 3m

                                      Three marks means three separate points, not one point written three times. Plan them on your fingers before writing. Use a connector between each so the marker can see them: 'Firstly… In addition… Finally…'

                                      Question: Explain how the writer creates a sense of danger in paragraph 4. (3m)

                                      ❌ Weak: The writer makes it sound scary by describing the storm.

                                      ✅ Strong: Firstly, the writer uses short sentences such as 'The rope snapped.' to make events feel sudden. In addition, the sounds described — the groaning of the timber and the shriek of the wind — suggest the structure is about to fail. Finally, the narrator's own body betrays her fear: her fingers are described as numb and useless.

                                      Three distinct points, clearly signposted.

                                      How to work through a comprehension passage

                                      1. Read the questions first. Two minutes spent here saves ten later — you read the passage knowing what to look for.
                                      2. Read the passage once, without stopping. Do not annotate yet. Get the whole shape of it.
                                      3. Read again with a pencil. Underline anything that answers a question, and write the question number in the margin beside it.
                                      4. Check the marks. One mark means one point. Three marks means three separate points. Never write a paragraph for a one-mark question, and never write one sentence for a three-mark question.
                                      5. Answer in full sentences, unless the question asks for a single word.
                                      6. Re-read your answer against the question. The commonest error in the whole paper is answering a related question rather than the one printed.

                                      The lifting trap

                                      Lifting means copying a phrase straight from the passage. It is allowed for some questions and fatal for others:

                                      Question says Lifting
                                      "Give evidence" / "Quote" ✅ Expected — copy exactly
                                      Nothing about wording ⚠️ Allowed, but adapt so it reads as an answer
                                      "In your own words" ❌ Zero marks if you lift the key words

                                      Part 2 — Practice Passages

                                      Model answers follow each passage. Cover them, write your own answers first, then compare.

                                      The Kite

                                      Narrative · about 330 words · 8 questions · 14 marks · suggested for P4 and above

                                      Ah Kong made the kite himself, on the floor of the corridor outside our flat. He split the bamboo with a knife so old the handle had worn smooth, and he bent each strip over a candle flame until it curved exactly the way he wanted. It took him four evenings. I sat beside him the whole time, passing him string he did not ask for.

                                      "Why don't we just buy one?" I asked on the third evening. There was a shop at the void deck selling kites shaped like eagles, with printed feathers and plastic tails.

                                      Ah Kong did not look up. "You can buy a kite," he said. "You cannot buy a kite that knows you."

                                      I did not understand that, but I nodded anyway.

                                      On Sunday we walked to the open field behind the school. The wind was strong and the sky was the pale, washed-out blue that comes after heavy rain. Ah Kong held the kite above his head and told me to run. I ran until my chest burned, and when I turned around the kite was up, small and steady, tugging at the line like something alive.

                                      For nearly an hour it stayed there. Then the wind changed. The line went slack, then snapped taut, and before I could loosen my grip the string broke somewhere far above my hands. The kite tumbled sideways across the sky and disappeared behind the trees at the edge of the field.

                                      I stood there with the empty spool in my fist. Four evenings of bamboo and candle flame, gone in three seconds. My eyes stung and I turned away so Ah Kong would not see.

                                      He came and stood beside me, looking at the trees.

                                      "Good," he said.

                                      I stared at him.

                                      "Now," he said, "you know how to make one."

                                      We walked home. That evening he took out the knife and put a fresh strip of bamboo in my hands, and this time he did not touch it at all. He only watched, and told me when to move the flame closer.

                                      Questions

                                      1. How long did Ah Kong take to make the first kite? (1m)

                                      2. Why did the narrator suggest buying a kite instead? (1m)

                                      3. What did Ah Kong mean when he said, "You cannot buy a kite that knows you"? (2m)

                                      4. In your own words, describe the weather on Sunday. (2m)

                                      5. What does the phrase "tugging at the line like something alive" suggest about the kite? (1m)

                                      6. How did the narrator feel when the kite was lost? How do you know? (2m)

                                      7. Why do you think Ah Kong said "Good" when the kite was lost? (2m)

                                      8. How is the last paragraph different from the beginning of the story? Explain what this shows. (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. Four evenings. [1m]

                                      A literal question — the answer is stated directly. Don't over-write it.

                                      2. Because there was a shop at the void deck selling ready-made kites shaped like eagles, so it would have been much quicker and easier than making one. [1m]

                                      Start with 'Because'. The reason is implied by the detail about the shop.

                                      3. He meant that a kite you have made yourself has value that a bought one does not, because you have put your own time and effort into it and understand how every part of it works. [2m]

                                      Inference. The answer is nowhere in the passage — you build it from what he does afterwards.

                                      4. It was breezy, and the sky was a faint, faded blue because a heavy shower had fallen earlier. [2m]

                                      'Pale, washed-out blue' and 'after heavy rain' must both be reworded, not copied.

                                      5. It suggests that the kite pulled strongly and unpredictably, as though it had a will of its own rather than being an ordinary object. [1m]

                                      Vocabulary-in-context: explain the extra meaning the comparison creates.

                                      6. He felt devastated and close to tears. I know this because his eyes stung and he deliberately turned away so that Ah Kong would not see him crying. [2m]

                                      One mark for a precise emotion, one for the evidence. 'Sad' alone would be weak.

                                      7. Because he was not upset about losing the kite itself. He saw that his grandson had now watched the whole process closely enough to build one himself, which was what he had wanted all along. [2m]

                                      'Why do you think' signals inference. Support it with the final paragraph.

                                      8. Firstly, at the beginning Ah Kong does all the work while the narrator only sits and passes string. In addition, at the end it is the narrator who holds the bamboo and the knife, while Ah Kong does not touch it at all. Finally, this shows that the narrator has moved from being a bystander to being the maker, which is the lesson Ah Kong intended. [3m]

                                      Three marks means three separate points. Signpost them.

                                      Mrs Fernandez

                                      Narrative · about 350 words · 8 questions · 16 marks · suggested for P5 and above

                                      We decided we hated her before she had said a word.

                                      She came in on the Monday after Mrs Koh went on maternity leave — a small, grey-haired woman in a cardigan the colour of weak tea, carrying a canvas bag that looked heavier than she was. She set the bag down, wrote MRS FERNANDEZ on the board in careful capitals, and then stood looking at us for what felt like a very long time.

                                      "She's ancient," Priya whispered. "She'll be hopeless."

                                      For the first fortnight, she was. She spoke too softly. She did not notice when Wei Jie flicked erasers across the room. When she asked a question and nobody answered, she simply waited, sometimes for half a minute, until the silence became unbearable and somebody muttered something just to end it. We complained loudly to one another at recess. Someone said she should retire.

                                      Then, in the third week, she handed back our compositions.

                                      Mine came back covered in small, neat pencil marks. Not crosses — questions. Beside a sentence where I had written that my character was angry, she had written: What did his hands do? Beside my ending, where I had explained the moral in two tidy lines, she had written: You already showed me this. Trust me to see it.

                                      Nobody had ever written to me in the margin of my own work before. Teachers wrote grades and 'good effort'. Mrs Fernandez had read the thing.
