                                      I looked around. Priya was frowning at her own page, turning it over, reading the back. Wei Jie, who had not written more than half a page all year, was reading his in complete silence.

                                      "Rewrite them if you want to," Mrs Fernandez said. "I'll read them again. I'll read them as many times as you like."

                                      Twenty-six of us rewrote them. Some of us rewrote them twice.

                                      She was with us for eleven weeks. I cannot remember a single thing she said in front of the class. I remember every word she wrote in my margins.

                                      Questions

                                      1. Why was Mrs Fernandez teaching the class? (1m)

                                      2. Give two reasons why the class disliked Mrs Fernandez at first. (2m)

                                      3. What does the phrase "a cardigan the colour of weak tea" suggest about the impression Mrs Fernandez made? (2m)

                                      4. In your own words, explain what was unusual about the marks on the narrator's composition. (2m)

                                      5. What did Mrs Fernandez mean by "You already showed me this. Trust me to see it."? (2m)

                                      6. Why do you think the writer mentions that Wei Jie read his composition "in complete silence"? (2m)

                                      7. "The narrator's opinion of Mrs Fernandez changed gradually." True or false? Give evidence. (2m)

                                      8. Explain why the last two sentences are an effective ending to the story. (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. Because their usual teacher, Mrs Koh, had gone on maternity leave. [1m]

                                      Literal. One line is enough.

                                      2. Firstly, she spoke too quietly for them to hear her easily. Secondly, she failed to control the class — she did not notice Wei Jie flicking erasers around the room. [2m]

                                      Two marks, two distinct reasons. Long silences would also be accepted.

                                      3. It suggests she looked faded and dull, and that nothing about her appearance was striking or impressive — which is exactly why the class dismissed her so quickly. [2m]

                                      Vocabulary in context. Explain the impression, not just the colour.

                                      4. Instead of correcting errors or giving a grade, she had written questions in the margin that pushed him to think about his own writing choices. [2m]

                                      'Not crosses — questions' must be reworded, not lifted.

                                      5. She meant that the narrator's story had already made its lesson clear through the events themselves, so spelling out the moral at the end was unnecessary and he should have confidence in his reader. [2m]

                                      Inference from a quoted line. Link it back to the composition advice about not announcing the moral.

                                      6. Because Wei Jie had been the most disruptive pupil and had barely written anything all year. His silence shows that even he had been affected by her comments, which proves how unusual her marking was. [2m]

                                      The detail is chosen deliberately. Ask why the writer picked that particular boy.

                                      7. True. The class hated her from the first day and still complained at recess for a fortnight, but it was only in the third week, after she returned their compositions, that his view began to change. [2m]

                                      One mark for true/false, one for the specific evidence.

                                      8. Firstly, they contrast what the narrator cannot remember with what he can, which makes the point sharply. In addition, they show that Mrs Fernandez's real influence was private and written rather than loud and public, overturning the class's early judgement that she was hopeless. Finally, the words 'every word' suggest her comments stayed with him long after she left, which tells us how much she mattered. [3m]

                                      Three marks, three points, signposted.

                                      What We Throw Away

                                      Non-narrative · about 340 words · 8 questions · 15 marks · suggested for P5 and above

                                      Every year, Singapore throws away enough food to fill more than 700 Olympic swimming pools. Around half of this waste comes not from restaurants or supermarkets, but from ordinary households — from kitchens like yours and mine.

                                      The reasons are surprisingly ordinary. Shoppers buy in bulk because larger packets appear cheaper, then find they cannot finish the food before it spoils. Others cook far more than their family can eat, because serving too little is considered impolite. And a great deal of perfectly good food is discarded simply because of the date printed on the packet.

                                      That date is widely misunderstood. A 'use by' date is a safety instruction: after it, the food may genuinely be unsafe. A 'best before' date is only a guide to quality. A packet of biscuits a week past its 'best before' date may be slightly less crisp, but it is not dangerous. Research suggests that confusion between these two labels alone accounts for a significant share of household food waste.

                                      The consequences reach further than most people realise. Food that is thrown away must be incinerated, and the ash is shipped to Pulau Semakau, Singapore's only landfill. Semakau is expected to run out of space within a few decades. Beyond that, every discarded meal represents wasted water, wasted fuel and wasted farmland, most of it in other countries, since Singapore imports over ninety per cent of what it eats.

                                      The solutions, fortunately, are also ordinary. Planning meals before shopping cuts impulse buying. Storing food correctly — vegetables in the right part of the fridge, rice in a sealed container — extends its life considerably. Cooking smaller portions and returning for a second helping wastes far less than filling every plate to the brim. Several community fridges now allow residents to leave surplus food for neighbours instead of binning it.

                                      None of these actions is dramatic. But food waste is not a problem created by a few careless people. It is created by millions of small, reasonable decisions — which means it can be undone the same way.

                                      Questions

                                      1. Where does about half of Singapore's food waste come from? (1m)

                                      2. Give two reasons, in your own words, why households buy or cook too much food. (2m)

                                      3. Explain the difference between a 'use by' date and a 'best before' date. (2m)

                                      4. What does the word 'discarded' mean in paragraph 2? (1m)

                                      5. Why is food waste a particular problem for Singapore? Give two reasons. (2m)

                                      6. Suggest two things a family could do this week to waste less food. (2m)

                                      7. What does the writer mean by "None of these actions is dramatic"? (2m)

                                      8. Explain how the final sentence sums up the writer's argument. (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. From ordinary households, rather than from restaurants or supermarkets. [1m]

                                      Literal retrieval from paragraph 1.

                                      2. Firstly, bigger packets look like better value, so people purchase more than they can finish before it goes bad. Secondly, offering guests or family too small a serving is seen as rude, so people prepare extra. [2m]

                                      Both reasons must be reworded. 'Impolite' and 'in bulk' should not appear.

                                      3. A 'use by' date warns that the food could become unsafe to eat after that day, whereas a 'best before' date only indicates when the food stops being at its best in taste or texture, though it remains safe. [2m]

                                      Two marks means both halves of the contrast must appear.

                                      4. Thrown away or got rid of. [1m]

                                      Give a synonym that fits grammatically — 'discarded' is a past participle, so 'thrown away' works.

                                      5. Firstly, the ash from incinerated waste goes to Pulau Semakau, the country's only landfill, which is expected to be full within a few decades. Secondly, Singapore imports more than ninety per cent of its food, so wasted meals also waste the water, fuel and farmland used to produce them overseas. [2m]

                                      Two distinct reasons, both from paragraph 4.

                                      6. They could plan their meals before going shopping so that they only buy what they will actually use, and serve smaller portions at meals, allowing anyone still hungry to take a second helping. [2m]

                                      An application question. Answers must come from or be consistent with the passage.

                                      7. The writer means that the solutions are all small, everyday changes rather than difficult or impressive measures, so anyone can carry them out without much effort. [2m]

                                      Explain the phrase, then say why the writer includes it.

                                      8. Firstly, it rejects the idea that food waste is caused by a small number of careless individuals. In addition, it explains that the problem is the result of countless small, sensible decisions made by ordinary people. Finally, it argues that because the cause is small and shared, the remedy can be small and shared too, which gives the reader reason to believe their own actions matter. [3m]

                                      Three points. The last one is the persuasive purpose of the sentence.

                                      The Last Bus

                                      Narrative · about 360 words · 8 questions · 16 marks · suggested for P6 and above

                                      The plan had been simple, which is how I know now that it was mine.

                                      Ravi was nine and slower than me at everything, so I told him to wait at the bench outside the library while I went to buy the birthday card. Ten minutes. Fifteen at most. He had his water bottle and the book he was halfway through, and he nodded at me the way he always did, as though whatever I said had already been decided by someone more important than either of us.

                                      The stationery shop had a queue. Then they did not have the card I wanted, so I walked to the second shop, which was two streets away, and then I saw Marcus and Hui Ling outside the bubble tea place and we talked about the school camp.

                                      When I looked at my phone it was 6.42 p.m.

                                      I ran. I remember the sound of my own bag hitting my back, over and over, and the way the shophouses blurred at the edges. The library steps were empty. The bench was empty. There was a water bottle underneath it, on its side.

                                      I called his name once, loudly, and it came back off the wall of the building and sounded like somebody else's voice.

                                      For four minutes I stood in the middle of the pavement and did nothing useful at all. I thought about the canal behind the library. I thought about what I would say to my mother. I thought, with a clarity that shames me still, about how none of this would have happened if he were faster.

                                      Then a bus pulled in at the stop across the road — the 168, the one we took home — and Ravi got off it.

                                      He had his book under his arm. He looked at my face and something in his own face changed, and he said, before I could speak, "I'm sorry. I thought you'd gone home. I thought I'd got it wrong."

                                      He apologised to me. I have thought about that a great deal since.

                                      I am seventeen now. Ravi is taller than me and beats me at everything. But I still check, every single time we leave somewhere, that he is behind me. He has noticed. He has never once mentioned it.

                                      Questions

                                      1. What was the narrator's plan? (1m)

                                      2. Give two reasons why the narrator took much longer than planned. (2m)

                                      3. What does the opening sentence, "The plan had been simple, which is how I know now that it was mine", suggest about the narrator? (2m)

                                      4. Why does the writer mention the water bottle lying on its side? (2m)

                                      5. In your own words, describe what the narrator did during the four minutes after she called out. (2m)

                                      6. The narrator says one of her thoughts "shames me still". Which thought, and why is she ashamed of it? (2m)

                                      7. Why do you think Ravi apologised to the narrator? (2m)

                                      8. Explain how the final paragraph shows that the narrator was changed by what happened. (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. To leave Ravi waiting on the bench outside the library for ten to fifteen minutes while she went to buy a birthday card. [1m]

                                      Literal, but include the time — it matters later.

                                      2. Firstly, the first stationery shop had a queue and did not stock the card she wanted, so she walked two streets to a second shop. Secondly, she then met Marcus and Hui Ling and stopped to chat about the school camp. [2m]

                                      Two separate delays. The second one is the one she is ashamed of.

                                      3. It suggests that she is looking back as an older person and judging her younger self, recognising that the plan seemed simple only because she had not thought about what could go wrong. [2m]

                                      Note the phrase 'know now' — the story is told in hindsight.

                                      4. Because it is evidence that Ravi had been there and has gone, and the fact that it is knocked over suggests he may have left in a hurry, which increases the narrator's alarm. [2m]

                                      Small physical details in narratives are almost always doing a job. Say what job.

                                      5. She stood still on the pavement, unable to take any helpful action, while frightening thoughts ran through her mind. [2m]

                                      'Did nothing useful at all' must be reworded.

                                      6. The thought that none of it would have happened if Ravi had been faster. She is ashamed because in a moment when her brother might have been in danger, she was blaming him for a situation she herself had caused. [2m]

                                      Identify the thought, then explain the shame. Two clear parts.

                                      7. Because he assumed he had made the mistake himself by misunderstanding her instructions, and because he saw how upset she looked and wanted to make things better — he was used to accepting that she was in charge. [2m]

                                      Link back to paragraph 2, where he defers to her.

                                      8. Firstly, although many years have passed and Ravi is now the more capable of the two, she still checks that he is behind her every time they leave a place. In addition, the phrase 'every single time' shows this has become a permanent habit rather than an occasional worry. Finally, the detail that Ravi has noticed but never mentioned it suggests he understands why she does it, and that the incident quietly shaped both of them. [3m]

                                      Three marks, three points. The final one is about Ravi, not just the narrator.

                                      The Spare Room

                                      Narrative · about 320 words · 8 questions · 16 marks · suggested for P4 and above

                                      When my grandmother came to live with us, she was given the spare room, and the spare room was where I had kept everything that mattered to me.

                                      It was not really a bedroom. It had a folding bed nobody used, three boxes of my father's old files, and — most importantly — a corner where I had built a city out of cardboard over two entire school holidays. It had a hospital. It had a river made of blue tissue paper. I had spent forty-one days on it, because I had counted.

                                      My mother told me on a Tuesday. Grandmother was moving in on Saturday, and the city would have to go.

                                      I did not argue, because in our house arguing about a decision that has already been made is considered a waste of everybody's afternoon. I took the city apart myself on Friday evening, piece by piece, and put it in the recycling bin downstairs. It took eleven minutes. I remember being surprised by that.

                                      For the first two weeks, I did not go into the spare room at all.

                                      Then one evening Grandmother called me in. She was sitting on the edge of the bed with a shoebox on her lap, and inside the shoebox were about thirty small objects wrapped in newspaper — a brass thimble, a wooden elephant with one ear missing, a key to a house in Ipoh that had been sold in 1978.

                                      She unwrapped them one at a time and told me where each had come from. It took nearly an hour, and she did not hurry any of it.

                                      At the end she said, "Your mother tells me there was a city here."

                                      I said there had been.

                                      She thought about that. Then she said, "Mine is in a shoebox. Yours was on the floor. Neither is very sensible."

                                      I laughed before I could stop myself.

                                      We built a new one together over the December holidays, on a piece of board that slides under her bed. It is smaller than the first. It has a hospital, a blue tissue river, and, at Grandmother's insistence, a shop that sells nothing but thimbles.

                                      Questions

                                      1. What had the narrator built in the spare room? (1m)

                                      2. How long had the city taken to build, and how do we know the narrator cared about it? (2m)

                                      3. Why did the narrator not argue with his mother? (2m)

                                      4. Why do you think the narrator was surprised that it only took eleven minutes? (2m)

                                      5. Describe two of the objects in Grandmother's shoebox. (1m)

                                      6. What did Grandmother mean by "Mine is in a shoebox. Yours was on the floor. Neither is very sensible."? (3m)

                                      7. How did the narrator's feelings towards his grandmother change? Use evidence. (3m)

                                      8. Why is the detail about the thimble shop an effective ending? (2m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. A city made out of cardboard, complete with a hospital and a river made from blue tissue paper. [1m]

                                      Literal, but include a detail or two.

                                      2. It took forty-one days across two school holidays. We know he cared because he had counted the days exactly. [2m]

                                      Two parts to the question — answer both.

                                      3. Because in his family, arguing about something that has already been decided is regarded as pointless, so there was no expectation that complaining would change anything. [2m]

                                      The reason is stated, but must be reworded a little.

                                      4. Because something that had taken him forty-one days to build was destroyed in a few minutes, and the difference between the two made the loss feel sharper and somehow unfair. [2m]

                                      'Why do you think' — inference. Contrast the two numbers.

                                      5. A brass thimble and a wooden elephant missing one ear. [1m]

                                      One mark, so keep it very short.

                                      6. Firstly, she meant that she too keeps things that matter to her, so she understood his loss. In addition, she was pointing out that neither of them stores their treasures in a practical way. Finally, by joking about them both she put herself on his side rather than treating him as a child who had lost a toy. [3m]

                                      Three marks means three points. The third one is about her purpose in saying it.

                                      7. Firstly, at the start he resented her arrival, shown by his avoiding the spare room completely for a fortnight. In addition, after she showed him the shoebox and made her remark, he laughed before he could stop himself, which suggests his resistance broke. Finally, by December they were building a new city together, which shows the relationship had become a genuine friendship. [3m]

                                      Track the change across the whole passage: before, turning point, after.

                                      8. Because it shows the new city belongs to both of them rather than only to the narrator, and the small joke about her own treasured object proves that she has been fully included in something that once mattered only to him. [2m]

                                      Endings that use a small specific detail almost always carry a larger meaning.

                                      Why We Sleep Badly

                                      Non-narrative · about 340 words · 8 questions · 16 marks · suggested for P5 and above

                                      Ask a class of Primary Six pupils how many hours they slept last night and the answers will vary widely. Ask how many hours they should have slept, and most will guess correctly: nine to eleven. The gap between what children know and what they do is one of the more puzzling features of childhood sleep.

                                      Part of the explanation is biological. During adolescence, the body clock shifts later, so teenagers genuinely find it harder to fall asleep early. This shift begins earlier than most parents realise, sometimes as young as eleven. A child who says she is not tired at half past nine may be telling the truth.

                                      A larger part of the explanation, however, is environmental. Screens emit blue light, which suppresses melatonin, the hormone that signals to the body that it is time to sleep. Watching a video for thirty minutes before bed can delay the onset of sleep by considerably longer than thirty minutes. The problem is not simply that screens take up time; it is that they change what the body does with the time that remains.

                                      There is also the matter of what researchers call sleep debt. Many children lose an hour or two on school nights and attempt to repay it by sleeping late at weekends. This does not work as well as it feels like it should. Sleeping until noon on Sunday shifts the body clock later again, which makes Monday morning harder than it needed to be — a cycle sometimes called social jet lag.

                                      The consequences are not limited to feeling tired. Sleep is when the brain consolidates what was learnt during the day, moving information from short-term into long-term memory. A pupil who revises for two hours and then sleeps for five may retain less than one who revises for one hour and sleeps for nine.

                                      The remedies are unglamorous. A consistent bedtime, including at weekends. No screens for an hour before sleep. A dark, cool room. None of this is new advice, and none of it is difficult. It is simply, for most families, inconvenient.

                                      Questions

                                      1. How many hours of sleep should a Primary Six pupil get? (1m)

                                      2. What does the writer find puzzling? (2m)

                                      3. Explain, in your own words, why a child might honestly not feel tired at 9.30 p.m. (2m)

                                      4. How do screens affect sleep? (2m)

                                      5. What does the word 'suppresses' mean in paragraph 3? (1m)

                                      6. Explain why sleeping late on Sunday makes Monday harder. (2m)

                                      7. Why might a pupil who revises for one hour outperform one who revises for two? (3m)

                                      8. What does the writer mean by describing the remedies as "unglamorous" and the last sentence as "simply inconvenient"? (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. Between nine and eleven hours. [1m]

                                      Literal retrieval.

                                      2. That children can correctly state how much sleep they need, yet still do not get it — the gap between their knowledge and their behaviour. [2m]

                                      The word 'puzzling' points you to the last sentence of paragraph 1.

                                      3. As children approach their teenage years, their internal body clock naturally moves later, which means they are not yet ready for sleep at that hour even though they are not pretending. [2m]

                                      'Body clock shifts later' must be reworded.

                                      4. The blue light they give off reduces the body's production of melatonin, the hormone that tells the body it is time to sleep, so falling asleep is delayed well beyond the time actually spent looking at the screen. [2m]

                                      Two marks: name the mechanism and the effect.

                                      5. Reduces or holds back. [1m]

                                      Give a synonym that fits the grammar of the sentence.

                                      6. Because a long weekend lie-in pushes the body clock even later, so on Sunday night the child is not ready to sleep at the usual time and wakes on Monday having lost more sleep, not less. [2m]

                                      Follow the chain of cause and effect.

                                      7. Firstly, sleep is when the brain moves what has been learnt from short-term into long-term memory. In addition, the pupil who revises longer but sleeps only five hours has less time for this process to happen. Finally, the extra hour of revision is therefore wasted if it is taken out of the sleep that would have fixed the learning in place. [3m]

                                      Three marks, three linked points.

                                      8. Firstly, the writer means the solutions are ordinary and dull rather than clever or new. In addition, the word 'inconvenient' suggests families already know what to do but find it awkward to fit around homework, tuition and screens. Finally, the tone is gently critical: the writer is pointing out that the barrier is not difficulty or ignorance but unwillingness. [3m]

                                      Explain both phrases and then say what the writer's attitude is.

                                      The Substitute Goalkeeper

                                      Narrative · about 350 words · 8 questions · 18 marks · suggested for P6 and above

                                      I spent two seasons as the substitute goalkeeper, which meant that I trained four times a week in order to sit on a plastic bench and watch somebody else be better than me.

                                      His name was Farid and he was, irritatingly, a decent person. He never once made me feel like a spare part. He would jog over at half-time to tell me what the strikers were doing, as though I might be going on, and I never did.

                                      The final was in September. Ten minutes before kick-off, Farid landed badly during the warm-up and could not stand on his left ankle.

                                      I remember Coach Nathan turning around and looking at me for a fraction too long before he said my name, and I understood exactly what that pause meant.

                                      We lost four-one.

                                      Two of the goals were unquestionably my fault. The third I might have reached. The fourth went in during the last minute, when we had pushed everybody forward, and nobody could reasonably have blamed me for it, but I blamed me for it anyway.

                                      I did not cry in the changing room. I waited until I was home and in the shower, where it does not count.

                                      The following Tuesday I went to training because I did not know what else to do with a Tuesday. Farid was there on crutches. He waited until the others had gone out to the field and then he said, "The second one. Did you see it coming?"

                                      I said I had not.

                                      "You did," he said. "You moved. You moved half a second before he struck it, then you stopped yourself. I watched it four times."

                                      I told him that stopping myself was exactly the problem.

                                      "No," he said. "Not seeing it is the problem, and you don't have it. The rest is practice."

                                      I have replayed that conversation more often than I have replayed the goals.

                                      I never became a good goalkeeper. I played for one more season, then a growth spurt ruined whatever coordination I had, and I moved to hockey and was mediocre at that instead. But I have never forgotten the difference between the thing you cannot learn and the thing you simply have not learnt yet, and I have been unreasonably calm about failure ever since.

                                      Questions

                                      1. What does the narrator mean by "a spare part"? (2m)

                                      2. Why does the narrator describe Farid as "irritatingly, a decent person"? (2m)

                                      3. What did the narrator understand from Coach Nathan's pause? (2m)

                                      4. The narrator says he blamed himself for the fourth goal even though nobody else would. What does this tell us about him? (2m)

                                      5. Explain the phrase "in the shower, where it does not count". (2m)

                                      6. Why do you think Farid had watched the second goal four times? (2m)

                                      7. Explain what Farid meant by "Not seeing it is the problem, and you don't have it. The rest is practice." (3m)

                                      8. The narrator says he has been "unreasonably calm about failure ever since". Explain how the events of the passage led to this. (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. He means someone who is kept around only in case of emergency and is not really needed or valued by the team. [2m]

                                      Explain the phrase in your own words.

                                      2. Because it would have been easier to resent Farid if he had been arrogant, but his kindness meant the narrator could not even enjoy disliking the player who had taken his place. [2m]

                                      The humour is in the word 'irritatingly'. Explain why decency was annoying.

                                      3. That the coach had no confidence in him and was reluctant to put him on, and was only doing so because there was no alternative. [2m]

                                      Inference from a small physical detail.

                                      4. It shows that he judged himself far more harshly than the situation deserved, and that he took full responsibility for the defeat regardless of what was actually his fault. [2m]

                                      The question asks what it reveals about character, not what happened.

                                      5. He means that crying where nobody can see or hear him, and where the water hides the tears, allowed him to feel that it had not really happened and that he had not lost his composure. [2m]

                                      Two marks: what he did, and why the location mattered to him.

                                      6. Because he wanted to be certain of what he had seen before saying anything, so that his encouragement would be based on evidence rather than being empty kindness. [2m]

                                      Link it to the kind of person Farid is shown to be earlier.

                                      7. Firstly, he meant that the ability to read the game and anticipate a shot is the part that cannot easily be taught. In addition, he was telling the narrator that he clearly possessed this ability, since he had begun to move before the shot. Finally, everything else — the confidence to commit to the movement — was simply a skill that could be improved through training. [3m]

                                      Three marks, three separate ideas inside one short quotation.

                                      8. Firstly, he suffered a very public failure in the final and discovered that he survived it. In addition, Farid taught him to separate weaknesses that can be trained from limits that cannot, which made failure feel diagnosable rather than shameful. Finally, the word 'unreasonably' suggests he knows his calmness is greater than the situation warrants, which shows how deeply that one conversation changed him. [3m]

                                      The last mark comes from noticing the word 'unreasonably'.

                                      The Last Shophouse

                                      Narrative · about 355 words · 8 questions · 20 marks · suggested for P6 and above

                                      The letter arrived on a Thursday and my mother read it twice at the kitchen table before she said anything.

                                      The block was to be redeveloped. We had eleven months. There would be compensation, and priority for a flat in the new estate, and a list of dates for briefing sessions at the community centre.

                                      My grandfather had opened the shop in 1971. My mother had grown up behind the counter and had taken it over at twenty-six. I had done my homework at the small table by the window for the whole of primary school, under a ceiling fan that wobbled and had never once fallen.

                                      "Eleven months," my mother said. Then she got up and served a customer who wanted three tins of condensed milk.

                                      For a long time she said nothing further about it, and I made the mistake of thinking that she was fine.

                                      In the seventh month I came down early one morning and found her behind the counter with a notebook, writing. She had been going through the shelves, item by item, recording what each thing was and who bought it. Mrs Yeo, condensed milk, three tins, every second Wednesday. Mr Kamal, curry powder, the large tin, monthly. The boy from 217, one packet of prawn crackers on Fridays, always with exact change.

                                      There were four pages of it.

                                      I asked what it was for. She said she did not know yet.

                                      In the tenth month, she began telephoning them. Not all of them — she had no numbers for most — but the ones she could reach. She told each of them what she had written down about them, and where the new estate shops would be, and which of the other provision shops in the area carried the same brands.

                                      Mrs Yeo cried on the telephone. My mother did not.

                                      We closed on a Sunday. The last thing my mother did was take down the ceiling fan herself, with a screwdriver, and wrap it in a towel, and put it in the boot of the car.

                                      It is in the storeroom of our flat now. It has never been installed. My mother says the ceilings are the wrong height, which is true, and also not the reason.

                                      Questions

                                      1. What news did the letter contain? (2m)

                                      2. Why does the writer mention the ceiling fan in paragraph 3? (2m)

                                      3. What does the mother's reaction to the letter suggest about her? (3m)

                                      4. In your own words, describe what the mother was writing in her notebook. (2m)

                                      5. Why does the writer include the detail about the boy from 217 paying with exact change? (2m)

                                      6. What did the mother eventually do with the information she had collected? (2m)

                                      7. "Mrs Yeo cried on the telephone. My mother did not." Why do you think the writer places these two sentences together? (3m)

                                      8. Explain the final sentence: "My mother says the ceilings are the wrong height, which is true, and also not the reason." (4m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. That the block containing the family's shop was going to be redeveloped, and that they had eleven months before they would have to leave. [2m]

                                      Two marks: the news itself and the timeframe.

                                      2. It shows how familiar and constant the shop was throughout his childhood, and it introduces an object that becomes important at the end of the passage. [2m]

                                      Ask what job the detail does — here it does two.

                                      3. Firstly, she read it twice before speaking, which shows she was absorbing it carefully rather than reacting immediately. In addition, she said only 'Eleven months' and then served a customer, which suggests she deals with difficulty by continuing to work. Finally, her silence over the following months shows she keeps strong feelings private rather than sharing them. [3m]

                                      Three marks — use the whole paragraph, not just the first line.

                                      4. She was making a record of each regular customer, noting what they bought, how much, and how often. [2m]

                                      Do not lift 'item by item' or the examples.

                                      5. It shows how precisely his mother knew each customer, down to small personal habits, which makes clear that the shop was a set of relationships and not simply a business. [2m]

                                      The smallest detail in a list is usually the deliberate one.

                                      6. She telephoned the customers she had numbers for and told them what she had recorded about them, along with where the new shops would be and which nearby provision shops stocked the same brands. [2m]

                                      Answer the whole question — she did two things with it.

                                      7. Firstly, the contrast highlights how tightly the mother controls her feelings compared with her customers. In addition, the shortness and bluntness of the second sentence imitates her own manner. Finally, it invites the reader to suspect that she did feel just as much, but would not show it — which the ending then confirms. [3m]

                                      Three marks: the contrast, the style, and what it makes the reader think.

                                      8. Firstly, the practical explanation she gives is genuinely accurate, so she is not lying. In addition, the narrator is telling us that it is not her real reason for leaving the fan boxed up. Furthermore, the true reason is that installing it in a new flat would mean accepting that the shop is gone, which she is not ready to do. Finally, the sentence shows how well the narrator now understands his mother — he no longer mistakes her practical explanations for the whole truth, as he did in month one. [4m]

                                      Four marks. The last point links back to 'I made the mistake of thinking that she was fine.'

                                      The Pencil Case

                                      Narrative · about 320 words · 8 questions · 18 marks · suggested for P4 and above

                                      The pencil case went missing on a Wednesday, and by Thursday everybody knew that Devan had taken it.

                                      Nobody had seen him take it. That was not the point. The point was that the pencil case was new and expensive and belonged to Sara, and that Devan's own pencil case was a plastic bag with three stubs of pencil in it, and that he sat two seats away.

                                      By Friday, four people had stopped lending him things.

                                      I did not join in, but I did not say anything either, which I have since learnt is a decision and not the absence of one.

                                      On Monday, Mrs Rajan asked the class to stay behind for five minutes. She did not mention the pencil case. She said that she had lost her reading glasses on Friday and had spent the weekend certain that she had left them at the hawker centre, and that she had been quite rude to the stallholder about it on the telephone.

                                      Then she took the glasses out of her own desk drawer, where they had been the whole time.

                                      "I have written her a letter," she said. "It is not a good letter. There is no good letter for that."

                                      She let us think about it for a moment, and then she said we could go.

                                      The pencil case turned up on Tuesday, behind the cupboard, where it had fallen through the gap at the back of Sara's shelf.

                                      Nobody apologised to Devan. Not one of us, including me. He came back to school on Wednesday and everything carried on as though the week had not happened, and within a fortnight I think most people had genuinely forgotten.

                                      I have not forgotten. I am thirty-one, and I still think about the plastic bag with the three pencil stubs in it, and about how quickly we decided, and about how easy it would have been to say one sentence on the Friday.

                                      I have said the sentence a few times since, in other rooms, about other people. It is never easy. But it is always easier than remembering that you did not.

                                      Questions

                                      1. Why did the class decide that Devan had taken the pencil case? (2m)

                                      2. What does the narrator mean by "I did not say anything either, which I have since learnt is a decision and not the absence of one"? (2m)

                                      3. Why did Mrs Rajan tell the class the story about her reading glasses? (3m)

                                      4. What did Mrs Rajan mean by "There is no good letter for that"? (2m)

                                      5. Where was the pencil case found, and why is this detail important? (2m)

                                      6. "Nobody apologised to Devan." Why do you think this was? (2m)

                                      7. How do we know the incident affected the narrator more than the others? (3m)

                                      8. Explain the final sentence: "It is never easy. But it is always easier than remembering that you did not." (2m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. Because the pencil case was new and valuable while Devan's own was only a plastic bag containing three pencil stubs, and because he sat close to Sara — so they assumed he had both a motive and the opportunity. [2m]

                                      Two marks: the poverty assumption and the seating. Note that nobody actually saw anything.

                                      2. He means that staying silent was itself a choice with consequences, not a neutral act, and that by saying nothing he allowed the accusation to continue. [2m]

                                      The whole passage turns on this sentence. Explain it fully.

                                      3. Firstly, she wanted to show that she too had accused somebody without evidence. In addition, by using herself as the example she avoided naming Devan or embarrassing the class directly. Finally, her story demonstrated that such an accusation causes real harm that an apology cannot fully undo. [3m]

                                      Three marks. The third point comes from her remark about the letter.

                                      4. She meant that no apology, however carefully written, can undo the hurt of having been wrongly accused, so the letter would always be inadequate. [2m]

                                      5. It had fallen through a gap at the back of Sara's shelf and was behind the cupboard. It matters because it proves nobody had taken it at all, so the entire accusation had been built on assumption. [2m]

                                      Answer both halves — the location and its significance.

                                      6. Because admitting they had been wrong would have meant facing their own unfairness, and it was easier for the class to let the matter quietly drop than to confront what they had done. [2m]

                                      'Why do you think' — inference, not a stated reason.

                                      7. Firstly, he says that within a fortnight most people had forgotten, but that he has not. In addition, he is now thirty-one and still recalls the exact detail of the plastic bag and the three pencil stubs. Finally, he says he has since spoken up in other situations, showing the incident permanently changed how he behaves. [3m]

                                      Three marks, three pieces of evidence across the last two paragraphs.

                                      8. He means that speaking up against unfairness is always uncomfortable, but that the discomfort lasts only a moment, whereas the guilt of having stayed silent stays with you for years. [2m]

                                      Link it back to the fact that he is still thinking about this at thirty-one.

                                      Why Cities Are Getting Hotter

                                      Non-narrative · about 345 words · 8 questions · 15 marks · suggested for P5 and above

                                      On a still afternoon, the centre of a large city can be as much as seven degrees warmer than the countryside a few kilometres away. Scientists call this the urban heat island effect, and Singapore experiences one of the strongest examples in the world.

                                      The causes are mostly matters of material. Concrete, asphalt and brick absorb heat during the day and release it slowly through the night, which is why city nights cool down far less than rural ones. A dark road surface can reach sixty degrees in the afternoon sun. Grass in the same conditions stays close to air temperature, because plants release water vapour through their leaves, and evaporation cools the air around them.

                                      Shape matters as well as material. Tall buildings standing close together trap heat between them in what researchers call an urban canyon. Heat that would otherwise radiate upwards into the sky bounces instead from wall to wall. The same buildings block the wind that would carry warm air away.

                                      Then there is the heat we generate ourselves. Every air conditioner cools a room by moving heat outdoors. Every vehicle engine, every kitchen, every server room adds warmth to the street. On the hottest days, when air conditioners are working hardest, this contribution is at its greatest — which means the problem worsens precisely when it is least welcome.

                                      The consequences are not merely uncomfortable. Higher night temperatures disturb sleep, and poor sleep affects health and concentration. Elderly residents and those without air conditioning are most at risk. Energy use rises, which in turn generates more heat.

                                      There are remedies, though none is a complete answer. Planting trees along streets provides shade and evaporative cooling at the same time. Roofs painted white or planted with vegetation absorb far less heat than dark ones. Designing new estates so that buildings channel rather than block the prevailing wind can lower street temperatures measurably.

                                      None of these measures will make a tropical city cool. What they can do is prevent it from becoming several degrees hotter than it needs to be, which over a lifetime is not a small difference.

                                      Questions

                                      1. How much warmer can a city centre be than nearby countryside? (1m)

                                      2. Explain, in your own words, why grass stays cooler than a road surface. (2m)

                                      3. What is an 'urban canyon' and why does it make a city hotter? (2m)

                                      4. What does the word 'radiate' mean in paragraph 3? (1m)

                                      5. Why does the writer say the problem "worsens precisely when it is least welcome"? (2m)

                                      6. Give two consequences of higher night temperatures. (2m)

                                      7. Explain how planting street trees helps in two different ways. (2m)

                                      8. What is the writer's attitude in the final paragraph? Explain using the text. (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. As much as seven degrees warmer. [1m]

                                      Literal. One line.

                                      2. Plants give off water vapour from their leaves, and as that moisture evaporates it draws heat out of the surrounding air, keeping the temperature near the grass close to that of the air itself. [2m]

                                      'Evaporation cools' must be reworded, not lifted.

                                      3. It is the narrow space formed between tall buildings that stand close together. Heat that would normally escape upwards is reflected from one wall to another instead, and the buildings also block the wind that would otherwise remove the warm air. [2m]

                                      Two marks: define it, then give the effect.

                                      4. Spread outwards or be given off. [1m]

                                      A synonym that fits the sentence grammatically.

                                      5. Because air conditioners push heat out into the street, and they are used most heavily on the hottest days, so the outdoor temperature is pushed up further at exactly the time when people are already suffering most from the heat. [2m]

                                      Explain the irony the phrase is pointing at.

                                      6. People sleep badly, which damages their health and their ability to concentrate. Energy use also increases as more cooling is needed, and that in turn produces still more heat. [2m]

                                      Two distinct consequences from paragraph 5.

                                      7. Firstly, the trees cast shade so that surfaces beneath them absorb less heat from the sun. Secondly, they release water vapour from their leaves, and the evaporation cools the surrounding air. [2m]

                                      The passage says 'at the same time' — that signals two mechanisms.

                                      8. Firstly, the writer is realistic rather than optimistic, admitting openly that no measure is a complete answer and that a tropical city cannot be made cool. In addition, he still argues the remedies are worth pursuing, since they can stop the city becoming several degrees hotter than necessary. Finally, the phrase 'over a lifetime is not a small difference' shows he considers the gain genuinely important despite being modest. [3m]

                                      Three marks: name the attitude, support it twice.

                                      The Understudy

                                      Narrative · about 360 words · 8 questions · 18 marks · suggested for P6 and above

                                      I was cast as the understudy, which in our school production meant learning every line of a part I would almost certainly never perform.

                                      The lead was Priyanka. She had been the lead in everything since Primary Three, and she was, to be fair about it, extremely good. She did not gloat. She once spent a whole lunchtime helping me with a line I kept dropping, which made it harder rather than easier to resent her.

                                      I learnt the part anyway. Forty-one pages. I learnt it in the shower, on the bus, in the eleven minutes between finishing dinner and starting homework. My mother could recite two of the scenes by the third week.

                                      On the afternoon of the second performance, Priyanka's grandfather died.

                                      Mrs Sundaram found me in the corridor at four o'clock and told me, and then asked whether I was ready, and I said yes before I had decided whether it was true.

                                      I would like to report that it went brilliantly. It went adequately. I dropped a line in the second act and covered it clumsily, and my voice did something strange during the speech I had practised most. Nobody in the audience knew any different, because nobody in the audience had seen Priyanka do it the night before.

                                      But I knew.

                                      Afterwards, a parent I did not know told me I had been wonderful, and I said thank you, and I meant the thank you and did not believe the compliment, and I have since discovered that this is a fairly ordinary adult experience.

                                      Priyanka came back the following week. She had watched a recording. She said three specific things about my performance, two of them generous and one of them accurate, and the accurate one was about the speech where my voice had gone strange.

                                      "You were pushing," she said. "You don't have to push. It's already loud enough in there."

                                      I have thought about that more than I have thought about the performance.

                                      I did not become an actor. I stand up in front of rooms for a living, though, which is a related skill, and every time I feel myself pushing I hear a twelve-year-old telling me that the room is already quiet and I do not need to fill it.

                                      Questions

                                      1. What did being the understudy involve? (1m)

                                      2. Why does the narrator say Priyanka's kindness "made it harder rather than easier"? (2m)

                                      3. Give two details that show how hard the narrator worked. (2m)

                                      4. Why does the writer mention that nobody in the audience had seen Priyanka perform the night before? (2m)

                                      5. What is the effect of the two-word paragraph "But I knew."? (2m)

                                      6. Explain what the narrator means by "I meant the thank you and did not believe the compliment". (2m)

                                      7. Priyanka said three things, "two of them generous and one of them accurate". What does this tell us about her? (3m)

                                      8. Explain the final paragraph and why it is an effective ending. (4m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. Learning every line of the lead part despite being almost certain never to perform it. [1m]

                                      2. Because if she had been arrogant he could have resented her, but her generosity in helping him removed that excuse and left him with nothing but his own disappointment. [2m]

                                      The difficulty is emotional, not practical.

                                      3. He learnt all forty-one pages, using every spare moment such as time in the shower, on the bus and between dinner and homework. His mother heard it so often that she could recite two scenes herself by the third week. [2m]

                                      Two separate pieces of evidence.

                                      4. To explain that the audience had nothing to compare his performance with, so they could not tell it was weaker — which is why only he knew how it had really gone. [2m]

                                      It sets up the two-word paragraph that follows.

                                      5. Its shortness makes it land heavily after the longer paragraph before it, and it shifts the focus from the audience's judgement to his own, which is the one that actually matters to him. [2m]

                                      Comment on both the form and the meaning.

                                      6. He was sincerely grateful that the parent had bothered to be kind, but he did not accept that the praise was deserved, because he knew the performance had only been adequate. [2m]

                                      Two halves to the sentence — deal with both.

                                      7. Firstly, it shows she was kind enough to offer encouragement before criticism. In addition, it shows she was honest enough to say the one thing that was true rather than only what was comfortable. Finally, the fact that the accurate comment was about the exact moment he knew had gone wrong shows she was a genuinely perceptive judge of performance. [3m]

                                      Three marks. The third point comes from matching her comment to his own private knowledge.

                                      8. Firstly, it moves the story decades forward and reveals that the narrator now speaks publicly for a living. In addition, it shows Priyanka's advice about not pushing turned out to apply far beyond acting. Furthermore, describing her as 'a twelve-year-old' emphasises how young she was to have understood something he still uses as an adult. Finally, the ending gives the lasting value of the experience not to the performance itself but to one sentence of honest feedback, which quietly reverses what the reader expected the story to be about. [4m]

                                      Four marks. Save the strongest point — the reversal — for last.

                                      The Second Language

                                      Narrative · about 355 words · 8 questions · 19 marks · suggested for P6 and above

                                      My grandmother and I have never had a conversation.

                                      This is not a figure of speech. She speaks Teochew and a little Mandarin. I speak English and the kind of Mandarin that collapses the moment anybody says something I have not heard before. Between us we have perhaps two hundred words, and about forty of them are food.

                                      For most of my childhood this did not strike me as a loss. She was the person who appeared on Sundays with a tin of kueh and sat in the corner of the living room while the adults talked. She smiled at me. I smiled at her. Somebody translated when it mattered.

                                      Two years ago my mother mentioned, in passing, that my grandmother had been a schoolteacher in Chaozhou before she came here, and that she had taught for eleven years.

                                      I did not know this. I was twenty-four.

                                      I have since found out, in fragments, through my mother, that she taught mathematics, that she walked forty minutes each way to the school, and that she stopped teaching when she moved here because her qualifications were not recognised and her English was not good enough. She worked in a factory that made electrical switches for nineteen years.

                                      None of this is a secret. Nobody hid it. It simply never came up, because the person it belonged to could not tell me herself, and I had never thought to ask anybody else.

                                      I have started learning Teochew. I am extremely bad at it. I have a notebook and an app and a cousin in Penang who sends me voice messages I understand perhaps a third of.

                                      Last month I managed a full sentence. I asked her whether the kueh was difficult to make. She looked at me for a long moment — long enough that I thought I had said something else entirely — and then she laughed, and answered, and I understood almost none of the answer.

                                      But she answered for a long time. Longer than the question deserved. She was still going when my mother came in from the kitchen.

                                      I am thirty-one years behind. She is eighty-four. I am aware of the arithmetic.

                                      I am learning it anyway.

                                      Questions

                                      1. Why have the narrator and her grandmother never had a conversation? (2m)

                                      2. What is the effect of the detail that "about forty of them are food"? (2m)

                                      3. Why did the narrator not see the situation as a loss when she was a child? (2m)

                                      4. Summarise what the narrator later learnt about her grandmother's life. (3m)

                                      5. "None of this is a secret. Nobody hid it." Explain why the narrator did not know it. (2m)

                                      6. Why do you think the grandmother "looked at her for a long moment" before laughing? (2m)

                                      7. Why does the writer say the grandmother answered "longer than the question deserved"? (3m)

                                      8. Explain the last three short paragraphs and what they show about the narrator. (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. Because they share almost no common language — the grandmother speaks Teochew and a little Mandarin, while the narrator speaks English and only very limited Mandarin, leaving them with around two hundred shared words. [2m]

                                      The reason is stated but should be reworded.

                                      2. It is quietly humorous, but it also shows how narrow their shared vocabulary is — limited almost entirely to practical, everyday matters rather than anything personal. [2m]

                                      Comment on tone as well as meaning.

                                      3. Because as a child she accepted the arrangement as normal: her grandmother was simply a familiar presence who brought food and smiled, and an adult translated whenever something important needed saying. [2m]

                                      'Why' — start with 'Because'.

                                      4. Firstly, she had been a mathematics teacher in Chaozhou for eleven years, walking forty minutes each way to work. In addition, she gave up teaching on moving to Singapore because her qualifications were not accepted here and her English was insufficient. Finally, she then spent nineteen years working in a factory making electrical switches. [3m]

                                      Three marks means three distinct facts.

                                      5. Because the one person whose life it was could not tell her directly, owing to the language barrier, and it had never occurred to the narrator to ask anyone else about it. [2m]

                                      Both halves matter — the barrier and her own failure to ask.

                                      6. Because she was surprised to be addressed in her own language by her granddaughter for the first time, and she needed a moment to take in both the sentence and what it meant that it had been attempted. [2m]

                                      'Why do you think' — inference.

                                      7. Firstly, the question was a very simple one about making kueh, so a short reply would have been enough. In addition, the length of the answer suggests the grandmother was delighted to be spoken to and wanted the exchange to continue. Finally, it hints at how much she may have wanted to say over the years and never been able to. [3m]

                                      Three marks. Build from the literal to the emotional.

                                      8. Firstly, she states plainly that she is thirty-one years behind and that her grandmother is eighty-four, acknowledging she may have very little time. In addition, 'I am aware of the arithmetic' shows she has faced the likelihood that she will never become fluent enough for a real conversation. Finally, 'I am learning it anyway' shows she has decided the attempt is worth making regardless of whether it succeeds, which is the point of the whole passage. [3m]

                                      Three very short paragraphs — the brevity is deliberate. Explain the progression.

                                      The Slowest Runner

                                      Narrative · about 270 words · 8 questions · 16 marks · suggested for P3 and above

                                      Everybody in Primary Three knew that Kai was the slowest runner in the class.

                                      It was not something anyone was unkind about. It was simply a fact, like knowing that Nadia was the tallest or that Mr Rahim's classroom was the one with the broken clock. When we picked teams, Kai was picked last, and Kai did not seem to mind.

                                      On Sports Day, our class had to run a relay. Four runners, one baton, once around the field.

                                      Mr Rahim chose Kai to run the last leg.

                                      The whole class went very quiet.

                                      "Sir," said Nadia carefully, "shouldn't the fastest person go last?"

                                      "Usually," said Mr Rahim. "Not today."

                                      He did not explain, and there was no time to argue.

                                      On the day, our first three runners were wonderful. By the time the baton reached Kai, we were nearly ten metres ahead. Kai ran as fast as he could, which was not very fast, and two other runners passed him in the last twenty metres.

                                      We came third.

                                      Nobody said anything unkind, but nobody said anything at all either, which was somehow worse. Kai sat on the grass with his back to us.

                                      Then Mr Rahim knelt down beside him and said something none of us could hear, and Kai laughed.

                                      Afterwards, on the bus, Mr Rahim told us. Kai had asked him, three weeks earlier, whether he could please run in something, just once, and Mr Rahim had said yes.

                                      "He knew he would come third," Mr Rahim said. "He asked anyway. I think that is the bravest thing that happened on that field today."

                                      We won the relay the following year. Kai ran the last leg again, and we still won, because by then he had been practising for a year.

                                      Questions

                                      1. What did everybody know about Kai? (1m)

                                      2. Why was the class surprised that Kai ran the last leg? (2m)

                                      3. What happened during the race? (2m)

                                      4. Why does the writer say the silence was "somehow worse"? (2m)

                                      5. Why had Mr Rahim chosen Kai? (2m)

                                      6. What did Mr Rahim mean by calling it "the bravest thing that happened on that field"? (3m)

                                      7. What does the last paragraph tell us about Kai? (2m)

                                      8. Do you think Mr Rahim made the right decision? Give a reason. (2m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. That he was the slowest runner in the Primary Three class. [1m]

                                      Literal. One short sentence.

                                      2. Because the last leg is usually given to the fastest runner in the team, and Kai was the slowest, so they expected the team to lose their lead. [2m]

                                      Nadia's question tells you the reason.

                                      3. The first three runners built a lead of nearly ten metres, but two runners overtook Kai in the last twenty metres, so the class finished third. [2m]

                                      Two marks: the lead, then what happened to it.

                                      4. Because saying nothing at all made Kai feel blamed without anyone having to say so, which was harder to bear than an unkind remark he could have answered. [2m]

                                      'Why do you think' style — you have to work it out.

                                      5. Because Kai had asked him three weeks earlier whether he could take part in something just once, and Mr Rahim had agreed. [2m]

                                      6. Firstly, Kai knew before he started that he would probably lose the lead. In addition, he asked to run anyway, in front of the whole school. Finally, Mr Rahim is saying that choosing to try when you expect to fail takes more courage than winning does. [3m]

                                      Three marks means three points.

                                      7. That he kept practising for a whole year after the race, which shows he was determined and did not let the defeat stop him. [2m]

                                      The word 'because' at the end is doing the work.

                                      8. Yes, because although the class lost the race, Kai gained the confidence to keep practising, and the class learnt something about courage that mattered more than one relay. (An answer saying no is accepted if it is well reasoned.) [2m]

                                      Either answer can score, as long as you give a reason from the passage.

                                      Why Leaves Change Colour

                                      Non-narrative · about 290 words · 8 questions · 14 marks · suggested for P4 and above

                                      In many countries, the leaves on certain trees turn yellow, orange or red before they fall. In Singapore, this rarely happens. The reason has less to do with the trees themselves than with the weather.

                                      Leaves are green because they contain a substance called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll allows a plant to use sunlight to make its own food. Because there is so much of it in a healthy leaf, its strong green colour hides all the other colours that are also present.

                                      Those other colours have been there the whole time. Yellow and orange come from substances called carotenoids, the same ones that make carrots orange. They simply cannot be seen while the chlorophyll is there.

                                      In countries with cold winters, the days grow shorter in autumn and the temperature drops. The tree senses this and begins to shut down its leaves, because keeping them alive through winter would cost more energy than it gains. It stops making new chlorophyll, and the chlorophyll already in the leaf slowly breaks down.

                                      As the green fades, the yellows and oranges that were hidden underneath become visible. Some trees also produce a red substance at this time, which is why maple leaves turn such a bright red.

                                      Eventually the tree seals off the leaf completely, and it falls.

                                      Singapore has no cold season and very little change in day length, so most of our trees keep their leaves all year and stay green. A few, such as the sea almond, do drop their leaves and turn a reddish colour first — but they do it whenever they are ready, not all at the same time.

                                      So the colours of autumn are not new colours arriving. They are old colours being uncovered.

                                      Questions

                                      1. What makes leaves green? (1m)

                                      2. What does chlorophyll do for a plant? (1m)

                                      3. Why can we not normally see the yellow and orange in a leaf? (2m)

                                      4. In your own words, explain why a tree shuts down its leaves in autumn. (2m)

                                      5. What two signals tell the tree that autumn has arrived? (2m)

                                      6. Why do maple leaves turn bright red rather than yellow? (1m)

                                      7. Why do most trees in Singapore stay green? (2m)

                                      8. Explain the last sentence: "They are old colours being uncovered." (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. A substance called chlorophyll. [1m]

                                      Literal.

                                      2. It lets the plant use sunlight to make its own food. [1m]

                                      3. Because a healthy leaf contains so much chlorophyll that its strong green colour covers up the other colours, even though they are present all along. [2m]

                                      Two marks: the amount of chlorophyll, and the effect.

                                      4. Keeping the leaves alive during the cold months would use up more energy than the tree would get back from them, so it is not worth doing. [2m]

                                      'Cost more energy than it gains' must be reworded.

                                      5. The days become shorter and the temperature falls. [2m]

                                      Two things, so two marks.

                                      6. Because some trees also make a red substance at that time of year. [1m]

                                      7. Because Singapore has no cold season and the length of the day barely changes, so the trees never receive the signals that cause leaves to shut down. [2m]

                                      Link it back to the two signals in paragraph 4.

                                      8. Firstly, it means the yellows and oranges were inside the leaf all along. In addition, nothing new is made when a leaf changes colour — the green is simply removed. Finally, the sentence sums up the whole passage in a single idea, which is that autumn reveals rather than creates. [3m]

                                      Three marks. The third point is about why the writer ends there.

                                      The New Boy

                                      Narrative · about 363 words · 10 questions · 20 marks · suggested for P4 and above

                                      The new boy arrived in the third week of term, which is the worst possible time.

                                      By the third week, everybody already has somebody to sit with at recess. The seats are decided. Mrs Ong put him at the empty desk beside mine, said his name was Arjun, and went back to the whiteboard.
