                                      For four days, Arjun said nothing at all except "yes" and "thank you".

                                      At recess he sat at the end of the long table with his lunchbox and ate very slowly, one thing at a time, looking at the wall. I watched him from two tables away, where I sat with Wei Jie and Faizal, and I thought about going over, and then the bell rang, and then it was the next day.

                                      This happened four times.

                                      On the Friday, Wei Jie was away with a fever, and Faizal had a dental appointment, and at recess I found myself standing in the middle of the canteen holding a tray with nowhere obvious to go.

                                      So I sat down opposite Arjun, because it was that or eat standing up.

                                      He looked up. Then he pushed his box of biscuits into the middle of the table, which I understood to mean that I could take one.

                                      It turned out that Arjun had moved from Chennai six weeks earlier, that he had an older sister who was already at secondary school, and that he could name every bone in the human hand. He showed me on my own hand, pressing each knuckle and saying a word I could not repeat.

                                      We talked until the bell went.

                                      On Monday, Wei Jie came back, and the four of us sat together, and by the end of term I could not remember what the seating had been like before.

                                      I still think about those four days, though. I had wanted to go over the whole time. What stopped me was not unkindness. It was that going over would have meant walking across the canteen on my own while people watched, and at nine years old that felt like a great deal to ask.

                                      It took a fever and a dental appointment to make me brave.

                                      Questions

                                      1. Why does the narrator say the third week is "the worst possible time" to arrive? (2m)

                                      2. How do we know that Arjun was lonely during his first four days? (2m)

                                      3. What made the narrator finally sit with Arjun? (2m)

                                      4. What did Arjun mean by pushing his biscuits into the middle of the table? (2m)

                                      5. Give two things the narrator learnt about Arjun that day. (2m)

                                      6. "This happened four times." Why is this short sentence effective? (2m)

                                      7. The narrator says "What stopped me was not unkindness." What did stop him? (3m)

                                      8. Explain the last line: "It took a fever and a dental appointment to make me brave." (3m)

                                      9. Which word in the passage means 'cruelty'? (1m)

                                      10. Find a word in the passage that means 'clear to see, without needing to be told'. (1m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. Because by then everybody has already made friends and decided where they sit at recess, so there is no easy way for a newcomer to join a group. [2m]

                                      The reason is explained in paragraph 2. Reword it.

                                      2. He barely spoke, saying only 'yes' and 'thank you', and at recess the narrator sat alone at the end of the long table eating slowly and staring at the wall. [2m]

                                      Give the evidence, not just the conclusion.

                                      3. His two usual friends were both absent that Friday, so the narrator was left standing in the canteen with a tray and nowhere else to sit. [2m]

                                      It was not a decision to be kind — say what actually happened.

                                      4. He was offering to share them, which was his way of welcoming the narrator without having to say anything. [2m]

                                      Explain the gesture, then say why it mattered.

                                      5. Any two of: the narrator had moved from Chennai six weeks earlier; the narrator had an older sister already at secondary school; the narrator could name every bone in the human hand. [2m]

                                      Two facts are asked for. Any two of the three will do.

                                      6. Its shortness makes the repetition feel heavy and deliberate, and it shows that the narrator missed the same chance again and again rather than only once. [2m]

                                      Comment on both the form and what it tells us.

                                      7. Firstly, the narrator would have had to cross the canteen by himself. In addition, other pupils would have watched him do it. Finally, at nine years old that kind of public attention felt frightening, so his fear of being noticed outweighed his wish to be kind. [3m]

                                      Three marks. The third point is about how a nine-year-old feels, not what happened.

                                      8. Firstly, the narrator is admitting that the narrator did not choose to be brave — two accidents forced him into it. In addition, the ordinariness of a fever and a dental appointment makes his own courage sound very small by comparison. Finally, the line is gently self-critical, showing that as an older narrator the narrator can see how easily the friendship might never have happened. [3m]

                                      Three marks. Notice the humour and the self-criticism together.

                                      9. 'Unkindness'. [1m]

                                      Look in the last paragraph.

                                      10. 'Obvious'. [1m]

                                      It describes how plain something was.

                                      Why Some Animals Play Dead

                                      Non-narrative · about 300 words · 10 questions · 18 marks · suggested for P4 and above

                                      When an opossum is threatened, it does not run away. It falls over, opens its mouth, lets its tongue hang out and stops moving. It can stay like this for up to four hours.

                                      This behaviour is often called playing dead, but the name is misleading. The animal is not pretending. Scientists have found that the opossum's heart rate drops sharply and that it becomes genuinely unable to move. It is closer to fainting than to acting.

                                      The strategy works because of how predators hunt. Many hunting animals are triggered by movement, and a great many will not eat something they did not kill themselves, because an animal that is already dead may be diseased. A motionless opossum is therefore both harder to notice and less appetising.

                                      Opossums are not alone. Certain snakes roll onto their backs. Some beetles fold their legs and drop from leaves. A few species of frog do it. So do some fish. The behaviour has appeared separately in many unrelated animals, which suggests it works well enough to be worth evolving more than once.

                                      It is not without cost. An animal lying still cannot feed, cannot escape a second attacker and cannot protect its young. Some opossums have been run over because they froze in the road rather than moving. The strategy only makes sense against a predator that hunts by sight and movement, and it is useless against one that hunts by smell.

                                      There is also a limit to how long it can last. An opossum in this state slowly recovers whether or not the danger has passed, and a young opossum recovers faster than an adult.

                                      Like most things in nature, then, it is not a perfect defence. It is simply one that works often enough.

                                      Questions

                                      1. Describe what an opossum does when it is threatened. (2m)

                                      2. Why does the writer say that the name 'playing dead' is misleading? (2m)

                                      3. Give two reasons why lying still protects the opossum from predators. (2m)

                                      4. What does the word 'motionless' mean in paragraph 3? (1m)

                                      5. Why does the writer mention snakes, beetles, frogs and fish? (2m)

                                      6. Give two disadvantages of this strategy. (2m)

                                      7. Why are some opossums run over on roads? (2m)

                                      8. Explain the final sentence: "It is simply one that works often enough." (3m)

                                      9. Which word in the passage means 'not moving at all'? (1m)

                                      10. Find a word in the passage that means 'set off automatically, without being chosen'. (1m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. It collapses onto the ground with its mouth open and its tongue hanging out, and remains completely still, sometimes for as long as four hours. [2m]

                                      Include the detail and the duration.

                                      2. Because the animal is not deliberately pretending — its heart rate falls sharply and it genuinely cannot move, so the state is more like fainting than acting. [2m]

                                      Two marks: what people assume, and what actually happens.

                                      3. Firstly, many predators are triggered by movement, so a still animal is less likely to be noticed. Secondly, many hunters avoid eating animals they did not kill themselves, in case the carcass is diseased. [2m]

                                      Two distinct reasons from paragraph 3.

                                      4. Not moving at all. [1m]

                                      A short synonym is enough for one mark.

                                      5. To show that the behaviour has developed independently in many unrelated kinds of animal, which suggests it must be an effective defence. [2m]

                                      Do not just list them — say why the list is there.

                                      6. Any two of: it cannot feed while it lies still; it cannot escape if a second attacker arrives; it cannot protect its young; it is useless against a predator that hunts by smell. [2m]

                                      Two disadvantages are asked for. Any two will do.

                                      7. Because their instinct is to freeze when they sense danger, so they stop moving in the middle of the road instead of running clear of the vehicle. [2m]

                                      Link the behaviour to the outcome.

                                      8. Firstly, the writer is admitting that the defence fails in many situations. In addition, it does not need to succeed every time to be worth having — it only needs to work more often than it fails. Finally, the sentence sums up the whole passage's balanced view, that a natural defence is judged by how useful it usually is rather than by whether it is perfect. [3m]

                                      Three marks. The last point is about the writer's overall attitude.

                                      9. 'Motionless'. [1m]

                                      Look in the paragraph describing what the animal's body does.

                                      10. 'Triggered'. [1m]

                                      It describes how the response begins.

                                      The Wrong Trophy

                                      Narrative · about 320 words · 10 questions · 20 marks · suggested for P4 and above

                                      The trophy said MEI LING TAN, and my name is Mei Ling Tang.

                                      I noticed in the car on the way home, turning it over in my lap while my mother talked about what we would have for dinner. One letter. It had been engraved in gold on a small black plate, and whoever had typed it had left off the g.

                                      "They spelt it wrong," I said.

                                      My mother glanced at it at a traffic light. "So they did. Never mind. Everyone knows it's yours."

                                      But here is the thing. There is a Mei Ling Tan in Primary Five. She plays the erhu. She had also been at the prize-giving, because she won something for music, and her trophy had been handed out from the same table by the same teacher.

                                      I did not say this to my mother.

                                      For two days the trophy sat on the shelf above my desk, and every time I looked up it said somebody else's name.

                                      On Wednesday I took it to the general office and explained. The lady behind the counter, Mrs Selvam, looked at it, then looked at a list, and then made a small noise.

                                      It turned out that Mei Ling Tan's trophy said MEI LING TANG.

                                      She had noticed on the first night and said nothing, because she assumed it was hers and that somebody had simply added a letter. She had been looking at my name for two days while I looked at hers.

                                      Mrs Selvam swapped the little black plates over with a screwdriver in about ninety seconds.

                                      We met in the corridor afterwards, both holding the correct trophy at last, and we stood there for a moment not quite knowing what to say. Then she said, "Two days," and I said, "Two days," and we both laughed in a way that was slightly too loud for a corridor.

                                      I do not know her well even now. But we nod at each other, and it is a particular kind of nod, and neither of us has ever explained it to anybody.

                                      Questions

                                      1. What was wrong with the narrator's trophy? (1m)

                                      2. How did the narrator's mother react, and what does this show about her? (2m)

                                      3. Why did the mistake matter more to the narrator than to her mother? (3m)

                                      4. Why do you think the narrator did not tell her mother about the other Mei Ling? (2m)

                                      5. What had happened to the two trophies? (2m)

                                      6. Why had Mei Ling Tan not reported the mistake? (2m)

                                      7. Explain why the two girls laughed "in a way that was slightly too loud for a corridor". (3m)

                                      8. Explain the last paragraph, and why it is a good ending. (3m)

                                      9. Which word in the passage means 'exchanged one for the other'? (1m)

                                      10. Find a word in the passage that means 'took for granted without checking'. (1m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. It bore the name MEI LING TAN, not her own name MEI LING TANG. The plate on her trophy was in fact the other girl's name plate. [1m]

                                      One mark, so keep it short and precise.

                                      2. She glanced at it briefly at a traffic light and said it did not matter because everyone knew the trophy was her daughter's. This shows that she saw it as a trivial mistake not worth worrying about. [2m]

                                      Answer both halves — what she did and what it reveals.

                                      3. Firstly, there was a real Mei Ling Tan at the school, so the name on the trophy belonged to an actual other person. In addition, the narrator saw the wrong name every time she looked up from her desk, so it troubled her daily. Finally, it made the trophy feel as though it were not really hers. [3m]

                                      Three marks. The first point is the one the mother did not know.

                                      4. Because her mother had already dismissed the problem, and explaining would have meant arguing about something her mother thought was unimportant — so it was easier to deal with it herself. [2m]

                                      'Why do you think' — this is inference, not stated.

                                      5. The engraving plates had been swapped by mistake, so the narrator's trophy carried the other girl's name and the other girl's trophy carried hers. [2m]

                                      Two marks: state the mix-up clearly in your own words.

                                      6. Because she assumed the trophy was hers and that somebody had simply added a letter to her name by accident, so she did not realise anything was wrong. [2m]

                                      Look at what each girl does once the mistake is discovered, not at what either of them says.

                                      7. Firstly, they had both spent two days privately bothered by the same odd problem without knowing the other existed. In addition, the coincidence was genuinely funny once it was explained. Finally, the loudness suggests relief as much as amusement — each had been carrying a small worry alone and suddenly found somebody who understood it exactly. [3m]

                                      Three marks. Save the point about relief for last.

                                      8. Firstly, it admits honestly that the two girls did not become close friends, which is more believable than a neat friendship ending. In addition, the shared nod shows that one small experience can connect two people permanently even without conversation. Finally, the detail that neither has ever explained it to anybody makes the moment feel private and valuable, which is a quieter and more memorable close than a dramatic one. [3m]

                                      Three marks. Comment on the honesty of the ending as well as its meaning.

                                      9. 'Swapped'. [1m]

                                      Look at what turned out to have happened to the two name plates.

                                      10. 'Assumed'. [1m]

                                      It describes what the narrator did about the engraving.

                                      The Case Against Bottled Water

                                      Non-narrative · about 385 words · 10 questions · 20 marks · suggested for P5 and above

                                      Singapore has some of the cleanest tap water in the world. It is tested continuously, it meets international drinking standards, and it costs roughly one-thousandth of the price of the same volume sold in a plastic bottle. And yet bottled water sales continue to rise.

                                      The usual explanation is convenience, and there is truth in that. A bottle can be bought anywhere and carried away. But convenience does not explain the whole picture, because a refillable bottle is also portable and there are now water coolers in most malls, MRT stations and schools.

                                      A better explanation is habit. People buy bottled water because they have always bought it, because it is displayed at every counter, and because carrying a bottle of something is easier than remembering to bring one.

                                      The environmental cost is well known. A plastic bottle takes a few minutes to drink and several centuries to break down. Fewer than half are recycled, and even those that are usually become a lower-grade plastic that cannot be made into a bottle again.

                                      What is less often mentioned is the cost of moving water around. Bottled water is heavy, and much of it is transported considerable distances by road or sea, which uses fuel to deliver something that already comes out of a tap a few metres away.

                                      There is a second cost that rarely appears on any label. Producing the plastic for a single one-litre bottle uses roughly three litres of water, most of it in the factory rather than in the bottle. A drink sold on the promise of purity therefore costs several times its own volume before it reaches a shelf.

                                      There are exceptions, and an honest argument must acknowledge them. In an emergency, or in places where the tap water is genuinely unsafe, bottled water saves lives. Some people are advised by a doctor to drink water with a particular mineral content. These are real reasons.

                                      But they do not describe most purchases. Most bottles are bought by someone who walked past a water cooler on the way to the shop.

                                      The solution is neither dramatic nor new. A refillable bottle costs a few dollars and lasts for years. The difficulty has never been the technology. It has been remembering to pick it up on the way out of the door.

                                      Questions

                                      1. Give two facts the writer uses to show that Singapore's tap water is good. (2m)

                                      2. Why does the writer say that convenience "does not explain the whole picture"? (2m)

                                      3. In your own words, explain what the writer means by habit. (2m)

                                      4. Explain why recycling does not fully solve the problem. (2m)

                                      5. What point is the writer making about transport? (2m)

                                      6. Why does the writer include paragraph 6, about exceptions? (3m)

                                      7. Explain the sentence: "Most bottles are bought by someone who walked past a water cooler on the way to the shop." (2m)

                                      8. "The difficulty has never been the technology." What does the writer think the real difficulty is, and what does this suggest about the solution? (3m)

                                      9. Which word in the passage means 'able to be filled again'? (1m)

                                      10. Find a word in the passage that means 'large, worth taking seriously'. (1m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. It is tested continuously and meets international standards for drinking water, and it costs around a thousand times less than the same amount of bottled water. [2m]

                                      Two separate facts from paragraph 1.

                                      2. Because a refillable bottle is just as easy to carry, and water coolers are now available in most malls, MRT stations and schools, so buying a bottle is not the only convenient option. [2m]

                                      The counter-argument is in the same paragraph.

                                      3. People buy bottled water without really thinking about it, because they have always done so, because it is on sale everywhere they look, and because it takes less effort than planning ahead. [2m]

                                      Do not lift 'displayed at every counter'.

                                      4. Fewer than half of plastic bottles are recycled at all, and those that are usually become a poorer-quality plastic that cannot be turned back into a bottle. [2m]

                                      Two marks: the low rate, and what happens to what is recycled.

                                      5. That bottled water is heavy and is often carried long distances using fuel, which is wasteful when the same water is already available from a tap only a few metres away. [2m]

                                      Say what the fact is and why it matters.

                                      6. Firstly, it acknowledges that bottled water is genuinely necessary in emergencies, where tap water is unsafe, or where a doctor has advised it. In addition, including these cases shows the writer is being fair rather than one-sided. Finally, it makes the main argument stronger, because a reader is more likely to accept a case that has admitted its own limits. [3m]

                                      Three marks. The third point is about persuasive technique.

                                      7. It means that the majority of purchases are not made out of necessity at all — the buyer had a free alternative available moments earlier and simply did not use it. [2m]

                                      Explain what the sentence is really accusing people of.

                                      8. Firstly, the writer says the real difficulty is remembering to take a refillable bottle when leaving the house. In addition, this means the obstacle is a matter of personal habit rather than cost or invention. Finally, it suggests the problem is solvable by anyone immediately, without waiting for new products. [3m]

                                      Three marks. End with what the reader is meant to do about it.

                                      9. 'Refillable'. [1m]

                                      Look in the paragraph about what to carry instead.

                                      10. 'Considerable'. [1m]

                                      It describes the distances the bottles travel.

                                      The Metronome

                                      Narrative · about 479 words · 10 questions · 23 marks · suggested for P6 and above

                                      Mrs Arulappan never once told me I had played something well.

                                      I studied piano with her for seven years, from the age of eight, in a flat that smelt of floor polish and had a metronome on top of the upright that she set going before I had taken my coat off.

                                      Her method was the same every week. I played. She listened with her eyes closed. Then she named, without any preamble, the single thing that had gone wrong.

                                      "Bar nine. You rushed because it was getting difficult."

                                      "You are playing the left hand as though it were an accompaniment. It is not."

                                      "That was faster. It was not better."

                                      I hated it for about two years. My friends had teachers who put stickers on the page. At eleven I asked my mother whether I could change, and she said I could decide at the end of the year, and by the end of the year I had stopped asking, though I could not at the time have said why.

                                      What I understood much later is that Mrs Arulappan was never withholding praise in order to push me. She simply did not consider praise to be information. She had one hour a week, and she spent all of it on the thing that would make the next week better.

                                      In my final year she entered me for an examination I did not expect to pass. I passed it, with a mark that surprised both of us.

                                      I went to her flat afterwards with the certificate. She read it, put it on the piano, and said, "Bar nine of the Chopin. You still rush."

                                      Then she made me tea, which she had never done before in seven years, and we drank it without saying very much, and I understood that this was the entire celebration and that it was enough.

                                      I asked her once, in my fifth year, why she never said anything was good. She thought about it for long enough that I wished I had not asked. Then she said that there were a great many people who would tell me I was wonderful, and that they would all be trying to be kind, and that being kind and being useful were not always the same errand. She said I had one hour a week with somebody whose only job was to be useful, and that she did not intend to waste it.

                                      She died when I was twenty-six. I do not play often now, and when I do it is badly.

                                      But I have taught four people things since — nothing to do with music — and every single time I have caught myself doing it her way. One hour. One thing that is wrong. No stickers.

                                      I am aware that this makes me a difficult teacher. I have not been able to make myself stop.

                                      Questions

                                      1. Describe Mrs Arulappan's teaching method. (2m)

                                      2. Why did the narrator hate the lessons at first? (2m)

                                      3. "That was faster. It was not better." What does this remark tell us about her standards? (2m)

                                      4. Explain what the narrator means by "she did not consider praise to be information". (3m)

                                      5. Why does the writer mention that the narrator stopped asking to change teachers "though I could not at the time have said why"? (2m)

                                      6. Why is her response to the certificate significant? (3m)

                                      7. Why does the tea matter so much to the narrator? (3m)

                                      8. Explain the last two paragraphs and what they reveal about her influence. (4m)

                                      9. Which word in the passage means 'an introduction before getting to the point'? (1m)

                                      10. Find a word in the passage that means 'keeping something back deliberately'. (1m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. Every lesson she listened to him play with her eyes closed, then immediately named the one thing that had gone wrong, without any introduction or encouragement first. [2m]

                                      Two marks: what she did, and how she did it.

                                      2. Because the narrator never received any praise, while his friends had teachers who rewarded them with stickers on the page, so his lessons felt harsher by comparison. [2m]

                                      The comparison with his friends is the point.

                                      3. It shows she judged playing by its musical quality rather than by effort or speed, and that she would not accept an improvement in one thing as an excuse for a weakness in another. [2m]

                                      Explain what she valued, not just what she said.

                                      4. Firstly, the narrator means she saw praise as telling a pupil nothing they could act on. In addition, she believed her limited hour was better spent identifying the fault that would improve the following week. Finally, this shows her silence was not coldness or a deliberate tactic, but a considered view of what teaching time was for. [3m]

                                      Three marks. The last point corrects what the reader may have assumed.

                                      5. It shows that the narrator had begun to value her teaching before the narrator was old enough to understand what the narrator was getting from it, so his loyalty came from instinct rather than reasoning. [2m]

                                      Focus on the gap between feeling and understanding.

                                      6. Firstly, she did not congratulate him even on the day the narrator passed an examination neither of them had expected. In addition, she returned immediately to the same fault she had named for years, showing her standards did not relax for an occasion. Finally, it confirms that her approach was consistent rather than cruel, because she treated his success exactly as she had treated everything else. [3m]

                                      Three marks. The third point is about consistency.

                                      7. Firstly, she had never made him tea in seven years, so it was completely out of character. In addition, because she never praised him in words, this small unusual act had to carry all of her approval. Finally, the narrator says it was 'the entire celebration and that it was enough', which shows the narrator had learnt to read her meaning without needing it spoken. [3m]

                                      Three marks. Explain why a cup of tea can mean so much.

                                      8. Firstly, the narrator admits the narrator barely plays any more and plays badly, so her lasting effect was not musical. In addition, the narrator has copied her method exactly whenever the narrator has taught anyone anything — one hour, one fault, no rewards. Furthermore, the narrator acknowledges that this makes him a difficult teacher, so the narrator can see the cost of her approach as well as its value. Finally, 'I have not been able to make myself stop' shows the influence runs deeper than choice, which is a more honest measure of a teacher than any qualification. [4m]

                                      The last point is about the force of 'I have not been able to make myself stop' — far stronger than simply saying he still does it.

                                      9. 'Preamble'. [1m]

                                      It describes how the teacher began each lesson.

                                      10. 'Withholding'. [1m]

                                      It appears where the narrator explains what the teacher was doing.

                                      The Letter She Never Sent

                                      Narrative · about 461 words · 10 questions · 23 marks · suggested for P6 and above

                                      We found it while clearing the flat, in the third drawer of the dressing table, underneath a tin of buttons.

                                      It was addressed to a Mr Harold Tay at an address in Katong, and it had a stamp on it, and it had never been posted.

                                      My mother turned it over twice. The envelope was not sealed. She looked at me, and I looked at her, and neither of us said the obvious thing, which was that my grandmother had been dead for eleven days and could not now be asked.

                                      In the end we did not open it.

                                      I want to record that accurately, because I have since told the story several times and I have noticed a temptation to make us seem more certain than we were. We stood there for a long while. My mother's thumb was inside the flap at one point. We did not open it, but it was close, and I am not sure the decision was noble so much as postponed.

                                      We asked my aunt. She had never heard of Harold Tay.

                                      We looked him up. There was a Harold Tay who had died in 2004, and a Harold Tay who ran a printing business until the nineties, and no way of knowing whether either of them was the one.

                                      The letter is now in a box in my mother's wardrobe, still unopened, and it has been there for nine years.

                                      Once, about four years ago, my mother took the box down and put it on the kitchen table, and we both sat and looked at it for perhaps ten minutes. Then she carried it back to the wardrobe without either of us saying anything. We have not mentioned that afternoon since, and I am not sure which of us decided.

                                      I think about it more than I expected to. Not because I want to know what is in it — or rather, I do want to know, but that is not the interesting part. What I think about is that my grandmother wrote it, and stamped it, and then did not post it, and kept it for what must have been decades in a drawer she opened every day.

                                      She had a hundred chances to throw it away. She had a hundred chances to post it.

                                      She did neither, which is its own kind of answer, and I suspect it is the only one we are going to get.

                                      My mother says that opening it now would tell us about my grandmother, but it would tell us nothing about the version of her who decided not to send it, and that the second one is the one we actually lost.

                                      I have never been able to think of a good reply to that.

                                      Questions

                                      1. Where and how was the letter found? (2m)

                                      2. What two details show that the letter had been meant to be sent? (2m)

                                      3. Why does the narrator insist on recording the moment "accurately"? (3m)

                                      4. What did the family find out about Harold Tay? (2m)

                                      5. The narrator says she wants to know what is in the letter, "but that is not the interesting part". What does she find more interesting? (3m)

                                      6. Explain: "She had a hundred chances to throw it away. She had a hundred chances to post it." (2m)

                                      7. What does the mother mean by "the second one is the one we actually lost"? (3m)

                                      8. Why is "I have never been able to think of a good reply to that" an effective last line? (4m)

                                      9. Which word in the passage means 'the wish to do something you know you should not'? (1m)

                                      10. Find a word in the passage that means 'put off until a later time'. (1m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. It was found while the family was clearing out the flat, in the third drawer of the dressing table, underneath a tin of buttons. [2m]

                                      Two marks means include the circumstances as well as the place.

                                      2. It was addressed to a named person at a specific address in Katong, and it already had a stamp on it. [2m]

                                      Two pieces of evidence.

                                      3. Firstly, she has told the story several times since and has noticed herself being tempted to make the family sound more principled than they were. In addition, she admits her mother's thumb was inside the flap, so they came very close to opening it. Finally, she says the decision may have been postponed rather than noble, which shows she wants to be honest about her own motives rather than flattering. [3m]

                                      Three marks. This paragraph is about honesty, not about the letter.

                                      4. Very little — an aunt had never heard of him, and a search turned up two different men of that name with no way of telling whether either was the right one. [2m]

                                      Say what they found and why it did not help.

                                      5. Firstly, she is more interested in the fact that her grandmother wrote and stamped the letter but never sent it. In addition, she kept it for decades in a drawer she opened every day, so the decision was made repeatedly rather than once. Finally, this makes the grandmother's choice itself the mystery, rather than the contents of the envelope. [3m]

                                      Three marks. The repetition of the choice is the key point.

                                      6. It means she could easily have destroyed the letter or sent it at any time over many years, so keeping it unsent must have been deliberate rather than an oversight. [2m]

                                      Explain why the writer puts the two options side by side.

                                      7. Firstly, she means that reading the letter would reveal facts about the grandmother's life. In addition, it would not explain the woman who chose year after year not to send it. Finally, that version of her grandmother — her reasons, her hesitation — is the part that died with her and that no letter can bring back. [3m]

                                      Three marks. Distinguish the two 'versions' clearly.

                                      8. Firstly, it ends the passage without resolving anything, which matches a story about a question that cannot be answered. In addition, it shows the narrator accepts her mother's reasoning even though she still wants to open the letter. Furthermore, the admission that she has no reply is more convincing than agreement would be, because it shows the pull she still feels. Finally, the line quietly tells the reader that the letter will probably stay closed, without the narrator having to say so. [4m]

                                      Four marks. The final point is about what the line implies rather than states.

                                      9. 'Temptation'. [1m]

                                      It appears where the narrator is holding the envelope.

                                      10. 'Postponed'. [1m]

                                      It describes what was done again and again.

                                      The Egg in the Drain

                                      Narrative · about 316 words · 10 questions · 16 marks · suggested for P3 and above

                                      On Saturday morning, my sister Nadia and I heard a noise outside our flat.

                                      It was a small sound. It went cheep, then stopped, then cheep again.

                                      We looked over the corridor railing. We looked behind the bicycles. We looked under the letter boxes. We could not find it anywhere.

                                      Then Nadia lay flat on the floor and put her ear against the drain cover.

                                      "It is in here," she said.

                                      The drain cover was a metal grid with narrow slots. Through them we could see something small and grey. It was a baby bird, and it could not get out.

                                      I tried to lift the cover. It was far too heavy. We tried together, and it did not move at all.

                                      "We need an adult," Nadia said.

                                      Our father was asleep, because he had worked at night. Our mother had gone to the market. So we knocked on the door next to ours.

                                      Uncle Ravi opened it, holding a newspaper. We told him about the bird. He looked through the slots, then went back inside without a word.

                                      For a moment I thought he did not care.

                                      Then he came back with a screwdriver and a torch.

                                      It took him five minutes to lift the cover. Nadia held her jacket open like a net, Uncle Ravi guided the frightened bird into it, and then it was out.

                                      We put it in a shoebox. Uncle Ravi telephoned the bird rescue centre, and a lady came at four o'clock and took the box away.

                                      She told us it was a mynah chick. She said it would be fed every two hours and released when it could fly.

                                      That evening our father asked what we had done all day.

                                      Nadia said, "Nothing much."

                                      I did not say anything either. But I still remember how heavy that drain cover was, and how light the bird was in the jacket.

                                      Questions

                                      1. Where were Nadia and the narrator when they first heard the noise? (1m)

                                      2. Give two places the children searched before they found the bird. (2m)

                                      3. How did Nadia work out where the bird was? (1m)

                                      4. Why could the children not rescue the bird by themselves? (2m)

                                      5. Why did they go to Uncle Ravi instead of asking their own parents? (2m)

                                      6. Why did the narrator think for a moment that Uncle Ravi did not care? (2m)

                                      7. What did Nadia do to help catch the bird? (1m)

                                      8. What two things did the lady from the rescue centre say would happen to the bird? (2m)

                                      9. Which word in the passage means 'thin openings'? (1m)

                                      10. The narrator remembers 'how heavy that drain cover was, and how light the bird was'. Why do you think he remembers those two things together? (2m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. They were at their flat, and the sound came from outside in the corridor. [1m]

                                      Look at the first two paragraphs.

                                      2. Any two of: over the corridor railing; behind the bicycles; under the letter boxes. [2m]

                                      Two places are asked for. Any two will do.

                                      3. She lay down flat on the floor and put her ear against the drain cover. [1m]

                                      She used her ears, not her eyes.

                                      4. The metal drain cover was far too heavy for them to lift, even when they tried together. [2m]

                                      Look at what happened when they both tried.

                                      5. Their father was asleep after working at night, and their mother had gone to the market. [2m]

                                      Both parents are accounted for in the same paragraph.

                                      6. Because he looked through the slots and went back inside without saying anything, so it seemed as though he was ignoring them. In fact he had gone to fetch a screwdriver and a torch. [2m]

                                      Say what the narrator thought, and then what was really happening.

                                      7. She held her jacket open like a net so that Uncle Ravi could guide the bird into it. [1m]

                                      Look at the paragraph about lifting the cover.

                                      8. It would be fed every two hours, and it would be released when it was able to fly. [2m]

                                      Both facts are in the same short paragraph.

                                      9. 'Slots'. [1m]

                                      It describes the gaps in the drain cover.

                                      10. Because they are opposites, and putting them side by side shows how much effort went into saving something so small. It suggests that the size of the trouble was worth it. [2m]

                                      Think about why a writer would put a heavy thing and a light thing in the same sentence.

                                      The Wrong Shoes

                                      Narrative · about 244 words · 9 questions · 16 marks · suggested for P3 and above

                                      On the morning of the school excursion, I put on my shoes in the dark and ran for the bus.

                                      It was only when I sat down that I looked at my feet.

                                      One shoe was mine. The other belonged to my brother, who is two years younger and two sizes smaller.

                                      My left foot was already beginning to hurt.

                                      I did not tell anybody. I was afraid the teachers would send me home, and we were going to the bird park, which I had waited three weeks for.

                                      For the first hour I walked normally and pretended nothing was wrong. By the time we reached the flamingos I was limping.

                                      Nur noticed first. She did not laugh. She asked what was wrong, and when I showed her, she went very quiet and thought for a while.

                                      Then she took off her own shoes and handed me the left one.

                                      "We wear the same size," she said. "I will wear your brother's."

                                      Nur's feet are smaller than mine. My brother's shoe was far too tight for her, and I knew it.

                                      She wore it for the rest of the day and said nothing at all about it.

                                      On the bus home she took it off and I saw the red mark across her toes.

                                      I have thought about that mark many times since. She was not being kind for one minute, which is easy. She was being kind for five hours, which is not.

                                      Questions

                                      1. Why did the narrator put on the wrong shoes? (1m)

                                      2. How were the two shoes different? (2m)

                                      3. Why did the narrator not tell anybody? (2m)

                                      4. How do we know the narrator's foot was getting worse? (2m)

                                      5. What did Nur do when she found out? (2m)

                                      6. Why was Nur's offer a bigger sacrifice than it first seems? (2m)

                                      7. Which word in the passage means 'walking unevenly because of pain'? (1m)

                                      8. How did the narrator find out how much it had hurt her? (1m)

                                      9. Explain the last sentence in your own words. (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. He put them on in the dark, in a hurry to catch the bus for the excursion. [1m]

                                      Look at the very first sentence.

                                      2. One was his own. The other belonged to his younger brother, and was two sizes smaller. [2m]

                                      Two details are needed: whose it was, and how much smaller.

                                      3. He was afraid the teachers would send him home, and he had been looking forward to the bird park for three weeks. [2m]

                                      There are two reasons in the same sentence.

                                      4. At first he walked normally and pretended nothing was wrong, but by the time they reached the flamingos he was limping. [2m]

                                      Compare the first hour with later in the day.

                                      5. She took off her own shoes and gave him her left one, and wore his brother's small shoe instead. [2m]

                                      Say what she gave and what she took.

                                      6. Her feet were smaller than his, so his brother's shoe was far too tight for her, and she wore it for the rest of the day without complaining. [2m]

                                      Think about whose foot the small shoe fitted worst.

                                      7. 'Limping'. [1m]

                                      Look in the paragraph about the flamingos.

                                      8. On the bus home she took the shoe off and he saw a red mark across her toes. [1m]

                                      He saw it rather than being told.

                                      9. Being kind for a short moment is easy because it costs you almost nothing. Nur stayed uncomfortable for five hours without mentioning it, and choosing to keep going is much harder than starting. [3m]

                                      Contrast one minute with five hours, and say why the difference matters.

                                      Why We Queue

                                      Non-narrative · about 399 words · 9 questions · 19 marks · suggested for P5 and above

                                      Queuing is not natural. It has to be learnt, and different places learn it differently.

                                      In Singapore, a queue at a bus stop forms almost without discussion. People arrive, look, and place themselves at the end. Nobody appoints anybody. There is no line painted on the ground, and no official watching.

                                      What holds it together is not a rule but an agreement, and agreements are fragile in a particular way: they work completely until they do not work at all.

                                      Researchers who study queues have found that a single person stepping in near the front rarely causes an argument. Instead, something quieter happens. The people behind exchange glances. Bags are shifted. Somebody clears their throat. Very often the person who pushed in retreats without a single word being said to them.

                                      This is remarkably efficient. A rule needs an inspector, a penalty and somebody to collect it. Social disapproval needs nothing at all, and it arrives instantly.

                                      It is also fragile. In the same studies, once two or three people pushed in and nothing happened, the queue collapsed within a minute. Those who had been waiting patiently stopped waiting, because the cost of being patient had suddenly become obvious and the benefit had disappeared.

                                      Not every culture queues the same way. In some places a crowd at a counter is the norm, and what looks like disorder to a visitor is a system with its own rules about who is served next. Neither arrangement is naturally better. What matters is that everybody in the room has learnt the same one, which is why the most difficult queues in the world are at international airports.

                                      This is why queue systems in busy places increasingly use numbered tickets. A ticket does not make people more honest. It makes honesty unnecessary, which is a different thing and, in a crowded clinic on a Monday morning, a more reliable one.

                                      There is one exception worth noticing. People are far more willing to let somebody go ahead of them when a reason is given, even a thin one. In one well-known experiment, asking to skip a photocopier queue succeeded far more often when the request ended with the word 'because', regardless of what followed it.

                                      That finding is usually presented as evidence that people are easily fooled. It might equally show something better: that most of us would rather be reasonable than be first.

                                      Questions

                                      1. According to the passage, what makes a queue at a bus stop work? (2m)

                                      2. Give two of the ways the passage says people react to somebody pushing in. (2m)

                                      3. Why does the writer call social disapproval 'remarkably efficient'? (2m)

                                      4. Explain in your own words why a queue can collapse so quickly. (3m)

                                      5. What does the writer mean by saying a ticket 'makes honesty unnecessary'? (2m)

                                      6. Why does the writer mention a clinic on a Monday morning? (2m)

                                      7. What did the photocopier experiment find? (2m)

                                      8. Which word in the passage means 'easily broken'? (1m)

                                      9. The writer offers two ways of reading the photocopier finding. What are they, and which does the writer prefer? (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. Not an official rule, but an unspoken agreement between the people in it. Nobody appoints anybody and nobody is watching. [2m]

                                      The answer is a contrast between two kinds of authority.

                                      2. Any two of: they exchange glances; they shift their bags; somebody clears their throat. [2m]

                                      Three are listed; two will do.

                                      3. Because a rule needs an inspector, a penalty and somebody to collect it, whereas disapproval costs nothing and works instantly. [2m]

                                      The comparison with a formal rule is the point.

                                      4. Once a few people push in and nothing happens to them, waiting patiently starts to look pointless. The people who were waiting can now see that it costs them something and gains them nothing, so they stop. [3m]

                                      Use the ideas of cost and benefit in your own words.

                                      5. A numbered ticket does not persuade anybody to behave better. It removes the need to rely on good behaviour at all, because your place is recorded rather than trusted. [2m]

                                      Notice the difference between making people honest and not needing them to be.

                                      6. It is an example of a busy, crowded place where a queue depending on goodwill would be most likely to break down, so a ticket system is more reliable there. [2m]

                                      Ask why that particular example was chosen.

                                      7. People were far more likely to let somebody skip the queue when the request included the word 'because', whatever reason followed it. [2m]

                                      The key detail is that the reason itself did not matter.

                                      8. 'Fragile'. [1m]

                                      It is used twice, about agreements and about the system.

                                      9. It can be read as evidence that people are easily fooled by any reason at all. The writer prefers the second reading: that most people would rather behave reasonably than get to the front, so a reason gives them permission to be generous. The phrase 'It might equally show something better' shows the preference. [3m]

                                      Give both readings, then quote or point to the words that show the writer's own view.

                                      The Cat That Came to School

                                      Narrative · about 295 words · 9 questions · 17 marks · suggested for P4 and above

                                      The cat first appeared outside our classroom in the second week of January.

                                      It was grey, thin, and missing part of one ear. It sat on the ledge outside the window during Mathematics and left before recess, and it did this every day for a fortnight before anybody mentioned it out loud.

                                      Mr Devan pretended not to notice. We pretended not to notice that he was pretending.

                                      Then somebody brought food.

                                      It was Wei Ling, and she brought half a sausage from her lunchbox, and after that the cat stayed until the end of the day.

                                      Within a week, four people were bringing food. The cat grew visibly rounder. It also began to walk into the classroom.

                                      That was when Mr Devan stopped pretending.

                                      He did not shout. He asked us to sit down, and then he asked one question: what would happen to the cat in March, when we moved to a different block?

                                      Nobody had thought about March.

                                      He explained that a cat fed by children learns to expect children, and that a cat which has learnt to expect children and then finds none is in a worse position than a cat that never learnt anything.

                                      We argued for twenty minutes. Some of us were angry, mostly because he was right.

                                      In the end we did something better than feeding it. Wei Ling's mother knew somebody at a rescue centre. They came on a Thursday, caught it in about four minutes, and took it away to be checked and rehomed.

                                      We were sent a photograph in April. It lives with an elderly couple in Bedok and has become extremely fat.

                                      I still look at the window ledge sometimes during Mathematics. It is the right ending, and I know that, and I still look.

                                      Questions

                                      1. How long had the cat been visiting before anybody spoke about it? (1m)

                                      2. Give two details that describe how the cat looked when it first appeared. (2m)

                                      3. What does 'We pretended not to notice that he was pretending' tell us about the class? (2m)

                                      4. What changed after Wei Ling brought food? (2m)

                                      5. What was Mr Devan's argument against feeding the cat? (3m)

                                      6. Why were some pupils angry? (1m)

                                      7. Why does the writer say what they did in the end was 'better than feeding it'? (2m)

                                      8. Which word in the passage means 'given a new home'? (1m)

                                      9. Explain the last sentence: 'It is the right ending, and I know that, and I still look.' (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. A fortnight, which is two weeks. [1m]

                                      The passage gives the length in the second paragraph.

                                      2. Any two of: it was grey; it was thin; part of one ear was missing. [2m]

                                      Three details are given; two will do.

                                      3. They knew Mr Devan had seen the cat and was deliberately ignoring it, and they were happy to play along so that nothing would have to be done about it. [2m]

                                      Both the teacher and the class are choosing not to act.

                                      4. The cat began staying until the end of the day, four people started bringing food, it grew visibly rounder, and it began coming into the classroom. [2m]

                                      Several things changed; give at least two.

                                      5. A cat fed by children learns to expect children. When the class moved block in March there would be no children, and a cat that has learnt to expect food and then finds none is worse off than one that never learnt to expect it. [3m]

                                      His argument is about what happens after the feeding stops.

                                      6. Mostly because he was right, and they could not argue against it. [1m]

                                      The passage says so directly.

                                      7. Feeding the cat only helped while they were there. Having it caught, checked and rehomed gave it a permanent home, which solves the problem instead of postponing it. [2m]

                                      Compare a short-term help with a lasting one.

                                      8. 'Rehomed'. [1m]

                                      Look in the paragraph about the rescue centre.

                                      9. The narrator accepts that rehoming the cat was the right decision and does not regret it. Even so, he misses it, and the habit of looking at the ledge has stayed with him. Knowing something is right does not stop you feeling the loss of it. [3m]

                                      The sentence holds two things at once. Say what both are.

                                      The Understudy's Understudy

                                      Narrative · about 402 words · 9 questions · 17 marks · suggested for P5 and above

                                      There were three of us who could play the part, and I was the third.

                                      Pei Shan had it. Hafiz was her understudy, which meant he learnt every line and would go on only if she could not. I was Hafiz's understudy, which meant almost nothing at all.

                                      Mrs Fong was honest about it. "You will not perform," she told me in September. "Two people would both have to be ill. It has happened to me once in twenty-two years."

                                      I learnt the part anyway. I am not sure why. Possibly because being told something is nearly impossible is not quite the same as being told it is impossible.

                                      I went to every rehearsal. I sat at the side with the script on my knees and mouthed the lines while Pei Shan spoke them. For eleven weeks I was the least important person in the hall.

                                      What I did not expect was how much I would learn there.

                                      Because I was never on stage, I watched. I saw Mrs Fong ask Pei Shan to say one line six times, and I understood on the fourth attempt what she was listening for. I saw Hafiz solve a problem with a difficult entrance by changing where he stood two lines earlier. Nobody explained these things to me. I simply had nothing else to do but notice them.

                                      There was one afternoon in week nine when Pei Shan lost her voice and could not rehearse. Hafiz went on in her place, and Mrs Fong turned to me and said, "You are Hafiz today." I sat in his chair at the side of the hall for two hours, holding his script, and did not speak a single line. It was the closest I came all term, and it lasted one afternoon.

                                      On the night, Pei Shan was not ill and neither was Hafiz. I watched from the third row with my parents.

                                      She was very good. He would have been very good. I would have been adequate, and I knew it, because I had spent eleven weeks watching people who were better than me.

                                      That is the part nobody warned me about, and it is the part I am most grateful for.

                                      In March I auditioned for the next production and got a speaking part. Mrs Fong said something afterwards that I have kept.

                                      "You were the only one who had already been to every rehearsal."

                                      Questions

                                      1. Explain what an understudy is, using the passage. (1m)

                                      2. Why did the narrator's position mean 'almost nothing at all'? (2m)

                                      3. What did Mrs Fong tell the narrator in September, and why is her exact wording important? (3m)

                                      4. Give two things the narrator learnt by watching rather than performing. (2m)

                                      5. Why was the narrator able to notice these things? (2m)

                                      6. What happened on the night of the performance? (1m)

                                      7. Why does the narrator say he would have been only 'adequate'? (2m)

                                      8. Which word in the passage means 'good enough, but no better'? (1m)

                                      9. Why is Mrs Fong's last remark a good ending to the story? (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. Somebody who learns every line of a part and performs it only if the person who has the part cannot. [1m]

                                      The passage explains it when Hafiz is introduced.

                                      2. He was the understudy's understudy, so two people would both have had to be unable to perform before he would go on. [2m]

                                      The reason is arithmetical.

                                      3. She said he would not perform, because it would take two people being ill, which had happened once in twenty-two years. The wording matters because she said it was nearly impossible rather than impossible, and the narrator notices that difference and learns the part anyway. [3m]

                                      Give what she said and then explain what the narrator makes of it.

                                      4. Any two of: he understood what Mrs Fong was listening for when she made Pei Shan repeat a line; he saw how Hafiz fixed a difficult entrance by changing where he stood two lines earlier. [2m]

                                      Two examples are given in the same paragraph.

                                      5. Because he was never on stage he had nothing else to do but watch, so he had time to see things nobody explained to him. [2m]

                                      The reason is about what he was not doing.

                                      6. Neither Pei Shan nor Hafiz was ill, so the narrator did not perform. He watched from the third row with his parents. [1m]

                                      The outcome is plainly stated.

                                      7. Because he had spent eleven weeks watching two people who were better than he was, so he could judge his own level honestly. [2m]

                                      He gives the reason in the same sentence.

                                      8. 'Adequate'. [1m]

                                      It is used about himself, not about the others.

                                      9. It shows that the eleven weeks were not wasted after all. The thing that got him a speaking part was exactly the thing that had seemed pointless: turning up to every rehearsal when he had no chance of performing. It rewards the narrator without pretending he was talented, which is more honest and more satisfying. [3m]

                                      Connect her remark back to the weeks that seemed to be for nothing.

                                      The Borrowed Umbrella

                                      Narrative · about 289 words · 9 questions · 14 marks · suggested for P3 and above

                                      The rain began during the last lesson on Monday, and by the time the bell rang it was falling so hard that nobody wanted to step outside.

                                      I had forgotten my umbrella. Again.

                                      Mrs Devi was standing at the gate with a pile of umbrellas from the lost property cupboard. She lent me a small yellow one with a bent handle.

                                      "Bring it back tomorrow," she said. "It is not mine to give away."

                                      I promised that I would. Then I ran all the way to the bus stop, holding the yellow umbrella above my head with both hands.

                                      At home I shook the water off it and leaned it against the shoe rack so that I would see it in the morning.

                                      On Tuesday I did not see it. I was late, and I ran out of the house with one shoe half on.

                                      I remembered the umbrella at recess. My stomach went tight.

                                      I did not want to tell Mrs Devi, so for the whole afternoon I avoided walking past her desk. I took the long way to the water cooler. I even waited inside the classroom until she had left the corridor.

                                      At dismissal she found me anyway.

                                      "The umbrella?" she asked.

                                      "At home," I said. "Beside the shoe rack. I am sorry."

                                      Mrs Devi did not look cross. She looked relieved.

                                      "Thank you for telling me the truth," she said. "I thought it had been thrown away."

                                      I brought it back on Wednesday, dry and folded, and I put it into the cupboard myself. Then I bought a cheap blue umbrella of my own and left it in my bag, where it has stayed ever since.

                                      I have not forgotten an umbrella in two years.

                                      Questions

                                      1. When did the rain begin? (1m)

                                      2. Why did Mrs Devi have a pile of umbrellas at the gate? (1m)

                                      3. Describe the umbrella Mrs Devi lent the writer. (2m)

                                      4. Why did Mrs Devi say, "It is not mine to give away"? (2m)

                                      5. Why did the writer forget the umbrella on Tuesday morning? (1m)

                                      6. Give two things the writer did that afternoon to avoid Mrs Devi. (2m)

                                      7. Why do you think Mrs Devi looked relieved rather than cross? (2m)

                                      8. Which word in the passage means 'kept away from'? (1m)

                                      9. How do you know the writer learnt something from what happened? (2m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. During the last lesson on Monday. [1m]

                                      Look at the very first sentence.

                                      2. They came from the school's lost property cupboard. [1m]

                                      The third paragraph says where the umbrellas came from.

                                      3. It was small and yellow, with a bent handle. [2m]

                                      Three details are given in one sentence. Two of them will do.

                                      4. The umbrella belonged to somebody else, because it had been lost and put into the lost property cupboard. She was only lending it. [2m]

                                      Think about whose umbrella it really was.

                                      5. The writer was late and ran out of the house in a hurry, with one shoe only half on. [1m]

                                      Look at what was happening that morning.

                                      6. Any two of: took the long way to the water cooler; did not walk past her desk; waited inside the classroom until she had left the corridor. [2m]

                                      Two actions are asked for. The paragraph lists three.

                                      7. She had thought the umbrella was lost for good or thrown away, so hearing that it was safe at home was good news. [2m]

                                      Her next line tells you what she had been expecting to hear.

                                      8. 'Avoided'. [1m]

                                      Look in the paragraph about the afternoon.

                                      9. The writer bought a cheap blue umbrella to keep in the school bag, and has not forgotten an umbrella in two years. [2m]

                                      The last two paragraphs show a change in behaviour, not just a feeling.

                                      How Bees Tell One Another Where to Go

                                      Non-narrative · about 279 words · 9 questions · 13 marks · suggested for P3 and above

                                      A bee that finds a good patch of flowers has a problem. The flowers may be half a kilometre away, and the bee cannot carry its sisters there one by one.

                                      So it tells them instead. It does this by dancing.

                                      Back inside the dark hive, the bee climbs onto the honeycomb and runs forward in a straight line, shaking its body from side to side. Then it loops round and runs the same line again. From above, the path looks like the number eight.

                                      The straight run carries the message.

                                      The direction of the run tells the other bees which way to fly. The longer the run lasts, the further away the flowers are. A run of one second means the patch is about a kilometre away.

                                      The dancing bee also carries the smell of the flowers on its body, and it shares a drop of the nectar it collected. The other bees crowd round to taste it. Now they know the direction, the distance and the scent.

                                      Scientists did not always know this. In the 1940s a man named Karl von Frisch watched bees through a glass wall for years. He marked single bees with tiny spots of paint so that he could follow one at a time.

                                      What he discovered surprised people. Until then, most adults believed that insects were too simple to pass on anything so exact.

                                      A bee's dance is not speech. It does not have words, and it cannot describe anything that is not food, water or a new home. But it does something that very few animals can do: it tells another animal about a place that neither of them can see.

                                      Questions

                                      1. What problem does a bee have when it finds a good patch of flowers? (2m)

                                      2. Where does the bee dance? (1m)

                                      3. What shape does the dancing bee's path look like from above? (1m)
