                                      4. How do the other bees know how far away the flowers are? (2m)

                                      5. Apart from dancing, give two ways the bee passes on information about the flowers. (2m)

                                      6. Why did Karl von Frisch mark bees with spots of paint? (1m)

                                      7. Why were people surprised by what von Frisch discovered? (2m)

                                      8. Which word in the passage means 'the sweet liquid bees collect from flowers'? (1m)

                                      9. The passage says a bee's dance 'is not speech'. Give one way it is different from speech. (1m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. The flowers may be far away, and the bee cannot carry the other bees there one by one. [2m]

                                      The first paragraph states the problem.

                                      2. Inside the dark hive, on the honeycomb. [1m]

                                      Look at the third paragraph.

                                      3. The number eight. [1m]

                                      The end of the third paragraph describes the shape.

                                      4. From how long the straight run lasts. A longer run means the flowers are further away. [2m]

                                      One part of the dance carries the distance.

                                      5. Any two of: it carries the smell of the flowers on its body; it shares a drop of the nectar it collected so the others can taste it. [2m]

                                      Two ways are asked for, and both are in the same paragraph.

                                      6. So that he could follow one particular bee at a time among all the others. [1m]

                                      Think about what a hive full of identical bees would look like.

                                      7. Until then most people believed that insects were too simple to pass on information as exact as a direction and a distance. [2m]

                                      The paragraph after the discovery explains what people had believed before it.

                                      8. 'Nectar'. [1m]

                                      Look in the paragraph about smell and taste.

                                      9. Any one of: it has no words; it can only describe food, water or a new home, and nothing else. [1m]

                                      The last paragraph names two limits. One is enough.

                                      The Fourth Leg

                                      Narrative · about 371 words · 9 questions · 17 marks · suggested for P5 and above

                                      There are four legs in a relay and everybody wants the last one.

                                      I had run the second leg for two years, which is the leg nobody watches. You take the baton on a bend, you give it away on a bend, and the photographs are all of somebody else.

                                      So when Coach Lim read out the order for the inter-school final and my name came fourth, I did not believe it. I made him say it again.

                                      "Fourth," he said, without looking up from his clipboard. "Hui Ling, second."

                                      Hui Ling had run the fourth leg since Primary Three. She was the fastest of us over a hundred metres and everybody knew it, including her.

                                      She did not complain. That was the difficult part. She said, "Okay, Coach," and went to do her stretches by the long jump pit, alone, and at training that week she handed me the baton perfectly every single time.

                                      I asked her about it on the Thursday. She said she had asked to be moved.

                                      "You drop it when you're nervous," she said. "You don't drop it on the second leg because nobody's shouting. On the fourth leg everybody's shouting." She tightened a shoelace. "Coach thinks you should learn it now and not next year."

                                      I was not sure whether I had been promoted or sent to do something unpleasant.

                                      On the Saturday the stadium was as loud as she had promised. I stood in my box with my arm back and the noise came at me in a wall, and I could not pick out a single word of it, which turned out to be a mercy.

                                      Hui Ling came round the bend in second place. She did not shout; she slapped the baton into my palm so hard that my fingers closed by themselves.

                                      I ran the fourth leg. We finished second, four tenths of a second behind Rulang, and I did not drop anything.

                                      Afterwards the photographer took a picture of me holding the baton, because that is the leg they photograph.

                                      It is on the noticeboard outside the general office. Hui Ling is in it too, slightly out of focus, on the edge of the frame, with her hand still out.

                                      Questions

                                      1. Why does the narrator say the second leg is 'the leg nobody watches'? (2m)

                                      2. How do you know the narrator was surprised by Coach Lim's running order? (1m)

                                      3. Why would most people have expected Hui Ling to run the fourth leg? (2m)

                                      4. The narrator says Hui Ling not complaining 'was the difficult part'. Why was it difficult for the narrator? (2m)

                                      5. Give two things Hui Ling did that week which showed she was not sulking. (2m)

                                      6. In your own words, explain Hui Ling's reason for asking to be moved. (2m)

                                      7. Why does the narrator describe not being able to hear the words of the crowd as 'a mercy'? (2m)

                                      8. Which word in the passage means 'moved up to a more important position'? (1m)

                                      9. The last paragraph describes a photograph. What does the writer want the reader to notice about it? (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. It begins and ends on a bend, away from the finish, so the photographs are always of somebody else. [2m]

                                      The second paragraph gives two reasons in one sentence.

                                      2. The narrator did not believe it and made Coach Lim say it again. [1m]

                                      Look at what the narrator does immediately after hearing the order.

                                      3. She had run it since Primary 3 and was the fastest of them over a hundred metres. [2m]

                                      Two reasons are given in the same paragraph.

                                      4. If Hui Ling had complained, the narrator could have felt she was being unfair. Because she accepted it and then helped at training, the narrator had nothing to push against and had to face that she had given something up for him. [2m]

                                      Think about how an unfair reaction would have been easier to deal with than a generous one.

                                      5. Any two of: she said 'Okay, Coach' without arguing; she went to do her stretches; she handed the narrator the baton perfectly every time at training. [2m]

                                      Two actions are asked for. The paragraph offers three.

                                      6. The narrator drops the baton when nervous. The second leg is quiet, so the problem never shows there, while the fourth leg is noisy. She thought the narrator should learn to handle that pressure now rather than a year later. [2m]

                                      Her two short lines on the Thursday contain the whole reason. Do not copy them word for word.

                                      7. Because the noise was what the narrator was afraid of. Hearing it as one wall of sound rather than as separate voices made it easier to ignore and so easier to run. [2m]

                                      A mercy is something you are glad about. Ask what hearing the words clearly would have done.

                                      8. 'Promoted'. [1m]

                                      Look at the short paragraph just before the race.

                                      9. The narrator is the one photographed, but Hui Ling is in the picture too — out of focus, at the edge, with her hand still out. It is a way of saying that the narrator's moment was made possible by her, even though she is not the subject of it. [3m]

                                      Think about why the writer bothers to tell us where Hui Ling is in the frame and what her hand is doing.

                                      Stall 42

                                      Narrative · about 374 words · 9 questions · 17 marks · suggested for P5 and above

                                      My grandmother's stall is number 42, at the end of the row where the fan does not reach.

                                      She has sold the same three things for thirty-one years: mee rebus, lontong, and a tea so sweet that my father will not drink it. There is no signboard with photographs. There is a strip of red plastic with her name on it, and the paint has come off the second letter.

                                      I started helping on Saturdays when I was nine. My job was the drinks and the wiping. Her job was everything else, and she did it without hurrying and without ever once looking at the clock.

                                      In June the stall three doors down closed, and a bubble tea shop opened in its place. It had a machine that sealed the cups, a menu board that lit up, and a queue.

                                      For a few weeks my grandmother said nothing about it. Then one Saturday she asked me to write down what a bubble tea cost. I wrote it on the back of an order slip. She looked at the number for a long time and put the slip in her apron pocket.

                                      "One cup," she said, "is two plates of my lontong."

                                      I thought she was going to say it was ridiculous. Instead she said, "They are not selling drinks. They are selling somewhere to stand with your friends."

                                      The following Saturday she moved two of the plastic stools out from behind the stall and put them against the wall, in the shade, where the fan does reach. She told the secondary school boys who buy her tea that they could sit there.

                                      They sat there. They came back the next week with two more boys, and the week after that one of them took a photograph of the red plastic strip with her name on it and put it somewhere I do not fully understand.

                                      By August she was running out of lontong before one o'clock.

                                      She has still not put up a signboard. She says the stall has had the same number for thirty-one years and anybody who wants it can find it.

                                      But the stools are still against the wall, and on Saturdays I am now in charge of carrying them out.

                                      Questions

                                      1. Give two details that show the grandmother's stall is old-fashioned. (2m)

                                      2. What was the narrator's job at the stall? (1m)

                                      3. Give two ways the new bubble tea shop was different from the grandmother's stall. (2m)

                                      4. Why do you think the grandmother asked the narrator to write down the price of a bubble tea? (2m)

                                      5. Explain what the grandmother means when she says, "They are not selling drinks. They are selling somewhere to stand with your friends." (2m)

                                      6. What did the grandmother do as a result of that thought, and why was the place she chose a good one? (2m)

                                      7. What does the writer mean by saying the photograph was put 'somewhere I do not fully understand'? (2m)

                                      8. How do we know the grandmother's stall became busier? (1m)

                                      9. The grandmother changed one thing and refused to change another. What does this tell you about her? (3m)

                                      Model answers

                                      1. Any two of: it has sold the same three items for thirty-one years; it has no signboard with photographs, only a strip of red plastic; the paint has worn off a letter of her name. [2m]

                                      Two details are asked for. The second paragraph offers several.

                                      2. The drinks and the wiping. [1m]

                                      The third paragraph says it in one short sentence.

                                      3. Any two of: it had a machine that sealed the cups; it had a menu board that lit up; it had a queue. [2m]

                                      Three differences are listed in a single sentence.

                                      4. She wanted to understand what the new shop was charging and to compare it with her own prices, which she does out loud in the next paragraph. [2m]

                                      Look at what she says once she has the number.

                                      5. She means the shop's success does not come from the drink itself but from giving young people a place to gather, which is what they are really paying for. [2m]

                                      Her next action shows what she concluded from this, which is a clue to what she meant.

                                      6. She moved two plastic stools out and put them against the wall for the secondary school boys to sit on. The spot was good because it was in the shade and the fan reached it, unlike her own stall. [2m]

                                      Two parts: the action, and what was special about where she put the stools. The first paragraph tells you about the fan.

                                      7. The boy posted it online, on social media. The narrator knows roughly what happened but not how it works, and the grandmother would understand it even less. [2m]

                                      Think about what a secondary school boy does with a photograph he has just taken.

                                      8. By August she was running out of lontong before one o'clock. [1m]

                                      One short paragraph gives the evidence, without using the word 'busy'.

                                      9. She is willing to change how people use the space around her stall, because she listens to what customers actually want, but she will not change what she thinks makes the stall hers — the food, and being known by her number rather than by a signboard. She adapts without copying. [3m]

                                      Set the stools against the signboard. Ask what each one would have cost her.

                                      Document 08

                                      Model Answers — Writing (Paper 1)

                                      Four more annotated model compositions, three situational writing models, and a marking rubric so a parent can grade a composition at home without guessing.

                                      Part 1 — How to Mark a Composition at Home

                                      You do not need to be an English teacher. You need to apply the same two scales the examiner uses, and be consistent.

                                      Content — 20 marks

                                      Band Marks What it looks like
                                      A 17–20 Clearly on theme. One well-chosen incident, developed in depth. The climax is expanded, not rushed. We understand what the character thought and felt, and the ending shows genuine change or insight.
                                      B 13–16 On theme, complete plot, sensible detail. The climax is present but a little thin. Some insight, though the ending may state the lesson rather than show it.
                                      C 9–12 Relevant to the theme but thin, or too many events crammed in. Detail is general. Little sense of what the character felt.
                                      D 4–8 Only loosely connected to the theme, or the plot is confused or incomplete.
                                      E 0–3 Off theme, or too short to judge.

                                      Language — 20 marks

                                      Band Marks What it looks like
                                      A 17–20 Almost no grammatical errors. Varied sentence structures and openings. Vocabulary is precise and used correctly. Paragraphing is logical. Dialogue is punctuated correctly.
                                      B 13–16 A few errors that do not obscure meaning. Some sentence variety. Vocabulary is adequate with occasional reaching.
                                      C 9–12 Frequent errors, mostly in tense and subject–verb agreement. Mostly simple sentences. Repetitive vocabulary (said, went, nice, very).
                                      D 4–8 Errors in most sentences; meaning sometimes unclear.
                                      E 0–3 Very difficult to follow.

                                      The three questions to ask before assigning a mark

                                      1. Could I state the theme after reading it, without seeing the question? If not, content cannot reach band A.
                                      2. How many words does the climax take? If under 60, it has been rushed — cap content at band B.
                                      3. Count the tense and agreement errors. Zero to two → band A language. Three to six → band B. Seven or more → band C or below.

                                      Give one specific instruction, not five. A child who is told "improve your vocabulary, add more description, watch your tenses, vary your sentences and write a better ending" will change nothing. A child told "this week, expand the climax to at least eight sentences" will do it.

                                      Part 2 — Model Compositions

                                      Model 3 · Theme: Perseverance

                                      The Third Attempt

                                      I had failed the swimming test twice, and the second time was worse than the first.

                                      Everyone in my class had earned their bronze badge by October. Mine was still a blank space on the noticeboard where my name should have been, and every Tuesday Miss Faridah would read out the list of pupils going to the deep-end lane, and every Tuesday my name was not on it.

                                      The problem was not my arms. It was my breathing. Somewhere around the twelfth metre, my chest would tighten and my head would come up too early, and after that the whole stroke fell apart. I had been told what to do a hundred times. Knowing was not the difficulty.

                                      The third test was in November. I asked my father to take me to the public pool on Saturday mornings, and for six weeks we went at seven, before the crowds. He could not swim himself. He sat on the plastic bench at the shallow end with a flask of coffee and counted my strokes out loud, and when I stopped halfway he did not say anything encouraging at all. He just said the number I had reached, and waited.

                                      Fourteen. Then nineteen. Then twenty-two, then twenty-two again for three weeks in a row.

                                      On the last Saturday before the test, I reached thirty-one and touched the far wall. I stood up in the shallow end with water streaming off my face and looked at my father. He capped his flask and said, "Right. Breakfast."

                                      I passed on the Tuesday, in the second-slowest time in the class.

                                      The badge is in a drawer somewhere now and I could not tell you where. But I remember every one of those Saturday mornings, and I remember that twenty-two is not a wall. It is just a number you have not passed yet.

                                      Why it scores well: one narrow problem (breathing at twelve metres) rather than a vague "I was bad at swimming"; the father's restraint is more moving than encouragement would be; the numbers do the emotional work; the ending refuses the easy triumph — she finishes second-slowest — and lands on a genuine, earned idea.

                                      Model 4 · Theme: Kindness

                                      The Blue Chair

                                      Mr Tan had sat on the same blue plastic chair outside the provision shop for as long as I had been alive.

                                      He was there every morning when I left for school and every evening when I came back, one hand resting on a walking stick he did not really need, watching the carpark the way other people watch television. He was not friendly. If you greeted him he would nod, once, and look away again. My friends called him the guard.

                                      In March the chair was empty for four days.

                                      I noticed on the second day and said nothing. On the fourth day my grandmother asked the shopkeeper, who said Mr Tan's sister in Ipoh had passed away and he had gone up for the funeral, and that he had no one to feed his birds.

                                      I did not know he kept birds.

                                      That evening my grandmother handed me a key and a bag of millet and told me the flat number. I climbed to the eleventh floor expecting one cage. There were four, hanging along the corridor outside his door, and the moment I appeared all of them began to sing at once — a wall of sound so sudden and so loud that I nearly dropped the bag.

                                      I fed them every day for nine days.

                                      When Mr Tan came back, he did not thank me. He nodded once, the way he always did, and looked away. I was, I admit, a little disappointed.

                                      Then on Monday morning there was a second blue chair beside his, empty, and it was still there on Tuesday, and on Wednesday, and it is there now.

                                      I sit in it sometimes, before school. We do not talk much. It turns out we do not have to.

                                      Why it scores well: the kindness is small and practical, not heroic; the birds are a specific, surprising detail; the reward is withheld and then delivered as an object rather than a speech; the final three sentences show the change instead of announcing it.

                                      Model 5 · Theme: A Misunderstanding

                                      What I Thought I Saw

                                      I saw Priya take the money. I was completely certain, which is the dangerous part.

                                      Our class had been collecting for the Children's Home for three weeks, and the tin sat on the shelf beside the door, growing heavier. On Thursday, during recess, I came back for my water bottle and saw Priya standing at the shelf with the tin in both hands and her back to the door.

                                      She turned. She saw me. And her face did something complicated that I read, instantly and confidently, as guilt.

                                      I told Wei Jie at lunch. I made him promise not to tell anyone, which is a promise nobody has ever kept in the history of our school. By Friday morning, four people had stopped sitting with her. By Friday afternoon, six had.

                                      Priya did not defend herself. She did not say anything at all, which I took as further proof.

                                      On Monday, Mrs Kaur asked the class to give her their full attention and announced that the collection had reached four hundred and twelve dollars — sixty of which had been added by one pupil who had asked to remain anonymous, from money she had saved for a bicycle.

                                      She did not say a name. She did not have to. I watched Priya study the surface of her desk with tremendous concentration, and I felt the floor tilt underneath me.

                                      I apologised that afternoon. She said it was fine. It was not fine, and we both knew it, and it took most of the following term before she sat next to me again by choice.

                                      I still see that moment at the shelf sometimes — her turning, her face. I know now that what I read as guilt was simply the look of somebody caught doing something private. I have never trusted my own certainty in quite the same way since.

                                      Why it scores well: the reader is misled alongside the narrator; the consequences escalate believably through gossip; the reveal is indirect — the teacher never names Priya; the apology is not accepted neatly, which is far more honest than instant forgiveness.

                                      Model 6 · Theme: Facing a Fear

                                      Two Metres

                                      The diving board at the sports complex is two metres high. I have measured it. Two metres is nothing. You could stack two of my father on top of each other and still have room.

                                      I had climbed the ladder four times that year and come back down four times, past whoever was waiting behind me, with my ears burning.

                                      The fifth time was the day of the swimming carnival, and there was a queue.

                                      I remember the metal rungs, cold and slightly gritty under my feet, and the way the board felt different from the ground — softer, as though it might not hold. I walked to the end. Below me the water had stopped looking like water and started looking like a floor.

                                      Behind me somebody said, "Are you going or not?"

                                      That, strangely, was the thing that helped. Not encouragement. Impatience. I thought: I am going to be standing here for the rest of my life. There is no version of this where I climb down again and feel all right about it.

                                      So I stepped off.

                                      It is not a brave story. I did not dive; I fell, badly, and my legs came apart in the air and the water hit the side of my thigh so hard that the mark was still there a week later. Somebody laughed. I came up coughing and my goggles were somewhere near the bottom of the pool.

                                      But I had gone.

                                      I went again eleven minutes later, and the second time was easier than the first by an amount I cannot describe to anyone who has not stood on that board. The fear had not disappeared. It had simply become something I had already survived once, which turns out to be a completely different thing.

                                      Why it scores well: the fear is small and specific — two metres, five attempts — which makes it credible; the turning point is deliberately unromantic; the dive itself goes badly, which raises the honesty; the last sentence names the insight precisely without preaching.

                                      Part 3 — Situational Writing Models

                                      Model A · Formal complaint

                                      Task: You bought a school bag from Bright Stationers two weeks ago. The zip broke after three days. The shop has not replied to your earlier message. Write to the manager. Include: what you bought and when, what is wrong, what you have already done, and what you would like the shop to do.

                                      To: manager@brightstationers.com.sg
Subject: Faulty school bag purchased on 2 August (receipt no. 40318)

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing about a school bag I purchased from your Sengkang branch on
2 August. The receipt number is 40318.

The bag was in good condition when I bought it, but the main zip came away
from the fabric after three days of ordinary use. I have not dropped the bag
or overloaded it, and the damage appears to be a fault in the stitching rather
than the result of misuse.

I sent a message through the contact form on your website on 8 August but have
not received a reply. As the bag is still within the one-month warranty printed
on the receipt, I would be grateful if you could either repair the zip or
exchange the bag for one of the same model.

I have kept the receipt and the original packaging, and I can bring the bag to
the store at any time that is convenient. I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,
Rachel Tan

                                      Marker's view: all four bullet points covered, each with one supporting detail. Consistently formal — no contractions, no exclamation marks. The request is specific ("repair or exchange") rather than vague ("do something about it"). It offers cooperation at the end, which reads as reasonable rather than aggressive.

                                      Model B · Report to the principal

                                      Task: You are the Primary 6 class chairperson. Write a report to your principal on the class's visit to a nursing home. Include: what the class did, how the residents responded, one problem faced, and one recommendation.

                                      Report on the Primary 6 Resilience Visit to Sunrise Nursing Home
By: Rachel Tan, Class Chairperson
Date: 14 August 2026

Purpose
This report describes our class's visit to Sunrise Nursing Home on 8 August and
offers a recommendation for future visits.

What we did
Thirty-two pupils visited the home from 9 a.m. to 12 noon. We were divided into
four groups. Two groups performed songs and a short skit in the common hall,
while the other two spent the morning talking with residents in the day room
and helping with a simple craft activity.

Response of the residents
The response was warmer than we had expected. Several residents joined in the
singing, and one gentleman taught a group of pupils a Hokkien song none of us
had heard before. Staff told us afterwards that the day room is usually quiet
on weekday mornings.

Problem faced
The main difficulty was language. Many residents speak mainly dialect, and most
of our pupils could not hold a conversation beyond a greeting. Some pupils
became discouraged and stopped trying after the first ten minutes.

Recommendation
I recommend that pupils learn ten to fifteen useful phrases in Hokkien, Teochew
and Cantonese before the next visit, and that each group includes at least one
pupil who speaks a dialect at home. This would help conversations begin more
easily and would prevent pupils from giving up early.

                                      Marker's view: headings, factual tone, no chatty language. Each bullet point gets its own section. The problem is stated honestly rather than smoothed over, and the recommendation follows directly from it — that link is where the marks are.

                                      Model C · Informal thank-you

                                      Task: Your neighbour looked after your rabbit for two weeks while your family was overseas. Write to thank her. Include: what she did, something she did especially well, how the rabbit is now, and an offer to return the favour.

                                      To: mrs.rahman@email.com
Subject: Thank you for looking after Momo!

Dear Mrs Rahman,

Thank you so much for taking care of Momo while we were away in Penang. Two
weeks is a long time to look after somebody else's rabbit, and we are all very
grateful.

What I appreciated most was that you kept to his feeding times exactly. Momo is
fussy about routine, and last year when he stayed at the pet shop he stopped
eating for two days. This time he was completely settled when we got back — and
I noticed you had even been giving him the coriander he loves.

He is doing very well. He has gone straight back to sleeping under the sofa and
chewing the corner of my school bag, so nothing has changed at all.

If you and Mr Rahman are ever away, we would be very happy to water your plants
or feed your cat. Please just let us know, even at short notice.

Thank you again.

Your neighbour,
Rachel

                                      Marker's view: warm but not gushing. The specific detail — the coriander, the pet shop last year — is what makes the thanks feel real rather than formulaic. The offer at the end is concrete, and the tone stays informal from greeting to sign-off.

                                      Part 4 — Twelve More Composition Prompts

                                      Plan each in six minutes, write in forty-four, self-edit in five. One a week.

                                      # Theme A possible situation
                                      1 Honesty Finding a phone with the owner's messages visible on the screen
                                      2 Perseverance Rebuilding something you damaged, without being asked
                                      3 Kindness Noticing someone eating alone every day
                                      4 A difficult decision Choosing between a competition and a family event
                                      5 Regret The last time you saw someone before they moved away
                                      6 Courage Correcting an adult who was wrong
                                      7 Teamwork The one member of the group who would not cooperate
                                      8 A misunderstanding A message read by the wrong person
                                      9 An unexpected discovery Something found while clearing out a cupboard
                                      10 Gratitude Realising years later what a parent gave up
                                      11 Responsibility Being left in charge of something valuable
                                      12 Facing a fear Speaking at assembly after a bad experience

                                      Model answers show one way of doing it well, not the only way. If your composition is different and works, it is not wrong.

                                      Document 09

                                      Listening Comprehension — Reader's Script, Paper 1

                                      For the adult reading aloud. Do not show this document to the child.

                                      A parent, sibling or friend reads each text aloud TWICE, at a normal speaking pace, with a short pause between the two readings. The child reads the question and the four options first, then listens. Do not show the child the script. 20 marks.

                                      Passage A — for questions 11–15

                                      Good afternoon, everyone. I'm speaking to you today about our upcoming overnight camp at Pulau Ubin. We leave from the school gate at seven in the morning on the fifteenth of June and return at four in the afternoon on the sixteenth. The ferry ride takes about fifteen minutes.

                                      You will need to bring one change of clothes, a torch, insect repellent and a refillable water bottle. Do not bring mobile phones, snacks or money. Any snacks brought will be collected and returned to you at the end of the camp, because food attracts wild boar to the campsite.

                                      We will be cycling on the first afternoon. Helmets will be provided, but if you have your own and prefer it, you are welcome to bring it. Pupils who cannot cycle should tell Mr Rahim by Friday so that we can arrange the nature walk group instead. There is no need to feel embarrassed about this — last year, eleven pupils joined the walk.

                                      Finally, the consent form must be signed by a parent and handed in by next Wednesday. Pupils without a signed form will not be allowed to board the ferry, even if they turn up on the day.

                                      Passage B — for questions 16–20

                                      Interviewer: Madam Siti, you have been running the hawker stall for thirty-two years. What has changed the most?

                                      Madam Siti: The customers. When I started, almost everyone who came was from this neighbourhood. I knew their names, I knew what they ordered. Now half my customers find me on their phones, from an app. They come once, take a photograph of the food, and I never see them again.

                                      Interviewer: Is that a bad thing?

                                      Madam Siti: Not bad. Different. The queue is longer, which my son is very happy about. But cooking for a stranger is not the same as cooking for a neighbour. When Mr Tan came every Tuesday for eighteen years, I knew he liked extra gravy and no chilli. I did not need to ask.

                                      Interviewer: Will your children take over the stall?

                                      Madam Siti: My daughter is a nurse. My son says he will, but he says it the way people say things to make their mother happy. I have told him not to. It is fourteen hours a day and your back never forgives you. If he wants to cook, he should cook because he cannot stop himself, not because I did it first.

                                      Right, everyone, gather round for the briefing on the community garden project.

                                      We'll be working on the plot behind Block 219 every Saturday morning for the next six weeks, from eight until ten. Eight is early, I know, but by half past ten in March it becomes genuinely unpleasant out there, and we'd rather finish than faint.

                                      Bring a hat and a refillable water bottle. Do not bring your own tools — we have enough, and the ones we have are the right ones. Several people last year turned up with garden forks that were far too heavy for the soil here, which is mostly clay.

                                      In the first two weeks we'll be clearing and preparing the beds. That's the least interesting part and, unfortunately, the most necessary. Planting begins in week three. We're growing kangkong, chilli, sweet potato leaves and, if the soil behaves, a small patch of ginger.

                                      One more thing. Whatever we harvest goes to the residents on the assistance list first. Anything left after that is shared among the volunteers. Please don't turn up in week six expecting to fill a bag — that is not what this is for.

                                      Passage B — for questions 16–20

                                      Interviewer: You've been a school crossing warden for twenty-six years. Do you know the children by name?

                                      Mr Loke: Most of them. Not all. There are about four hundred at that school and they change every six years, so I gave up trying to know all of them a long time ago. But I know the regulars. I know who runs and who dawdles. I know which ones will step off the kerb without looking, and I position myself accordingly.

                                      Interviewer: Has anything ever gone badly wrong?

                                      Mr Loke: Once. Nineteen years ago. A car came through much faster than it should have and I had to pull a boy back by his bag. He was fine. I was not fine, for about a month. I still think about it when a car comes round that bend too quickly, which is most mornings.

                                      Interviewer: Have you ever thought of stopping?

                                      Mr Loke: Every February, when it rains for three weeks. Then it stops raining. And a child I have never spoken to says good morning to me because his older sister used to, and I think, well, another year.

                                      Interviewer: What would you want people to understand about the job?

                                      Mr Loke: That it is not about the sign. Anybody can hold a sign. It is about knowing, on a particular Tuesday, that the boy in the blue cap has had a bad morning and is not paying attention.

                                      Passage A — for questions 11–15

                                      Good afternoon. I'm here to explain how the Primary Six buddy reading programme will work this year, because it is a little different from last year.

                                      Each of you will be paired with a Primary One pupil. You will meet twice a week, on Tuesday and Thursday, during the second half of recess. That gives you about fifteen minutes each session. Fifteen minutes does not sound long, and it isn't, which is why preparation matters.

                                      Here is the change. Last year you chose the books. This year your buddy chooses, from a shelf of about sixty titles in the library corner. Some of you will find this frustrating. You may end up reading the same book about a truck eleven times. That is normal, and it is not a failure. Young children reread because rereading is how they build confidence.

                                      Your job is not to correct every mistake. If your buddy says a word wrongly but the sentence still makes sense, let it go. If the sentence stops making sense, wait three seconds, then help. Three seconds feels like a very long time. Count it in your head.

                                      Finally, keep the record card. One line per session: the title, and one thing your buddy did well. Not what they got wrong. One thing they did well. Hand it in at the end of term.

                                      Passage B — for questions 16–20

                                      Interviewer: You've repaired shoes on this street for forty-one years. Is the trade dying?

                                      Mr Teo: Everybody asks me that. The honest answer is that it changed, and then it changed back a little.

                                      Interviewer: Changed back?

                                      Mr Teo: In the nineties, nobody repaired anything. A shoe broke, you bought another shoe. My busiest years were the sixties and seventies, and then it went very quiet for about twenty years. I nearly closed twice.

                                      Interviewer: And now?

                                      Mr Teo: Now I have young customers. Twenty-five, thirty years old. They bring me expensive boots and they want them to last. Some of them ask me to teach them. I have taught four people, and three of them gave up within a month, which is about the usual rate.

                                      Interviewer: Why do they give up?

                                      Mr Teo: Because they expect to be good at it. Nobody is good at it. I was not good at it for six years. My teacher let me resole practice shoes that were going to be thrown away anyway, and he never once told me I was doing well, because I was not.

                                      Interviewer: That sounds harsh.

                                      Mr Teo: It was accurate. There is a difference. When I finally did something properly he said one word, and I have remembered that word for forty years. If he had said it every week it would have been worth nothing.

                                      Passage A — for questions 11–15

                                      Right, everyone, settle down. This is the briefing for the Primary Five science trip to the wetland reserve.

                                      We leave from the school gate at eight sharp on Thursday. The coach will not wait. If you are late, your parents will have to bring you, and the reserve is forty minutes away by car.

                                      Wear closed shoes. Not sandals, not slippers — closed shoes. Some of the boardwalk is wet and there are mangrove roots underneath it. Bring a hat, a refillable water bottle and your field notebook.

                                      Do not bring food. This is not about tidiness. The reserve has a resident population of long-tailed macaques, and a monkey that has been fed once will approach the next group of children it sees. Last year a pupil from another school had a bag taken straight off her shoulder.

                                      At the reserve you will be in groups of six with one parent volunteer each. Stay with your group. If you become separated, do not go looking — stop where you are and wait, and somebody will come back for you within a few minutes.

                                      Finally, your notebooks. You are recording three things at each of the four stations: what you can see, what you can hear, and one question you would like answered. The questions are the part I care about most. There are no marks for neat handwriting.

                                      Passage B — for questions 16–20

                                      Interviewer: You have been a swimming coach for thirty-four years. What have you changed your mind about?

                                      Coach Devi: Quite a lot. When I started, I believed that the child who wanted it most would win. I was completely wrong.

                                      Interviewer: Wrong how?

                                      Coach Devi: Wanting it is not rare. Nearly every child in that pool at six in the morning wants it. What is rare is being able to lose a race on Saturday and still be in the water on Monday. That is the thing I cannot teach, and it is the thing that decides almost everything.

                                      Interviewer: Can you spot it early?

                                      Coach Devi: Not from the swimming. I watch what happens in the ten minutes after a bad race. Some of them want to be told it was not their fault. A few go and look at the board to see the actual time. Those are the ones.

                                      Interviewer: What do you say to a child who has just swum badly?

                                      Coach Devi: As little as possible on the day. They are not able to hear it. I tell them one specific thing that was good, because there is always one, and then I leave them alone. We talk properly on Monday.

                                      Interviewer: And the parents?

                                      Coach Devi: The parents are usually harder than the children. A parent who says nothing in the car is worth more than any coach. I have told a great many of them that, and about half of them have listened.

                                      Document 10

                                      Oral Practice — Paper 4 (30 marks)

                                      Reading Aloud is worth 10 marks and Stimulus-based Conversation 20. Both are practised out loud. Reading silently will not prepare a child for either.

                                      Part 1 — Reading Aloud

                                      How to use these: give the child five minutes with the passage. They should read it silently once for meaning, mark the pauses, circle difficult words, and underline the words to stress. Then they read it aloud to you. Read the notes yourself first — they list what to listen for.

                                      Passage 1 · P4 and above

                                      Every morning before school, my grandfather waters the plants along our corridor. There are eleven pots altogether, and he knows exactly how much water each one needs. The chilli plant, he says, is the fussiest of the lot. If you give it too much, the leaves turn yellow within a week. Last month, he taught me how to check the soil with my finger before pouring. I get it wrong about half the time, but he never seems to mind. He simply says that plants are patient teachers, and that they will wait for me to learn.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • Pause slightly at every comma; take a full breath at each full stop.
                                      • Stress the numbers: eleven pots, half the time.
                                      • Watch the final consonants: waters, needs, leaves, plants, teachers.
                                      • 'Fussiest' has three syllables — FUSS-i-est, not 'fussest'.
                                      • Let your voice fall on the last sentence. It is the point of the passage.

                                      Passage 2 · P5 and above

                                      The old cinema on the corner closed down last year. For as long as I can remember, its red sign had glowed above the traffic, spelling out the name of whatever film was showing that week. My mother watched her first film there when she was nine. She says the seats squeaked terribly and the air conditioning was far too cold, and that she loved every minute of it. Now the building is boarded up, and somebody has stuck a notice on the door announcing that a supermarket will open in its place. My mother walked past it with me last Sunday. She did not say anything at all, which told me more than any complaint would have.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • 'Cinema' — CIN-e-ma, three syllables.
                                      • Slow down for the list in sentence four; the two 'and's need a small pause before each.
                                      • Stress 'nine' — the age matters to the story.
                                      • 'Boarded up' — sound the d clearly.
                                      • The last sentence should be read slowly and quietly. It carries the feeling.

                                      Passage 3 · P6 and above

                                      Singapore's first public library opened in 1845 with just a few hundred volumes, most of them donated. Today the network holds more than eight million items and lends out over thirty million a year. What has changed is not only the size of the collection but the purpose of the building itself. A library is no longer only a place to borrow books. It is a place where students revise for examinations, where retirees read newspapers in five languages, and where a child might attend her first storytelling session. The shelves matter, of course. But increasingly, what matters more is the space between them.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • Read the numbers clearly and slightly slower: eighteen forty-five, eight million, thirty million.
                                      • 'Volumes' here means books — read it with confidence, not hesitation.
                                      • The three 'where' clauses form a list. Keep the same rhythm for each and pause briefly between them.
                                      • Stress 'not only' and 'but'.
                                      • Final sentence: slight pause after 'But increasingly'. Land firmly on 'between them'.

                                      Passage 4 · P6 and above

                                      There is a particular sound a badminton shuttle makes when it is struck cleanly, and anybody who has played the game will recognise it at once. It is not loud. It is a short, dry click, quite unlike the dull thud of a mishit. My coach used to say that she could mark our technique with her eyes closed, simply by listening from the far end of the hall. At the time I assumed she was exaggerating. Years later, standing at the back of a school hall during a training session, I found that I could do exactly the same thing.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • 'Shuttle', 'struck', 'cleanly' — crisp consonant clusters, do not rush them.
                                      • 'A short, dry click' — pause at each comma. The rhythm imitates the sound.
                                      • Contrast 'click' with 'dull thud' in your tone: light, then heavy.
                                      • 'Exaggerating' — five syllables, eg-ZAJ-er-ay-ting.
                                      • The last sentence is a quiet realisation. Do not raise your voice for it.

                                      Passage 5 · P4 and above

                                      The lift in our block has been broken twice this month. The first time, it stopped between the fourth and fifth floors with three people inside, including Mrs Osman from the ninth floor. She told us afterwards that she had not been frightened at all, which nobody believed, and that she had spent the twenty minutes teaching the other two passengers a card game. The engineers say the motor is old and needs replacing. Until then, we take the stairs and grumble, and Mrs Osman takes the stairs and does not.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • 'Osman' — OSS-man, stress the first syllable.
                                      • Pause at each comma in the long third sentence; it has three parts.
                                      • Stress 'twice', 'three' and 'twenty' — the numbers carry the story.
                                      • Final consonants: stopped, believed, replacing, grumble.
                                      • The last sentence is the joke. Slow down slightly and let the contrast land.

                                      Passage 6 · P5 and above

                                      Every Thursday my grandmother cooks for eleven people, although only four of us live in the house. The rest of the food is packed into containers and delivered, by me, to three flats on our floor. She has been doing this since before I was born and has never once described it as charity. When I asked her why she cooks so much, she looked at me as though I had asked why she breathes, and said that a pot is a pot and the difference between four and eleven is one more handful of rice.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • 'Although' — do not swallow the first syllable.
                                      • Pause after 'delivered, by me,' — the phrase is deliberately interrupted.
                                      • Stress 'eleven' and 'four' both times; the numbers are the point.
                                      • 'Charity' — CHA-ri-ty, three syllables.
                                      • The final sentence is long. Breathe after 'breathes' and finish steadily.

                                      Passage 7 · P6 and above

                                      The Singapore Botanic Gardens received its UNESCO listing in 2015, more than a century and a half after it was first laid out. What strikes most visitors is not the rarest orchid or the tallest tree, but the ordinary Saturday use of the place: families spreading mats on the lawn, students revising under the rain trees, an elderly couple walking the same loop they have walked for decades. A garden that is only admired becomes a museum. A garden that is used becomes part of a city's daily life, and that, arguably, is the harder thing to achieve.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • 'UNESCO' — read it as a word, you-NESS-ko, not letter by letter.
                                      • '2015' — twenty fifteen.
                                      • The list in the middle has three items. Keep the same rhythm and pause between them.
                                      • Contrast the two short sentences near the end: drop your voice slightly on 'museum', lift it on 'daily life'.
                                      • 'Arguably' — AR-gyoo-ably, four syllables. Do not rush it.

                                      Passage 8 · P6 and above

                                      There is a particular silence in a hall thirty seconds before a performance begins. It is not the absence of sound — somebody is always coughing, a chair always creaks — but the absence of anybody wanting to make any. I have felt it from both sides now, as a performer waiting in the wings and as a parent sitting eleven rows back, and I could not honestly tell you which is worse. What I do know is that the silence ends the instant the first note is played, and that everyone in the room, without exception, breathes out.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • 'Particular' — four syllables, par-TIC-u-lar.
                                      • The dashes mark an interruption. Drop your pitch slightly for 'somebody is always coughing, a chair always creaks' and come back up.
                                      • Stress 'both' in 'from both sides now'.
                                      • 'Without exception' — separate the two words clearly; do not run them together.
                                      • End on 'breathes out' gently. It is a quiet realisation, not an announcement.

                                      Passage 9 · P4 and above

                                      My father has kept the same wooden toolbox for twenty-three years. The handle is worn smooth, one hinge is held on with wire, and inside there is a jumble of screwdrivers, a hammer with a chipped head and a tin of nails that he refuses to throw away. Last month my mother bought him a new plastic toolbox for his birthday, with neat compartments and a lock. He thanked her warmly, admired it for a while, and then carried it into the store room. The old one is still by the door, where he can reach it.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • 'twenty-three' — keep both parts clear; do not swallow the 'three'.
                                      • The list in the second sentence has four items. Pause slightly at each comma so the list can be heard.
                                      • Final consonants: kept, worn, chipped, refuses, thanked, admired, carried.
                                      • Stress 'new' in the third sentence and 'old' in the last one — the contrast is the point of the passage.
                                      • The last sentence is the punchline. Slow down and let 'where he can reach it' land.

                                      Passage 10 · P5 and above

                                      Hawker centres were not built for food. They were built for order. In the nineteen sixties, thousands of street hawkers cooked over open fires along the five-foot ways of Singapore, and the government wanted them licensed, plumbed and inspected. So it put up halls with concrete floors and numbered stalls, and moved everybody indoors. Nobody at the time imagined that these plain buildings would one day be listed by UNESCO, or that queues would form at seven in the morning for a bowl of noodles cooked by a man in his eighties who has never changed his recipe.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • Open with a firm, almost flat delivery on the first two sentences — they are a surprising claim and work best when stated plainly.
                                      • 'nineteen sixties', 'five-foot ways', 'UNESCO' — say each of these slowly; they are the hard ones.
                                      • 'licensed, plumbed and inspected' — three past participles in a row. Sound the final -ed on each.
                                      • Pause after 'So it put up halls with concrete floors and numbered stalls,' before 'and moved everybody indoors'.
                                      • Lift your voice on 'never changed his recipe' at the end — it carries the admiration.

                                      Passage 11 · P6 and above

                                      The first person to swim across the Straits of Johor for charity did it in nineteen eighty-two, and she was fifty-six years old. She had learnt to swim at the age of forty-nine, in a public pool, from a teacher who charged her nothing. When reporters asked what the hardest part had been, they expected her to say the current, or the cold, or the jellyfish. She said it was the first morning at the pool, standing at the shallow end in a borrowed swimming costume while children half her height swam past her. Everything after that, she said, was merely water.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • Say 'nineteen eighty-two' and 'fifty-six' distinctly — the two numbers are the hook of the passage.
                                      • 'the current, or the cold, or the jellyfish' — a list of three. Give each one equal weight and pause before the last.
                                      • The fourth sentence is long. Breathe after 'shallow end' and again after 'costume'.
                                      • Stress 'first morning' — it answers the reporters' question and overturns their expectation.
                                      • 'was merely water' — drop your voice and slow right down. Do not rush the final three words.

                                      Passage 12 · P6 and above

                                      Consider the humble queue. It is one of the few things in public life that works entirely on agreement: there is no law compelling you to stand behind the person who arrived before you, and yet almost everybody does. Watch what happens when somebody steps in near the front. Nobody shouts. Instead there is a ripple of glances, a shifting of bags, a pointed clearing of the throat, and very often the offender retreats without a word being spoken to them. It is a remarkably efficient system, held together by nothing more solid than the fear of being looked at.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • Open conversationally on 'Consider the humble queue' — you are inviting the listener to notice something.
                                      • 'compelling', 'offender', 'remarkably', 'efficient' — practise these four aloud before you begin.
                                      • The list in the fourth sentence builds: glances, bags, throat. Let each one get slightly more emphasis.
                                      • Pause after 'Nobody shouts.' It is a short sentence on purpose, and the pause does the work.
                                      • Land firmly on 'the fear of being looked at' — this is the joke and the point at the same time.

                                      Passage 13 · P3 and above

                                      Our class has a tortoise called Bruce. He is older than everybody in the room, including Mrs Ong. He moves so slowly that we once thought he had stopped moving altogether, and Faizal nearly cried. Then Bruce turned his head, very slightly, and looked at us as though we had been extremely rude. He eats cabbage on Thursdays, sleeps most of the rest of the week, and has never once done anything exciting. He is the most popular member of our class.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • 'Bruce' — one clear syllable. Do not rush past it; the name is part of the joke.
                                      • Pause at the commas in the fifth sentence (“He eats cabbage on Thursdays…”). It has three parts.
                                      • Final consonants: moves, stopped, turned, looked, eats, sleeps.
                                      • Stress 'never once' and 'most popular' — the contrast is the point of the passage.
                                      • Slow down for the last sentence and let it land. Do not smile it away.

                                      Passage 14 · P4 and above

                                      There is a bird in Singapore that can copy almost any sound it hears. The common mynah has been recorded imitating car alarms, mobile phone ringtones and, in one case, the whistle a man used to call his dog. The dog, it is said, came running three times before anybody worked out what was happening. Scientists think mynahs copy sounds to mark out territory. Whatever the reason, it means that some of the noises you hear outside your window in the morning were not made by a machine at all.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • 'mynah' — MY-na. Say it clearly the first time; it is the key word.
                                      • The list in the second sentence has three items. Pause before 'and, in one case'.
                                      • Final consonants: recorded, imitating, worked, mark, machine.
                                      • Stress 'three times' — it is the funny detail.
                                      • The last sentence is a mild surprise. Slow slightly on 'not made by a machine at all'.

                                      Passage 15 · P4 and above

                                      My mother keeps a list on the fridge of everything she has ever lent to a neighbour. There are fourteen items on it. Next to eleven of them she has written a date, a name and a small tick. Next to the other three she has written a date and a name and nothing else, and she has been writing nothing else beside those three for about six years. She says she is not annoyed. She says she keeps the list only so that she remembers what she owns. Nobody in our family believes this, and nobody says so.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • Numbers carry this passage: 'fourteen', 'eleven', 'three', 'six years'. Say each one clearly.
                                      • Pause after 'a date, a name and a small tick' before the next sentence.
                                      • Do not rush 'and she has been writing nothing else beside those three for about six years'. Breathe after 'three'.
                                      • The two sentences beginning 'She says' should sound flat and innocent. That is where the humour is.
                                      • Land firmly on the last sentence, and pause a beat before 'and nobody says so'.

                                      Passage 16 · P5 and above

                                      The lift in my grandmother's block has a mirror on the back wall, and for about a year it was cracked right across the middle. Everybody complained. Somebody wrote to the town council twice. Then one Tuesday it was replaced, and within a week three different neighbours had told my grandmother that the lift felt bigger. It is exactly the same lift. Nothing about it changed except that you can now see the whole of yourself in it, which I find a strange and rather cheerful thing to know about people.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • 'grandmother's' — sound the possessive s; do not let it run into 'block'.
                                      • Pause at each full stop in the short middle sentences. They are short on purpose.
                                      • Final consonants: cracked, complained, replaced, changed.
                                      • Stress 'exactly the same lift' — the contrast is the whole point of the passage.
                                      • Slow down for the last clause and let 'cheerful' sound warm rather than clever.

                                      Passage 17 · P5 and above

                                      A hawker in Chinatown has sold the same three dishes for thirty-one years and has never put a photograph on his stall. When a food blogger asked him why, he said that a photograph tells you what a dish looks like, which is the least important thing about it. He then refused to be photographed himself. The queue that morning was eleven people long, and nobody in it was holding a phone up, which may have been the point he was making all along.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • 'thirty-one' — keep both parts clear.
                                      • The second sentence is long. Breathe after 'why', and again after 'looks like'.
                                      • Final consonants: sold, asked, refused, holding.
                                      • Stress 'least important' — it is the surprising part of what he says.
                                      • The last clause is dry. Do not over-emphasise it; let it sit.

                                      Passage 18 · P6 and above

                                      There is a kind of silence peculiar to a school hall in the minute before a performance begins. It is not quiet — four hundred people cannot be quiet — but it is attentive, which is a different thing altogether. Chairs stop scraping. Somebody's grandmother is still unwrapping a sweet and everybody can hear her doing it. Then the lights drop, and the sound that follows is the only applause of the evening that is given for nothing at all, before a single note has been played.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • 'peculiar' — pe-CUL-iar, three syllables, stress the second.
                                      • The dashes in the second sentence are pauses. Lift your voice slightly inside them.
                                      • Final consonants: begins, scraping, unwrapping, played.
                                      • 'the only applause of the evening that is given for nothing at all' — do not rush this; it is the idea the whole passage is built towards.
                                      • End quietly. The last five words should be almost spoken rather than read.

                                      Passage 19 · P3 and above

                                      My little brother collects bus tickets. He has a shoebox full of them under his bed, and he knows where every single one came from. Last week he found an old ticket on the pavement outside our block. It was wet and the printing had gone, so nobody could tell which bus it was from. He kept it anyway. He says it is the most interesting one, because it is the only one that is a mystery.

                                      Listen for:

                                      • Short, simple sentences. Pause fully at each full stop and do not run them together.
                                      • 'shoebox' — one word, two clear parts.
                                      • Final consonants: collects, knows, found, kept, says.
                                      • Stress 'anyway' — it is the surprise in the story.
                                      • Smile slightly on the last sentence. It is meant to be funny and fond.

                                      Part 2 — Stimulus-based Conversation

                                      Three questions follow each stimulus. The child looks at the stimulus for a short while, then answers aloud. Model answers are given — they are one good version, not the only one. What matters is the shape: Point, Elaborate, Example, Link.

                                      The single most common mistake is a one-sentence answer. Four to six sentences is the target for every question.

                                      Screen time · P5 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: HEALTH PROMOTION BOARD How much is too much? 4h 12m average daily screen time, Singapore children aged 7–12 2h recommended daily limit outside schoolwork Children who spend more than three hours a day on screens are more likely to report poor sleep, eye strain and difficulty concentrating in class. Try this: no screens in the bedroom · a device-free dinner table · one screen-free day each week

                                      Q1. What are your thoughts on the information in this poster?

                                      I find the difference between the two figures quite striking. The poster says children my age spend over four hours a day on screens, which is double the recommended limit of two hours. Personally, I think this is a fair reflection of what I see around me — during the holidays, several of my classmates spend most of the afternoon gaming or watching videos. What worries me most is the point about concentration, because that affects schoolwork without anyone noticing the cause. I do think the poster is a little simplistic, though, since not all screen time is the same: doing research for a project is different from scrolling through videos.

                                      Q2. Tell me about a time when you spent too long on a screen. What happened?

                                      During the December holidays last year, I started watching a series on a Saturday afternoon and did not stop until nearly midnight. I had told myself I would watch two episodes. The next morning I woke up at eleven with a headache, and I felt irritable for most of the day. Worse, I had promised my mother I would help her clear the storeroom that morning, and I was in no state to do it. She did not scold me, which somehow made it worse. Since then I have started setting an alarm before I begin watching anything, which helps more than I expected.

                                      Q3. Do you think schools should teach pupils about managing screen time?

                                      Yes, I believe they should, and I would go further than a single assembly talk. This is because most of us know that too much screen time is bad for us, but knowing is not the difficulty — managing the habit is. For instance, my school held a talk last year with very similar statistics to this poster, and nothing changed afterwards. What might work better is a practical activity, such as tracking our own usage for a week and then discussing the results in class, because seeing your own number is far more convincing than seeing an average. Overall, I think schools are the right place for this, provided the lesson is practical rather than just informative.

                                      Neighbourhood volunteering · P6 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: SENGKANG RESIDENTS' NETWORK Two hours. One Saturday. Your block. We are looking for 40 volunteers aged 10 and above. Meal delivery Bring hot meals to residents who cannot leave their flats. Reading buddies Read with children at the study corner. Garden plot Water, weed and harvest the community garden. Tech help Help older residents use their phones. Last year, 12 of our 40 volunteers came back for a second session. We would like that number to be higher. Tell us what would make you return.

                                      Q1. Which of these activities would you choose, and why?

                                      I would choose the reading buddies role. This is because I have a younger cousin whom I read with most weekends, so I already have some idea of how to keep a child interested when the book gets difficult. I also think it is the role where a primary school pupil can genuinely be useful rather than just present — a younger child may find it easier to read aloud to someone close to their own age than to an adult. Tech help appeals to me too, but I suspect I would be less patient than the job requires.

                                      Q2. The poster says only 12 out of 40 volunteers came back. Why do you think that is?

                                      I think there are a few reasons. Firstly, people often sign up for a one-off event without intending it to become a commitment, especially if a school or a parent encouraged them. Secondly, if volunteers are not told what difference they made, the experience can feel forgettable. For instance, when my class collected donations last year, we never found out what happened to the money, and I noticed that fewer people volunteered the second time. Finally, two hours on a Saturday competes with tuition and family time, which is a real obstacle for children my age. I would suggest the organisers send a short follow-up message telling volunteers exactly what their work achieved.

                                      Q3. Some people say children are too young to volunteer. What do you think?

                                      I disagree, although I understand the concern. The worry is presumably that children may get in the way or need supervising themselves, and for some tasks that is fair — I would not expect a ten-year-old to deliver meals alone to a stranger's flat. However, there are many roles where being young is actually an advantage. Reading with a small child is one. Helping an elderly resident with a phone is another, because most of us grew up with these devices and can explain them simply. In my view the question is not whether children are too young, but whether the task has been matched properly to the volunteer.

                                      Food waste at the school canteen · P6 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: RIVERBANK PRIMARY · CANTEEN AUDIT What ends up in the bin Food thrown away per week, by stall Rice & noodles Mixed veg rice Drinks stall Snacks 48 kg 32 kg 8 kg 5 kg Most of the waste is rice left on plates, not unsold food. Pupils were asked why. The two most common answers were “the portion was too big” and “I didn't have time to finish” .
