                                      Q1. What does this audit tell you about food waste in your canteen?

                                      The chart shows that the rice and noodle stall throws away by far the most, at forty-eight kilograms a week, which is nearly ten times the snack stall. What I find most revealing is the note underneath: the waste is mainly rice left on plates rather than food that went unsold. That means the problem is not the stallholders ordering too much, but what happens after the food is served. The two reasons pupils gave — portions being too large and not having enough time — suggest this is more about how recess is organised than about pupils being careless.

                                      Q2. Have you ever thrown away food at school? Why?

                                      Yes, more often than I would like to admit. Last term I frequently left half my rice, mostly because recess is only twenty-five minutes and I would spend the first ten queueing. By the time I sat down I had about eight minutes to eat, and if my friends finished first I would give up and follow them out. Looking back, the food itself was fine — I simply did not allow myself time. Since then I have started going to the shorter queue even when it is not my favourite stall, which has helped.

                                      Q3. What one change would you suggest to reduce this waste?

                                      I would suggest offering a smaller rice portion at a slightly lower price, and making pupils choose the size when they order. This is because the audit points directly at portion size as one of the two main reasons, and it is the easier of the two to fix — lengthening recess would need the whole timetable to change. A smaller option also rewards pupils for choosing it, rather than lecturing them. For instance, my cousin's school introduced a 'small rice' option last year and the canteen reported noticeably less waste within a month. Overall, I think practical changes work better than posters telling us not to waste food.

                                      Learning a musical instrument · P5 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: NATIONAL ARTS COUNCIL · YOUTH SURVEY Why children stop playing Too little time Practice is boring Not improving Exam pressure 63% 48% 37% 30% Of children who began an instrument before age ten, 54% had stopped by age fourteen. Among those who continued, the most common reason given was “I play with other people.”

                                      Q1. What do you think of the information in this survey?

                                      What surprises me most is that more than half of the children who start an instrument have given up by fourteen. I would have guessed it was high, but not that high. Looking at the reasons, I notice that the top two — not enough time and practice being boring — are really about how practice feels day to day, rather than about the instrument itself. I also think the last line is the most interesting part of the whole survey: the children who kept going said it was because they played with other people. That suggests the problem may be less about discipline and more about doing it alone in a room.

                                      Q2. Tell me about something you learnt that was difficult at first.

                                      I started learning the guzheng in Primary Three and I very nearly stopped in the first year. The finger picks kept slipping and my playing sounded nothing like my teacher's, which was discouraging. What changed was joining the school ensemble in Primary Four. Suddenly I was one part of a sound rather than the whole of it, and even when my own part was imperfect the music still worked. I practised more after that, not because anyone told me to, but because I did not want to be the one letting the group down. I have been playing for four years now.

                                      Q3. Should every child be required to learn an instrument in school?

                                      I agree to a certain extent, though I would not make it compulsory for years on end. This is because there is real value in every child discovering whether they enjoy music, and many would never find out otherwise, particularly if instruments are expensive at home. However, forcing a child to continue for six years when they clearly dislike it seems likely to produce exactly the outcome this survey describes. What I would suggest is a compulsory year of group music in lower primary, followed by a genuine choice. That way everyone gets the chance, and the ones who continue are continuing because they want to, which the survey suggests is what makes people stay.

                                      Helping elderly neighbours · P6 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: SILVER GENERATION OFFICE One in four lives alone Residents aged 65 and above in our estate 26% live alone 41% say they speak to no one on a typical weekday 12% have difficulty using a smartphone for appointments 3 in 5 say they would rather not be visited by strangers The office is recruiting volunteers for weekly check-ins. Training is provided. Volunteers must be 13 or above, or accompanied by an adult.

                                      Q1. Which figure on this poster stands out most to you, and why?

                                      The one that strikes me is that forty-one per cent say they speak to no one on a typical weekday. The figure about living alone is sad but expected; going a whole day without a single conversation is something I find much harder to imagine. What makes it more difficult is the last box, which says three in five would rather not be visited by strangers. So the people who most need company are also the ones least likely to accept it from someone they do not know. That seems to me the real problem the poster is pointing at, even though it does not say so directly.

                                      Q2. Have you ever helped an older person? What happened?

                                      My grandmother's neighbour, Mr Chia, is eighty-one and lives by himself two doors down. Last year his phone stopped receiving his clinic appointment reminders and he missed one, which upset him a great deal. I spent about half an hour with him going through the settings, and then I wrote the steps out on a piece of card in large handwriting and taped it inside his cupboard door. What I learnt was that the writing-down part mattered more than the fixing part, because he could then do it himself the next time. He has not needed to ask me again.

                                      Q3. What could a school do to help elderly residents nearby?

                                      I think a school is actually well placed to help, but it has to be done carefully given that most elderly residents do not want strangers at the door. My suggestion would be a regular activity at the community centre rather than home visits — for example, a fortnightly session where pupils help with phones and appointment apps, with the same pupils returning each time. Familiarity is the key point, because after three or four sessions we would no longer be strangers. I would also keep it practical rather than purely social, since asking for help with a phone feels easier for many people than admitting to being lonely.

                                      Reading for pleasure · P6 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: NATIONAL LIBRARY BOARD · READING HABITS Minutes read per day, age 10–12 Excluding schoolwork 2015 2020 2025 34 min 22 min 15 min Children who read for pleasure at least twenty minutes a day scored, on average, nine months ahead in reading age compared with those who read under five minutes. The most common reason given for not reading: “I can’t find a book I like.”

                                      Q1. What does this chart tell you, and does it worry you?

                                      The chart shows that daily reading for pleasure has fallen from thirty-four minutes in 2015 to fifteen in 2025, so it has dropped by more than half in ten years. It does concern me, mainly because of the second figure underneath: children who read at least twenty minutes a day are around nine months ahead in reading age. That means the gap is not only about enjoyment but about ability. What I find slightly more hopeful is the last line, because 'I can't find a book I like' is a solvable problem, unlike simply not wanting to read at all.

                                      Q2. What do you read, and how did you find it?

                                      I mostly read mysteries and non-fiction about animals. I came to mysteries entirely by accident — my aunt gave me a detective novel two Christmases ago that I assumed I would hate, and I finished it in three days. Since then I have read eleven books in the same series. What I have noticed is that I almost never find books by browsing; I find them because somebody who knows me hands me one. The library has thousands of books and I usually leave empty-handed, but a single recommendation from a friend works almost every time.

                                      Q3. How would you get more children in your school reading?

                                      I would focus on the reason the poster gives, which is that children cannot find a book they like. Telling people to read more does not solve that. My suggestion would be a shelf at the back of each classroom where pupils leave a book they loved with a handwritten note explaining why, signed with their name. This would work because a recommendation from someone in your own class carries far more weight than a poster or a teacher's list. For instance, everyone in my class read the same graphic novel last year purely because one boy would not stop talking about it. Overall, I think the answer is matching children to books, not asking them to try harder.

                                      Sleep and school start times · P5 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: HEALTH PROMOTION BOARD · PUPIL SURVEY How much sleep do we actually get? Primary 1–2 Primary 3–4 Primary 5–6 Secondary 1–2 9h 24m 8h 54m 8h 06m 7h 12m Doctors recommend 9 to 11 hours a night for children aged 6 to 13. Pupils in the survey who slept fewer than 8 hours were twice as likely to report falling asleep in class. The most common reason given for a late bedtime was not homework but screens in the bedroom .

                                      Q1. What do you find most interesting about the information in this survey?

                                      The part I find most interesting is that the amount of sleep drops steadily as pupils get older, when you might expect the opposite, because older children have more homework but are also better at organising themselves. What struck me even more was the reason given at the bottom. I had assumed homework was the main cause of late bedtimes, so learning that screens in the bedroom mattered more than homework was surprising. It suggests the problem is not that children have too much to do, but that we find it very hard to stop once we have started watching something.

                                      Q2. Tell me about your own bedtime routine. Is it something you would change?

                                      On school nights I am supposed to be in bed by half past nine, and most of the time I am. What actually happens is that I lie there with my tablet for another twenty minutes, so I fall asleep closer to ten. I would change one thing: I would leave the tablet charging in the living room instead of on my bedside table. My mother suggested that months ago and I resisted, but looking at this survey I can see she was right. The nights I sleep best are the ones when I have left it outside, usually because I forgot it there.

                                      Q3. Some people say primary schools should start later in the morning. What do you think?

                                      I agree to a certain extent, though I do not think it would solve the problem on its own. Starting at eight instead of half past seven would certainly help pupils who travel a long way, because some of my classmates leave home before six. However, I suspect that many children would simply sleep later rather than sleep longer, since the real cause according to this survey is what happens at bedtime, not what happens in the morning. What I would suggest instead is a later start twice a week, perhaps on the two days with the heaviest lessons, together with a rule that phones and tablets are charged outside the bedroom. That way we would be tackling both ends of the night rather than just one.

                                      Learning to cook at home · P4 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: SCHOOL NEWSLETTER · HOME SKILLS Can you cook one meal on your own? Boil an egg Cook rice Fry an egg Cook a vegetable dish 71% 54% 38% 19% In a survey of 480 Primary 4 to 6 pupils, 62% said they had never cooked anything using a stove. The most common thing pupils could prepare without help was instant noodles. Of the pupils who cooked regularly at home, almost all said they had learnt from a grandparent , not from a lesson or a video.

                                      Q1. What can you tell me about the information in this newsletter?

                                      The newsletter shows that most pupils in my level cannot cook very much. More than seven in ten can boil an egg, but fewer than two in ten can cook a vegetable dish, which needs cutting, heating oil and judging when something is done. I also noticed that nearly two thirds have never used a stove at all. The last sentence is the one I keep thinking about, though. The pupils who can cook learnt it from a grandparent rather than from a video, which tells me this is a skill that gets passed on by standing next to someone, not by watching a screen.

                                      Q2. Have you ever helped to prepare a meal? Tell me what happened.

                                      Yes, I have. Last year my mother taught me to make tomato and egg, which is the first dish she ever learnt herself. The first time, I put the eggs in before the pan was hot enough and they turned into a grey lump that stuck to the bottom. She made me scrub the pan and then let me try again the same evening, which I did not enjoy at the time. Now I can make it properly and I cook it on Saturdays when my parents are both working. My younger brother says it is better than my mother's, but he says that only when she is in the room.

                                      Q3. Do you think cooking should be taught in primary school? Why?

                                      I strongly believe it should, because cooking is one of the few subjects that every single person will use for the rest of their life, whatever job they end up doing. Knowing how to cook simple food also makes people healthier, since someone who can prepare a vegetable dish in fifteen minutes is far less likely to buy fried food every day. I know that schools worry about safety with stoves and knives, and that is a fair concern, so I would begin with dishes that need no heat at all in the lower primary levels, such as sandwiches and salads, and move on to the stove only in Primary 5 and 6 in small groups. Even a single term of lessons would mean that nobody leaves primary school able to cook only instant noodles.

                                      Litter in the neighbourhood · P6 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: TOWN COUNCIL · CLEANLINESS REPORT Who actually picks it up? Drink cups and cans Cigarette ends Food packaging Tissue paper 34% 27% 23% 16% Our town council employs 38 cleaners to sweep the estate every day. A one-week count found that 82% of the litter collected was dropped within ten metres of a bin . In a trial, painting bright footprints on the ground leading to the bins reduced litter in that block by a third , without any fines being issued.

                                      Q1. What do you think is the most important point in this report?

                                      For me the most important figure is that 82% of the litter was dropped within ten metres of a bin. That changes how I understand the problem completely. If the litter were far from any bin, the answer would be to build more bins, but it is not, so the issue is not convenience at all. People walk past a bin and drop something anyway. The footprint trial at the end supports that reading, because painting footprints does not make the bins any closer or any emptier. It only makes people notice them, and that alone cut the litter by a third without a single fine.

                                      Q2. Tell me about a time you saw someone drop litter. What did you do?

                                      A few months ago I was walking home from the market with my father when a man ahead of us finished a drink and left the plastic cup on top of an electrical box beside the lift lobby. There was a bin at the foot of the block, perhaps five steps away. I did not say anything to him, partly because I was nervous and partly because my father had already put his hand on my shoulder. After the man had gone into the lift, my father picked the cup up and threw it away, and he said one thing: that somebody always clears it, and it is never the person who left it. I have thought about that sentence many times since, and it is why I now pick things up on my own floor.

                                      Q3. What would you do to keep your neighbourhood clean, if it were up to you?

                                      I would spend the money on making bins impossible to ignore rather than on fines. The footprint trial in this report cut litter by a third for the price of some paint, which is remarkable, so I would paint footprints in every block and repaint them when they fade. Secondly, I would put a small bin at the entrance of every lift lobby, because that is where people finish their drinks while waiting. Thirdly, and this matters most to me, I would have primary school classes spend one morning a term clearing their own estate with the cleaners. It is easy to drop a cup when litter feels like somebody else's job, and much harder once you have spent a morning bending down to pick it up yourself. Fines punish the few people who are caught. Changing how the place feels changes everybody.

                                      Walking or riding to school · P4 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: SCHOOL NEWSLETTER · HOW WE GET HERE How our pupils travel to school Car School bus Walking Public bus or MRT 41% 27% 21% 11% Of the pupils who live within one kilometre of the school, 56% still come by car. The most common reason parents gave was the morning rush , not distance or weather.

                                      Q1. Looking at this chart, what stands out to you?

                                      The chart shows that the car is by far the most common way pupils get to school, at 41%, while only about one in five walks. What I find most surprising is the line underneath. More than half of the pupils who live within one kilometre still come by car, and a kilometre is a walk of about twelve minutes. So the problem is not really distance. The newsletter says the main reason parents gave was the morning rush, which suggests that families are short of time rather than short of options.

                                      Q2. How do you get to school, and what do you like or dislike about it?

                                      I walk, because I live in the block behind the school, and it takes me about eight minutes. What I like best is that I walk with my neighbour Siti and we talk the whole way, which means I arrive awake instead of half asleep. What I dislike is the rain. Twice last term I arrived with wet socks and had to sit in them all morning, and on those days I did wish we had a car.

                                      Q3. What could a school do to encourage more pupils to walk?

                                      I think a school should make walking feel organised rather than just allowed. One idea I have read about is a walking bus, where a parent walks a fixed route at a fixed time and children join along the way. That would help with the morning rush, because parents would not each have to make their own trip. Secondly, I would put up a covered walkway on the busiest path, since rain is the reason most people give up walking. Finally, I would give each class a chart of how many walking days it has managed in a month, because my class will compete over absolutely anything.

                                      Looking after a pet · P4 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: PET SHOP NOTICE · BEFORE YOU BUY Is your family ready for a pet? Fresh food and water Cleaning the cage Time out of the cage Visit to the vet every day twice a week every day once a year A rabbit lives for 8 to 12 years . It needs fresh hay every day, a clean cage twice a week, and time outside the cage. Many rabbits are given away in their first year, and the most common reason is that nobody had time .

                                      Q1. What does this notice tell you about keeping a rabbit?

                                      It tells me that a rabbit is a lot more work than I would have guessed. It needs fresh hay every single day and time outside its cage every day, and the cage has to be cleaned twice a week. The part that surprised me most is that a rabbit can live for eight to twelve years, which is almost as long as I have been alive. The notice also says many rabbits are given away in the first year because nobody had time, so I think the shop is trying to make families think carefully first.

                                      Q2. Tell me about an animal you have looked after, or one you would like to look after.

                                      My family looks after my neighbour's cat, Tiger, whenever they travel. It is my job to feed him in the morning and change his water. The first time, I put down too much food and my mother said he would be sick, so now I use the small cup that came with the packet. What I like is that he waits by the door at the same time every morning. What I did not expect is how much he sheds. I have to sweep the corridor outside our flat every day he stays with us.

                                      Q3. What should a family think about before getting a pet?

                                      I think the first thing to ask is who will actually do the work, because in my experience the person who wants the pet most is not always the person who ends up feeding it. The second thing is time. This notice says rabbits need something every single day, so a family that is out from morning until night should probably choose a pet that needs less, or none at all. The last thing I would think about is how long the animal lives. If a rabbit lives for ten years, a Primary 3 pupil getting one now will be in secondary school before it is old, and somebody has to plan for that.

                                      Helping at home · P4 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: FAMILY LIFE SURVEY · PRIMARY PUPILS Which jobs do children do at home? Tidy their own room Clear the table Wash up Hang the laundry 62% 48% 29% 17% In a survey of 600 primary pupils, 18% said they did no household jobs at all. Pupils who had one regular job they were in charge of were far more likely to keep doing it than pupils who were asked each time.

                                      Q1. What do you notice about this survey?

                                      I notice that the jobs children do most are the ones closest to themselves. More than half tidy their own room, but fewer than one in five hangs the laundry, which is a job for the whole family rather than just for you. I also noticed that 18% said they did nothing at all, which is about one child in every six. The most useful part is the last sentence: children who were in charge of one job kept doing it, and children who were asked each time did not. That suggests the job should be yours rather than something you are told to do.

                                      Q2. What jobs do you do at home? Tell me about one of them.

                                      I am in charge of the rubbish. Every evening after dinner I tie the bag and take it down to the chute on our floor. It is not a difficult job, but I have to remember it without being told, and at the beginning I forgot about three times a week. What helped was that my father stopped reminding me. The first time the kitchen started to smell, I noticed it myself, and I have not forgotten since. I also wash the rice now on Sundays, because my grandmother taught me how many times to rinse it.

                                      Q3. Do you think children should have to help at home? Why?

                                      Yes, I think so, for two reasons. The first is fairness. Everybody in a family uses the plates and makes the mess, so it is not right for one or two people to do all the clearing up. The second reason is that these are things we will all need to do one day anyway, and it is much easier to learn them at nine than to learn them all at once when you are older. I would add one thing, though. I think it works better when a child is given one job to own rather than being asked to help with whatever is left, because this survey says exactly that.

                                      Second-hand things · P5 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: NATIONAL ENVIRONMENT AGENCY · HOUSEHOLD WASTE What we throw away that still works Still working Needs a small repair Beyond repair Unsafe or recalled 41% 27% 22% 10% A survey of items left at five housing estates found that 41% of the discarded electrical goods were still in working order. The commonest reason given for replacing a working item was wanting a newer model , not breakage.

                                      Q1. What do you make of the information in this survey?

                                      The figure that stands out is that 41% of the electrical goods thrown away were still working. If you add the 27% that needed only a small repair, then more than two thirds of what was discarded did not actually need to be discarded at all. What I find most telling is the reason given underneath. People were not replacing things because they had broken, but because a newer model had come out, which means this is a problem about how we think rather than a problem about how well things are made.

                                      Q2. Tell me about something in your home that was passed on to you or repaired.

                                      My desk lamp was my cousin's before it was mine. The switch had stopped working, and my father and I opened it one Saturday and found that a wire had simply come loose from the base. It took about twenty minutes to fix. What I remember is how surprised I was that it was something that small, because when it stopped working we all assumed it was finished. I have had it for three years now and I would not swap it for a new one, partly because I know what is inside it.

                                      Q3. How could a school encourage pupils to repair things rather than replace them?

                                      I think a school should make repairing visible, because at the moment it happens out of sight and replacing happens in front of everybody. One idea would be a repair corner at recess, once a month, where a teacher or a parent who is good with tools helps pupils mend bags, zips and water bottles. Secondly, I would ask the art and science departments to run a project where pupils take something broken apart to see how it works, because you cannot want to fix what you do not understand. Finally, and this matters most, I would stop the school rewarding new things. When everybody notices a new bag and nobody notices a mended one, no amount of encouragement will change what pupils actually do.

                                      Learning from mistakes · P5 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: SCHOOL COUNSELLING SERVICE · PUPIL SURVEY What pupils do after getting something wrong Looked at the mark only Reread the questions alone Went through it with somebody Redid the paper 58% 24% 13% 5% Of 520 pupils asked what they did after a poor test result, 58% said they looked at the mark and put the paper away. Pupils who went through their wrong answers with somebody scored on average nine marks higher on the next test of the same topic.

                                      Q1. What does this survey tell you?

                                      It tells me that most pupils, well over half, treat a test as something that is finished once they know the mark. Only about one in eight goes through the wrong answers with another person, and yet that is the group whose next result was nine marks better. What makes the figure persuasive to me is that it compares the same topic, so it is not simply that the cleverer pupils talk about their work. It suggests the talking is what does the work.

                                      Q2. Tell me about a mistake of your own that you learnt something from.

                                      In Primary 4 I lost nine marks in a Science paper because I answered the question I had expected rather than the one that was printed. It asked why the plant in the dark box survived for two weeks, and I wrote everything I knew about photosynthesis instead. My teacher made me read the question aloud, twice, and then asked me what the word 'survived' was doing in it. I have underlined the verb in every question since. I still lose marks, but not for that.

                                      Q3. Should schools give pupils time in class to go over their mistakes?

                                      I strongly believe they should, for a reason this survey makes plain: pupils will not do it on their own. Only 13% went through their wrong answers with anybody, so leaving it to homework means it mostly does not happen. A lesson spent on the paper you have just sat is also more useful than a new lesson, because you already care about the answers. I would add one condition, though. It has to be done in a way that is not embarrassing. If going over mistakes means reading your score out, pupils will hide the paper, and the school will have made the problem worse rather than better.

                                      Helping at a hawker centre · P4 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: COMMUNITY CENTRE · YOUTH NOTICE Tray Return Champions Trays left on tables Trays returned by diners about 300 about 420 Our estate's hawker centre still has about 300 trays left on tables every lunchtime. Six cleaners clear them. Four of the six are over sixty-five years old.

                                      Q1. What can you tell me about this notice?

                                      The notice says that about 300 trays are still left on tables every lunchtime, while about 420 are returned, so a little under half of all diners are not returning theirs. The part that stays with me is the last line: four of the six cleaners are over sixty-five. That turns it from a tidiness problem into something about who ends up doing the carrying, and I think that is why the notice mentions their ages at all.

                                      Q2. Do you return your tray when you eat out? Tell me about it.

                                      Yes, usually, although I did not always. My grandmother started making me do it when I was about seven, and at first I thought it was pointless because somebody was paid to clear the tables anyway. What changed my mind was watching an auntie at our hawker centre carry four trays at once with her wrists bent right back. Now I do it without thinking, and I feel uncomfortable when I see a table of people walk away from six trays.

                                      Q3. What would make more people return their trays?

                                      I think the rules are already clear, so the problem is not that people do not know. What I would change is where the racks are. At our hawker centre the rack is at the back near the toilets, so returning a tray means walking away from the exit. If the racks were next to the doors, returning one would be on your way out instead of a detour. I would also get schools to bring classes to eat there once a term, because habits are easier to start at nine than to change at forty.

                                      Homework and free time · P6 and above

                                      (The stimulus for this topic is shown in the app under Practice. A description is given below so the conversation can also be done from this document.)

                                      Stimulus summary: STRAITS RESEARCH · PRIMARY 6 TIME DIARY Where a Primary 6 day goes School and travel Homework and tuition Meals and chores Free time, unstructured 9h 06m 3h 24m 1h 36m 54m Pupils kept a diary for one school week. The averages below exclude sleep. Of the pupils who reported under half an hour of unstructured free time a day, 71% also reported finding it hard to think of something to do when they did have time.

                                      Q1. What is the most striking thing in this diary study?

                                      The bare numbers are striking enough: nine hours on school and travel against fifty-four minutes of unstructured time. But the sentence underneath is what I keep returning to. Among the pupils with the least free time, 71% said they found it hard to think of what to do when they finally had some. I would have assumed those pupils would be the most eager to use it. It suggests that deciding what to do with yourself is a skill, and that it gets rusty if every hour of your week has already been decided for you by somebody else.

                                      Q2. How does your own week compare?

                                      Mine is close to this, though my homework is nearer two and a half hours because I do not have tuition on Wednesdays. The free time figure feels about right, and I recognise the problem in that last sentence. On the first Saturday of the June holidays I genuinely did not know what to do with myself and ended up scrolling for two hours, which I did not enjoy. What I have since found works is having one or two things I am slowly working at — at the moment it is learning to juggle — so that free time arrives with something already waiting in it.

                                      Q3. Some people say children today have too little free time. What do you think?

                                      I agree, but I want to be careful about why, because the usual argument is that children are tired, and tiredness is only part of it. What this study points to is more interesting: free time is where you find out what you actually like, and that cannot be scheduled for you. A child whose whole week is arranged may do very well at school and still reach secondary school without knowing what they would choose to do with an afternoon. I would not argue for less work. I would argue for protecting one genuinely empty afternoon a week and resisting the temptation to fill it, which I think is harder for parents than it sounds.

                                      Marking Reading Aloud at home

                                      Out of 10 What it sounds like
                                      9–10 Fluent throughout, clear final consonants, expression matches the meaning, well-judged pace
                                      7–8 Mostly fluent, one or two stumbles, some expression
                                      5–6 Several stumbles or mispronunciations, flat delivery, rushed
                                      3–4 Frequent hesitation, words guessed, little sense of the meaning
                                      1–2 Very halting

                                      Marking the Conversation at home

                                      Out of 20 What it sounds like
                                      17–20 Every answer developed over several sentences with a personal example, clear opinions, natural delivery, good eye contact
                                      13–16 Answers developed but one is short, or examples are general rather than personal
                                      9–12 Answers of one or two sentences, opinions stated but not explained
                                      5–8 Very short answers, long pauses, needs prompting
                                      1–4 Barely responds

                                      Score the child honestly, tell them the one thing to change, and do the same stimulus again a week later. The improvement between attempt one and attempt two is usually larger than anything a term of lessons produces.

                                      Document 11

                                      Situational Writing — Twenty Tasks with Model Answers

                                      Paper 1 Part 1 is worth 15 marks: 9 for task fulfilment and 6 for language and organisation. Task fulfilment is worth more, which means covering every bullet point matters more than elegant writing.

                                      Work through one task a week. Write your own answer first, cover the model, then compare.

                                      The marking bands

                                      Task fulfilment Language and organisation
                                      8–9 · All four points covered, each with a supporting detail 9 6 · Correct format, consistent tone, almost no errors 6
                                      6–7 · All four covered, but one or two are thin 7 5 · Correct format, a few errors, tone mostly right 5
                                      4–5 · Three points covered 5 3–4 · Format mostly right, several errors or tone slips 4
                                      2–3 · Two points covered 3 2 · Format or tone clearly wrong, frequent errors 2
                                      0–1 · One point, or largely off task 1 0–1 · Hard to follow 1

                                      Task 1 · Formal email · request

                                      The task

                                      Your class would like to hold a small farewell party for Mdm Lim, the school cleaner on your floor, who is retiring at the end of the month. You need the principal's permission.

                                      Write an email to your principal, Mr Chandra. You should include: • who the party is for and why • when and where you would like to hold it • what your class will do to keep the disruption small • what you would like him to allow

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to request permission. Audience: the principal — formal. Context: four bullet points, each needing one supporting detail.

                                      Model answer

                                      To: chandra_r@riverbankpri.edu.sg
Subject: Request to hold a short farewell for Mdm Lim on 29 May

Dear Mr Chandra,

I am writing on behalf of Primary 6 Resilience. Mdm Lim, who has cleaned our floor for the past six years, will be retiring at the end of this month, and we would like to thank her properly before she leaves.

We hope to hold a short gathering in our own classroom on Friday 29 May, during the second half of recess, lasting about twenty minutes.

To keep the disruption to a minimum, we will use our own classroom rather than the hall, bring the refreshments ourselves, and clear everything away before the bell. Two pupils have volunteered to stay behind to check the room is spotless.

May we have your permission to go ahead, and would you be willing to let Mdm Lim know she is expected somewhere at that time without telling her why?

Thank you very much for considering our request.

Yours sincerely,
Rachel Tan
Primary 6 Resilience

                                      Why it scores: All four points covered, each with one specific detail. Formal throughout — no contractions, no exclamation marks. The final request is concrete and even anticipates a practical problem.

                                      Task 2 · Formal email · complaint

                                      The task

                                      Your family ordered a birthday cake from Sweet Corner Bakery for collection on Saturday. When you collected it, the name written on it was wrong and the cake was a different flavour from the one ordered.

                                      Write an email to the bakery manager. You should include: • what you ordered and when • what was wrong with the cake • how this affected your family • what you would like the bakery to do

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to complain and seek a remedy. Audience: a manager you do not know — formal. Stay polite; anger loses marks.

                                      Model answer

                                      To: manager@sweetcornerbakery.com.sg
Subject: Incorrect cake collected on Saturday 14 June (order no. 2187)

Dear Sir or Madam,

On Tuesday 10 June my mother ordered a chocolate cake for collection on Saturday 14 June, under order number 2187. The name "Arun" was to be written on it.

When we collected the cake, the name on it read "Aaron", and the cake was a strawberry sponge rather than the chocolate one we had chosen and paid for.

We only discovered this after we had returned home, by which time the guests had arrived, so we had to serve the cake as it was. My younger brother, whose birthday it was, was quite upset that his name had been spelt incorrectly in front of everyone.

I would be grateful if you could look into how the order was recorded, and I hope you will consider a refund or a replacement cake. I have kept the receipt and a photograph of the cake as it was given to us.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Yours faithfully,
Rachel Tan

                                      Why it scores: Specific order details make the complaint credible. The effect on the family is described without exaggeration. The remedy requested is reasonable and the writer offers evidence rather than demanding.

                                      Task 3 · Informal email · invitation

                                      The task

                                      Your cousin Mei Hui lives in Penang. Your school is holding its first Open House and your class is running a stall. You would like her to come when she next visits.

                                      Write an email to Mei Hui. You should include: • what the Open House is and when it is • what your class stall will be doing • why you would like her to come • one practical detail she needs to know

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to invite. Audience: a cousin your own age — informal. Contractions and questions are fine here.

                                      Model answer

                                      To: meihui.ong@email.com
Subject: Come to our Open House in September!

Hi Mei Hui,

How are things in Penang? I've got something to tell you about.

Our school is holding its very first Open House on Saturday 12 September, from ten in the morning until three in the afternoon. The whole school will be open and every class is running something.

Our class is doing a Science stall. We're building a marble run out of recycled cardboard, and visitors get to add one section to it, so by the end of the day it should stretch right across the classroom. I'm in charge of testing whether the marbles actually get to the bottom, which so far they mostly don't.

I'd really like you to come because you're the only person I know who'd enjoy this more than I do, and because I haven't seen you since Chinese New Year. You could stay over on the Friday night if your parents agree.

One thing to know: there's no parking at school that day, so your family would need to come by MRT and walk from Sengkang station. It's about eight minutes.

Let me know if you can make it!

Love,
Rachel

                                      Why it scores: Warm and specific without gushing. The self-deprecating joke about the marbles sounds like a real child. The practical detail at the end is genuinely useful, not padding.

                                      Task 4 · Report

                                      The task

                                      You are the class environment representative. Write a report to your form teacher on your class's two-week effort to reduce paper waste.

                                      You should include: • what the class did • the results • one problem faced • one recommendation

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to report factually. Audience: your form teacher. Use headings and a neutral tone — no chatty language.

                                      Model answer

                                      Report on the Primary 6 Resilience Paper Reduction Effort
By: Rachel Tan, Class Environment Representative
Date: 30 May 2026

Purpose
This report sets out what our class did during the two-week paper reduction effort from 18 to 29 May, and recommends one change for next term.

What we did
We placed a single scrap-paper tray beside the printer and agreed that no sheet would be thrown away until both sides had been used. Worksheets were printed double-sided. Three pupils volunteered to check the recycling bin each afternoon for paper that had been thrown away by mistake.

Results
Our class recycling bin was weighed each Friday. In the week before the effort began, it held 4.6 kilograms. In the second week of the effort, it held 1.9 kilograms, a reduction of just under sixty per cent.

Problem faced
The main difficulty was the scrap tray itself. Because it sat beside the printer, pupils frequently took clean paper from it by mistake, which caused some confusion and a few lost worksheets.

Recommendation
I recommend that the scrap tray be moved to the shelf by the door and labelled clearly on both sides. This would separate it from the clean paper and make it obvious what the tray is for.

                                      Why it scores: Headings, factual tone, real numbers. The problem is admitted honestly and the recommendation follows directly from it — that link is where the marks are.

                                      Task 5 · Formal email · enquiry

                                      The task

                                      You have seen a notice about a free holiday coding workshop at the community centre but the notice is missing several details.

                                      Write an email to the community centre. You should include: • where you saw the notice and which workshop you mean • two questions you need answered • why you are interested • how they can reach you

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to enquire. Audience: staff you do not know — formal. Questions must be clear and answerable.

                                      Model answer

                                      To: enquiries@sengkangcc.org.sg
Subject: Enquiry about the December Junior Coding Workshop

Dear Sir or Madam,

I saw a notice about the Junior Coding Workshop on the board outside your Level 2 counter last Saturday. The notice gave the dates as 1 to 5 December but did not state the timings.

I would be grateful if you could answer two questions. Firstly, what time does each session begin and end? Secondly, is the workshop suitable for someone who has never written any code before, or is some experience expected?

I am interested because I have been using a block-based coding app at school and would like to learn to write proper programs. My school does not offer this beyond Primary 6.

You can reply to this email address, or telephone my mother on 9123 4567 in the evenings.

Thank you very much for your help.

Yours faithfully,
Rachel Tan

                                      Why it scores: Identifies the notice precisely, asks two genuinely distinct questions, gives a real reason for interest, and supplies two contact routes.

                                      Task 6 · Informal email · apology

                                      The task

                                      You promised your friend Daniel you would help him prepare for a chess tournament on Sunday, but you forgot and went out with your family instead. He played and lost badly.

                                      Write an email to Daniel. You should include: • what you did wrong • why it happened, without making excuses • how you think it affected him • what you will do about it

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to apologise. Audience: a close friend — informal, but sincerity matters more than tone here. Avoid excuses.

                                      Model answer

                                      To: daniel.ong@email.com
Subject: I'm sorry about Sunday

Daniel,

I let you down on Sunday and I want to say so properly rather than just mumbling it at recess tomorrow.

I promised I'd come over on Saturday evening to go through openings with you before the tournament, and I forgot. My aunt arrived unexpectedly and we went out for dinner, and it simply went out of my head. I'm not offering that as an excuse — I could have sent you one message from the restaurant and I didn't.

I know you'd been preparing for a month, and I think going in without that last run-through probably shook your confidence before you'd even sat down. You told me twice that the openings were the part you were least sure of.

The next tournament is in August. If you still want my help, I'll come over every Saturday from July, and I'll put it in my mother's calendar so it can't happen again. If you'd rather ask somebody else, I'll understand.

I'm sorry.

Rachel

                                      Why it scores: Owns the failure without softening it, and explicitly refuses to hide behind the excuse. Acknowledges the actual effect on Daniel. The remedy is concrete and leaves him the choice.

                                      Task 7 · Formal email · suggestion

                                      The task

                                      Your school canteen has long queues at the drinks stall every recess, and many pupils run out of time to eat.

                                      Write an email to the head of the canteen committee. You should include: • what the problem is • evidence that it is a real problem • one suggestion • why your suggestion would work

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to suggest a change. Audience: a teacher in charge — formal. A suggestion is far stronger with evidence behind it.

                                      Model answer

                                      To: canteen_committee@riverbankpri.edu.sg
Subject: Suggestion to reduce the drinks stall queue at recess

Dear Mrs Devi,

I am writing about the queue at the drinks stall during the first recess.

Over the past two weeks, some classmates and I timed the queue on eight occasions. The shortest wait was six minutes and the longest was thirteen. Recess is twenty-five minutes, so a pupil who queues for drinks and then queues again for food often has under eight minutes left to eat.

I would like to suggest that bottled water and packet drinks be sold from a separate table at the far end of the canteen, staffed by a prefect, with exact change only.

This would help because roughly half the pupils in the queue are buying only a bottled drink, and they do not need the stallholder at all. Removing them from the main queue would shorten it considerably without requiring any extra staff or equipment.

I would be happy to help organise a trial for a week if that would be useful.

Thank you for considering this.

Yours sincerely,
Rachel Tan
Primary 6 Resilience

                                      Why it scores: The evidence is the strongest part: actual timings, not an impression. The suggestion is cheap and specific, and the reasoning explains exactly why it would work.

                                      Task 8 · Informal message · declining

                                      The task

                                      Your friend Priya has invited you to her birthday outing on Saturday, but you have your grandmother's eightieth birthday dinner the same evening. You want to decline without hurting her feelings.

                                      Write a message to Priya. You should include: • thank her for the invitation • explain clearly why you cannot come • show you are genuinely sorry to miss it • suggest something else

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to decline warmly. Audience: a close friend — informal and short. A declining message goes wrong when it is vague.

                                      Model answer

                                      Hi Priya,

Thank you so much for inviting me on Saturday — I was really pleased you thought of me.

I'm afraid I can't come. It's my grandmother's eightieth birthday that evening and the whole family is going for dinner. It's been booked since March and I'd never hear the end of it if I missed it, and honestly I wouldn't want to.

I'm genuinely sorry, because the trampoline park was the one thing I actually wanted to do this holiday, and I know you planned it around everyone's schedules.

Could I take you out for bubble tea the following Saturday instead, just the two of us? My treat, and you can tell me everything I missed.

Have a brilliant day.

Rachel

                                      Why it scores: Thanks first, reason second, and the reason is specific enough to be believable. The regret is genuine rather than formulaic, and the alternative offered is concrete with a date.

                                      Task 9 · Formal email · appreciation

                                      The task

                                      Mr Devan, a veterinarian, gave a talk to your level about caring for pets. Your form teacher has asked you to write to him on behalf of the class.

                                      Write an email to Mr Devan. You should include: • what you are thanking him for • one thing from the talk that your class found most useful • what some pupils have done differently since the talk • an invitation to a school event he might like to attend

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to thank, and to invite. Audience: an adult visitor you do not know well — formal. Context: four bullet points. The second and third are where most pupils go thin; each needs one specific example, not a general compliment.

                                      Model answer

                                      To: devan@greenlanevet.com.sg
Subject: Thank you for your talk to our Primary 5 pupils

Dear Mr Devan,

I am writing on behalf of Primary 5 Integrity to thank you for the talk you gave us last Wednesday on caring for pets. You gave up an entire afternoon of your working week for us, and we are very grateful.

The part the class found most useful was your explanation of how to tell when an animal is in pain. Many of us had assumed that a hamster or a rabbit would cry out if something were wrong. Learning that small animals hide their pain, and that a change in eating or grooming is often the only sign, was new to almost everybody in the room.

Since the talk, several pupils have begun keeping a short weekly note of what their pet eats. One of my classmates noticed that her rabbit had stopped finishing its hay, took it to a clinic, and found that it had a tooth problem that was caught early. She asked me to tell you that.

Our school is holding its Green Fair on Saturday 18 July from nine in the morning until noon, and there will be a stall on responsible pet ownership run by our class. We would be delighted if you could come, although we understand that weekends may be busy for you.

Thank you once again for your time and your patience with our many questions.

Yours sincerely,
Nathan Wong
Primary 5 Integrity
Green Lane Primary School

                                      Why it scores: All four points covered, and each one carries a specific detail rather than a general compliment. The third point is the strongest move in the whole answer: instead of saying "we all take better care of our pets now", it tells one small true-sounding story with an outcome. Formal register is held from the greeting to the sign-off — no contractions, no exclamation marks — and the invitation is polite without being pushy.

                                      Task 10 · Informal email · instructions

                                      The task

                                      Your friend Haziq is coming to your flat on Saturday for the first time to work on a group project. He has never been to your estate.

                                      Write an email to Haziq. You should include: • how to get to your block from the MRT station • what time to come and how long you expect the work to take • what he should bring • what to do if he cannot find the place

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to give directions and instructions. Audience: a friend — informal. Context: four bullet points. Directions must be in a sensible order, and the last point needs a real fallback, not "just call me".

                                      Model answer

                                      To: haziq.rahman@email.com
Subject: Getting to my place on Saturday

Hi Haziq,

Here's how to find my flat so you don't end up wandering around Yishun for half an hour.

Come out of Yishun MRT at Exit B, the one facing the bus interchange. Walk past the interchange and keep the big supermarket on your left. At the traffic light, cross over and you'll see three identical blocks — mine is the middle one, Block 726. The lift lobby is behind the bicycle racks, and I'm on the eleventh floor, unit 11-142. It's about eight minutes' walk in total.

Can you come at ten? I reckon we'll need about three hours for the model and the write-up, so we should be done by one. My mother says she'll feed us lunch, so don't eat before you come.

Bring your half of the research notes, a ruler and the glue gun if yours still works — mine gave up last week. I've already got the cardboard, the paint and the printer, so you don't need to worry about those.

If you get lost, call me on 9123 4567. If I don't pick up because I'm in the shower, wait at the mama shop next to the bicycle racks and I'll come down and find you — it's the only shop at the foot of my block, so you can't miss it.

See you Saturday!

Your friend,
Nathan

                                      Why it scores: The directions run in the order the reader will walk them, with landmarks rather than street names, which is what actually helps. Informal tone throughout: contractions, a joke in the opening line, a question rather than an instruction about the time. The last point gives a genuine backup place to wait instead of the usual "just call me", which is what separates full task-fulfilment marks from partial ones.

                                      Task 11 · Report · to a teacher

                                      The task

                                      You are the class librarian. Your class ran a Reading Buddies scheme this term, in which Primary 6 pupils read with Primary 1 pupils every Friday. Your form teacher has asked for a report.

                                      Write a report for your form teacher, Mrs Halim. You should include: • how the scheme was run • what went well • one problem faced • one recommendation for next term

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to report. Audience: your form teacher — formal and factual. Context: a report, so use headings, no greeting, no chatty language, and no "I think it was fun".

                                      Model answer

                                      Report on the Primary 6 Reading Buddies Scheme
By: Nathan Wong, Class Librarian, Primary 6 Integrity
Date: 14 August 2026

Purpose
This report describes how the Reading Buddies scheme ran in Term 3 and recommends one change for Term 4.

How the scheme was run
Twenty-four Primary 6 pupils were each paired with one Primary 1 pupil. The pairs met in the school library every Friday from 1.30 p.m. to 2.15 p.m. over eight weeks. Each Primary 6 pupil chose two picture books a week from a shelf set aside by the librarian, read one aloud to the younger child, and then listened while the child attempted the second. A record card was signed after every session.

What went well
Attendance was high: 21 of the 24 pairs met in at least seven of the eight weeks. The younger pupils grew noticeably more willing to read aloud; nine of them read a whole book unaided by Week 8, compared with two in Week 1. Several Primary 6 pupils reported that having to explain words made them think harder about meanings themselves.

Problem faced
The library was too noisy. Twenty-four pairs reading aloud in one room meant that many pupils could not hear their partner and began to read more loudly, which made the problem worse. Three pairs moved into the corridor without asking, which was unsafe.

Recommendation
The scheme should be split into two groups of twelve pairs meeting on alternate Fridays, or the second group should be given the use of an empty classroom. Twelve pairs in the library would allow each pair to hear each other without raising their voices.

                                      Why it scores: Report format handled properly: a title, the writer's role, a date, and four headings — no "Dear Mrs Halim" and no sign-off. The language is factual and the evidence is numerical, which is what a report is for. The problem is a real operational one with a named consequence, and the recommendation follows directly from it rather than being a general wish for improvement.

                                      Task 12 · Notice · to schoolmates

                                      The task

                                      Your school is collecting used story books for children at a nearby welfare home. You have been asked to write a notice to be put up on the noticeboard at every level.

                                      Write a notice. You should include: • what is being collected and who it is for • what condition the books must be in • where and when to bring them • who to approach with questions

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to inform and persuade. Audience: pupils across the whole school, including Primary 1 — semi-formal and very plain. Context: a notice, so use a heading, short lines, and no greeting or sign-off. A notice that a Primary 2 pupil cannot read has failed.

                                      Model answer

                                      BOOK DRIVE: GIVE A STORY A SECOND HOME

WHAT WE NEED
We are collecting used story books for the children at Sunrise Children's Home. They have a reading room with almost empty shelves. Picture books and easy chapter books are the most useful, because most of the children there are between five and ten years old.

WHAT WE CANNOT ACCEPT
Books must be clean, complete and readable. Please do not bring books with torn or missing pages, books that have been written in, or books that are damp. Textbooks and assessment books cannot be used.

WHERE AND WHEN
Bring your books to the two blue boxes outside the school library.
Collection runs from Monday 3 August to Friday 14 August, before school and during both recesses.
Please do not leave books on the floor if a box is full — tell the librarian instead.

QUESTIONS?
Speak to Nathan Wong of Primary 6 Integrity, or to Mrs Halim in the staff room.

One book from each of us fills a shelf. Thank you.

                                      Why it scores: A notice has no greeting and no sign-off, and this one does not pretend to be a letter. Headings in capitals let a reader find one piece of information without reading the rest. The condition point is handled as a short "cannot accept" list, which is far clearer than a sentence, and the sentences stay short enough for a Primary 2 reader. The closing line persuades in seven words without slipping into an excitable tone.

                                      Task 13 · Formal email · explanation and appeal

                                      The task

                                      You borrowed a book from the public library and returned it three weeks late because it was left in your grandmother's flat in Malaysia during the holidays. You have been fined $6.30. You would like the library to reduce the fine.

                                      Write an email to the library. You should include: • the details of the book and the fine • why the book was returned late • what you have done about it • what you are asking the library to do

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to explain and to appeal. Audience: a library officer you do not know — formal, and Dear Sir or Madam with Yours faithfully. Context: an appeal must accept responsibility first. A response that blames the library or sounds as though the fine is unfair loses language marks even when all four points are covered.

                                      Model answer

                                      To: enquiries@nlb.gov.sg
Subject: Appeal regarding an overdue fine of $6.30 — member 30098

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am a Primary 6 pupil and a member of the Punggol Regional Library. I returned a book called *The Boy at the Back of the Class* on 12 June, three weeks after it was due, and I have been charged an overdue fine of $6.30.

The book was late because I took it with me to my grandmother's home in Johor Bahru during the school holidays and left it in her flat by mistake. We did not travel back until the first weekend of June, which was when I recovered it. I understand that this was my own carelessness and not the library's fault.

I returned the book on the same day that it came back into my hands, and it is undamaged. I have since written the due dates of my loans on the calendar in my kitchen so that this does not happen again, and I have paid $2.00 of the fine from my own pocket money.

I would be grateful if the library would consider reducing the remainder of the fine, as $6.30 is a large amount for me to pay out of my allowance. If that is not possible, I would like to ask whether I may pay the balance in instalments over the next two months. I will accept whichever decision you reach.

Thank you for taking the time to read my appeal.

Yours faithfully,
Nathan Wong
Member number 30098

                                      Why it scores: The first line identifies the writer and the matter in one sentence, which is what a formal opening is for. Responsibility is accepted explicitly — "my own carelessness and not the library's fault" — and this is the move that makes an appeal work. The fourth point offers an alternative in case the request is refused, which shows a genuine grasp of audience. Dear Sir or Madam is correctly paired with Yours faithfully, and the reference number appears in the subject line where an officer needs it.

                                      Task 14 · Informal email · breaking disappointing news

                                      The task

                                      You and your friend Priya were chosen for the school's badminton pair for the zonal finals. You have injured your wrist and the coach has replaced you. Priya does not know yet.

                                      Write an email to Priya. You should include: • what has happened • how it happened and what the doctor said • who will play with her instead, and what you think of that • what you will do to support her

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to tell a friend bad news kindly. Audience: a close friend — informal, but not flippant. Context: the difficulty here is tone. The news is disappointing for the reader too, so an email that is only about your own feelings has missed the audience.

                                      Model answer

                                      To: priya.s@email.com
Subject: Some bad news about the finals — read this before training

Hi Priya,

I wanted you to hear this from me before you heard it in the hall. I can't play in the zonal finals with you. Coach Tan told me this morning that he has to replace me.

It's my right wrist. I landed badly on it during the last set on Tuesday and it swelled up overnight. My mother took me to the clinic on Wednesday and the doctor said it's a sprain, not a break, but I have to keep the splint on for three weeks and I'm not allowed to hold a racket at all. The finals are in nine days, so there was no way around it. I did ask.

Coach has put Wei Ling in with you. I know she plays from further back than I do and you'll have to cover more of the net at first, but she has a much better smash than mine and she doesn't panic. Honestly, I think the two of you could go further than we would have. It took me until yesterday evening to be able to write that sentence and mean it.

I'll be at every training session, and I'll be the loudest person in the gallery on the day. If it helps, I can film your games so you and Wei Ling can watch them back — I've got nothing else to do with my hands for three weeks. And I still owe you a rematch once this splint comes off.

Don't let this throw you. You were the better half of that pair anyway.

Your friend,
Nathan

                                      Why it scores: The subject line tells the reader why to open the message now, and the first sentence delivers the news without a paragraph of build-up. The third point does the hardest thing in the task: it says something generous about the replacement and admits how hard that was to write, which is both honest and kind. The support offered is concrete — filming the games — rather than "I'll support you". The tone stays informal through contractions and short sentences without becoming jokey about news the reader will find upsetting.

                                      Task 15 · Informal note · to a classmate

                                      The task

                                      Your classmate Hui Ling was absent yesterday. Write her a short note.

                                      You should include: • what she missed in class • the homework that was given • an offer to help

                                      Write about 60 to 80 words.

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to tell her what happened. Audience: a classmate — informal. Context: three points, each needing one detail.

                                      Model answer

                                      Hi Hui Ling,

I hope you are feeling better. You missed quite a lot yesterday.

In Science we started the new topic on magnets, and Mr Lee did an experiment with iron filings on a sheet of paper. It was the best lesson we have had this term.

For homework we have to finish Workbook pages 24 to 26, and write five sentences about what we saw in the experiment. It is due on Friday.

If you like, I can come over on Wednesday after school and show you my notes, because the experiment is hard to explain in writing.

Get well soon!

Your friend,
Dinesh

                                      Why it scores: All three points are covered and each one carries a detail: not just 'we did Science' but which topic and which experiment; not just 'there is homework' but the pages and the due date; not just 'I can help' but when, and why helping in person would be better. The tone is friendly throughout and the note opens and closes properly.

                                      Task 16 · Informal email · thanking

                                      The task

                                      Your aunt sent you a birthday present. Write her an email.

                                      You should include: • thanks for the present • what you have done with it so far • news about something happening at school

                                      Write about 60 to 80 words.

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to thank and to share news. Audience: an aunt you know well — warm and informal. Context: three points.

                                      Model answer

                                      To: aunty_meena@email.com
Subject: Thank you for the paint set!

Dear Aunty Meena,

Thank you so much for the watercolour set you sent for my birthday. It arrived on Saturday morning, and I was very surprised because I had not told anybody that I wanted one.

I have already used it twice. On Sunday I painted the tree outside our kitchen window, and yesterday I painted our neighbour's cat, which came out looking more like a rabbit. My mother has put both of them on the fridge anyway.

At school we are getting ready for Racial Harmony Day next month. My class is doing a dance, and I have been chosen to be in the second row, which I am quite pleased about.

Thank you again. I will send you a photograph of my next painting, if it goes better than the cat did.

Love,
Sarah

                                      Why it scores: The thanks are specific rather than general, and the second point does the most work: two real paintings, one of which went wrong, which is far more interesting than 'I have used it a lot'. The school news is a genuine piece of news with a detail attached. The closing line ties back to the joke, which is a nice touch at this level but not required.

                                      Task 17 · Short message · apologising

                                      The task

                                      You borrowed your cousin's book and spilt a drink on it. Write him a message.

                                      You should include: • what happened • an apology • what you will do about it

                                      Write about 60 to 80 words.

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to apologise. Audience: a cousin — informal, but the tone must be genuinely sorry, not jokey.

                                      Model answer

                                      Hi Marcus,

I have some bad news about your book. I was reading it at the kitchen table yesterday evening and I knocked over a glass of Milo. The first twenty pages are stained brown and two of them are stuck together at the corner.

I am really sorry. It was completely my fault — I should not have been drinking anything next to it.

I have looked the book up online and it costs $14.90. I have $9 saved and I will have the rest by the end of the month, so I would like to buy you a new copy. If you would rather have it sooner, I can ask my mother and pay her back.

Sorry again. I will not borrow anything of yours near a drink again.

Dinesh

                                      Why it scores: The apology works because the damage is described honestly and in detail before the sorry, rather than after it. Blame is accepted without excuses. The third point is concrete — a price, an amount saved, a date, and an alternative — which is what turns an apology into a solution.

                                      Task 18 · Informal email · inviting

                                      The task

                                      Your school is holding a Sports Day. Write an email inviting your grandfather.

                                      You should include: • when and where it is • what you will be taking part in • how he can get there

                                      Write about 60 to 80 words.

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to invite. Audience: your grandfather — warm and clear. Context: he needs practical information, so the third point matters as much as the first two.

                                      Model answer

                                      To: ah_gong@email.com
Subject: Come to my Sports Day!

Dear Ah Gong,
