Our school Sports Day is on Saturday 12 July, from 8 a.m. to 12 noon, on the school field.

I am running in the 100 metres at about 9.15, and I am in the class relay, which is the last event.

You can take bus 156 from your block and get off at the fourth stop, right outside our gate. If you would rather not, my father can fetch you at half past seven.

Please come!

Love,
Sarah

                                      Why it scores: Every one of the three points carries a real detail, and the third — bus number, which stop, how long, plus an alternative — is the one most pupils leave thin. The joke about Amirul keeps the tone warm without losing the information. Notice that the writer tells him where she will be looking for him, which shows she has thought about the reader.

                                      Task 19 · Notice · to the class

                                      The task

                                      You are the class monitor. The classroom cupboard is untidy. Write a notice for the class noticeboard.

                                      You should include: • what the problem is • what everybody should do • when it must be done by

                                      Write about 60 to 80 words.

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to tell everybody what to do. Audience: your classmates — plain and polite, not bossy. Context: a notice, so no greeting and no sign-off, but put your name at the end.

                                      Model answer

                                      PLEASE HELP: OUR CLASS CUPBOARD

THE PROBLEM
The cupboard at the back of the classroom is so full that the door no longer shuts properly. Two files fell out on Monday and the pages got mixed up. There are also three lunchboxes in there that have been left for more than a week.

WHAT TO DO
Please take out anything of yours that does not belong in school and bring it home. Put files on the top shelf, art materials on the middle shelf, and PE things on the bottom shelf. If something is not yours, leave it on my desk and I will try to find the owner.

BY WHEN
Please do this before recess on Friday. Mrs Ong will be checking the cupboard that afternoon.

Thank you!
Sarah (class monitor)

                                      Why it scores: A notice has no 'Dear' and no 'Yours sincerely', and this one does not pretend to be a letter. The three headings let a classmate find what they need without reading it all. The instructions are specific enough to follow — which shelf for what — and the deadline has a reason attached, which makes it far more likely to be obeyed than a bare date.

                                      Task 20 · Informal email · describing

                                      The task

                                      You went on a school excursion last week. Write to your friend who has moved away.

                                      You should include: • where you went • the best part of the day • one thing that went wrong

                                      Write about 60 to 80 words.

                                      Before you write: Purpose: to describe. Audience: a friend — informal and chatty. Context: three points; the third is the one that makes the email worth reading.

                                      Model answer

                                      To: jia_wei@email.com
Subject: Our trip to the wetland reserve

Hi Jia Wei,

You missed a good one. Last Thursday our level went to the wetland reserve at Sungei Buloh.

The best part was the mudskippers. One hopped onto a root a metre from the boardwalk and sat staring at us.

The thing that went wrong was our worksheet. Faizal put it on the railing for one second and the wind took it into the water, so we redid it from memory on the bus.

How is your new school?

Your friend,
Dinesh

                                      Why it scores: The three points are all covered with detail, and the writer knows that the disaster is the most entertaining part, so it gets the fullest paragraph. Small precise facts — eleven minutes of rain, eight centimetres, station three — do more than adjectives. The two questions at the end keep it a real conversation rather than a report.

                                      The five most common ways marks are lost

                                      1. A bullet point missed entirely. Tick them off on the question paper as you write.
                                      2. A bullet point mentioned but not developed. Each point needs one supporting detail, not a bare sentence.
                                      3. Tone drifting. "Dear Sir or Madam" followed by "Hey, so anyway" loses language marks immediately.
                                      4. A vague request. "Please do something about it" earns less than "Please repair the zip or exchange the bag".
                                      5. Inventing facts that contradict the question. If the question says two weeks ago, do not write last month.
                                      Document 12

                                      Picture Composition — Primary 3 and 4

                                      At Primary 3 and 4, composition is a four-picture series. The pictures tell a story in order, and the child writes it out in about 120 to 180 words. It is marked out of 20: 10 for content, 10 for language.

                                      This is a different exam from the Primary 5–6 one. There is no theme to interpret and no choice of pictures — all four must be used, in order. The skill being tested is telling a clear story in correct past tense, not inventing a plot.

                                      What the marks are for

                                      Content — 10 Language — 10
                                      9–10 · All four pictures used in order, with extra details of your own and a clear ending 10 9–10 · Past tense throughout, full sentences, capital letters and full stops correct, some good words 10
                                      7–8 · All four pictures used, but few details added 8 7–8 · A few mistakes in tense or punctuation, but easy to read 8
                                      5–6 · One picture missed, or the order is muddled 6 5–6 · Several tense or full-stop mistakes; short repeated sentences 6
                                      3–4 · Only two pictures used, or the story is hard to follow 4 3–4 · Many mistakes; meaning sometimes unclear 4
                                      0–2 · Does not match the pictures 2 0–2 · Very hard to read 2

                                      The three things that lift a P3 composition

                                      1. Add what the pictures cannot show. The day, the weather, a name, why the child was there, what they were thinking. A story that only describes the four drawings stays in the middle band.
                                      2. Stay in the past tense. This is where most language marks are lost at this level. I saw, I ran, she smiled — not I see, I run, she smiles.
                                      3. End with a feeling and a reason. "I was happy" earns little. "I was happy, but not because of the chocolates" earns a great deal more.

                                      Before writing — three boxes, two minutes

                                      1 BEGINNING — who, where, when
2 PROBLEM — what went wrong (pictures 2 and 3)
3 ENDING — how it was solved, and how you felt

                                      The twelve tasks

                                      Write your own story first. Then read the model and the note underneath it.

                                      1. The Wallet on the Bench · Honesty

                                      The four pictures

                                      1. A boy sees a wallet on a bench
                                      2. He looks around but nobody is there
                                      3. He hands it to a shopkeeper
                                      4. A woman thanks him

                                      Model composition

                                      Last Saturday afternoon, I was walking home through the park when I saw a brown wallet lying on a wooden bench.

                                      I picked it up. It was heavy, and when I opened it I could see several notes inside. I looked all around the park, but there was nobody nearby. My heart began to beat faster. For a moment I thought about the model aeroplane I had been saving for.

                                      Then I remembered what my mother always says: never take what is not yours. I walked quickly to the provision shop at the corner and gave the wallet to Uncle Lim, the shopkeeper. He wrote down my name and my block number.

                                      Two days later, a lady came to our flat. She was the owner of the wallet and she had been looking for it everywhere. She thanked me warmly and gave me a small box of chocolates.

                                      I was very happy, but not because of the chocolates. I was happy because I had done the right thing.

                                      What makes it work: All four pictures are used in order. The writer adds details the pictures do not show — the day, the park, the model aeroplane, Uncle Lim's name — which is what lifts content into the top band. The ending says how he felt and why, instead of stopping at 'she thanked me'.

                                      2. The Fallen Groceries · Kindness

                                      The four pictures

                                      1. An elderly man carries a heavy bag
                                      2. The bag tears and the fruit rolls away
                                      3. A girl helps him pick everything up
                                      4. She carries the bag to his door

                                      Model composition

                                      One evening, I was walking back from the playground when I noticed an elderly man struggling with a large paper bag of groceries. He was walking very slowly and the bag looked far too heavy for him.

                                      Suddenly, the bottom of the bag tore open. Apples, oranges and a cabbage rolled all over the pavement. The old man bent down stiffly and tried to gather them, but he could hardly reach.

                                      I ran over at once and began picking up the fruit. "Thank you, girl," he said softly. Together we collected everything and put it into my empty school bag.

                                      I offered to carry the bag home for him. He lived on the second floor of the next block, so it did not take long. At his door, he smiled and said that I reminded him of his own granddaughter.

                                      It had taken me only ten minutes, but he looked so pleased. Now I always slow down when I pass an elderly neighbour.

                                      What makes it work: Uses all four pictures and adds the school bag, the second floor and the granddaughter — details invented by the writer. The last two sentences show what changed, which is what turns a description of pictures into a story.

                                      3. The Kite in the Tree · Problem solving

                                      The four pictures

                                      1. Two children fly a kite in the field
                                      2. The kite gets stuck high in a tree
                                      3. They ask a gardener for help
                                      4. The kite is flying again

                                      Model composition

                                      Last Sunday morning, my cousin Daniel and I took our new kite to the open field behind our block. The wind was strong and the kite climbed higher and higher until it was only a red dot in the sky.

                                      Then the wind changed direction suddenly. Before I could pull the string, the kite swooped sideways and became tangled in the branches of a tall angsana tree. Daniel and I jumped and jumped, but the kite was far beyond our reach.

                                      We were about to give up when we saw a gardener trimming the hedges nearby. We ran over and explained what had happened. He smiled and said he had exactly the right tool.

                                      Using his long pole, the gardener gently hooked the kite and lowered it down. Amazingly, it was not torn at all.

                                      We thanked him again and again. Within minutes our kite was soaring above the field once more. I have learnt that it is never foolish to ask an adult for help.

                                      What makes it work: Good use of specific words — angsana, swooped, tangled, soaring. The problem is solved by asking for help rather than by magic, which keeps the story believable. Note how paragraph 3 builds a small moment of hopelessness before the solution arrives.

                                      4. Caught in the Rain · Friendship

                                      The four pictures

                                      1. A boy walks to school under a grey sky
                                      2. Heavy rain begins and he has no umbrella
                                      3. A friend shares her umbrella
                                      4. They arrive at school dry and laughing

                                      Model composition

                                      One Monday morning, I set off for school without checking the sky. Thick grey clouds were gathering above the void deck, but I was already late and did not want to run back upstairs for my umbrella.

                                      I had walked only halfway when the rain came down. It was not a light drizzle but a proper downpour. Within seconds my shirt was soaked and my school bag was dripping. I stood under a tree, shivering and wondering what to do.

                                      Just then I heard someone calling my name. It was Mei Ling, my classmate, holding a big red umbrella. She hurried over and held it above both of us.

                                      We walked the rest of the way together, our shoulders bumping under the umbrella, laughing every time a car splashed past. By the time we reached the school gate, I was almost dry again.

                                      I thanked Mei Ling and promised to bring an extra umbrella from then on. A good friend, I realised, always appears at the right moment.

                                      What makes it work: The first paragraph explains why he has no umbrella, which the pictures cannot show. 'Our shoulders bumping under the umbrella' is a small invented detail that makes the scene real. Notice the past tense is used throughout, without slipping.

                                      5. The Spilt Paint · Owning up

                                      The four pictures

                                      1. Children painting in the art room
                                      2. A boy knocks over a pot of paint
                                      3. He tells the teacher what happened
                                      4. They clean it up together

                                      Model composition

                                      Last Friday, our class had an art lesson in the art room. We were painting posters for Racial Harmony Day, and every table was covered with brushes, water pots and jars of paint.

                                      I reached across the table for a brush without looking. My elbow caught the jar of red paint and knocked it right over. The paint poured across the table and dripped onto the floor in a bright red puddle. For a moment I froze. Nobody had seen me do it.

                                      I thought about saying nothing. Then I put down my brush and walked to Mrs Devi's desk. I told her that I had knocked over the paint and that I was sorry.

                                      Mrs Devi did not scold me at all. She thanked me for telling her straight away, fetched a bucket and some cloths, and helped me clean up the mess.

                                      It took us fifteen minutes. My shoes still have a faint pink mark on them, and I do not mind at all.

                                      What makes it work: The short sentence 'For a moment I froze' slows the story at exactly the right point. 'Nobody had seen me do it' shows the temptation, which is what makes owning up worth writing about. The last sentence is understated rather than preachy.

                                      6. The Injured Bird · Caring for animals

                                      The four pictures

                                      1. A girl finds a small bird on the ground
                                      2. She puts it gently into a box
                                      3. Her father takes it to the vet
                                      4. The bird flies away

                                      Model composition

                                      One morning, while I was watering the plants along our corridor, I heard a weak chirping sound. On the ground near the staircase lay a small brown bird. One of its wings was bent at an odd angle and it could not fly.

                                      I ran inside and found an empty shoebox. My mother helped me line it with an old towel so that the bird would be warm. Very carefully, I lifted the tiny creature with both hands and placed it inside. It was lighter than I had expected and its heart was beating very fast.

                                      That afternoon, my father drove us to an animal clinic near the market. The vet examined the bird and told us that the wing was only bruised, not broken. She gave us some medicine and told us to keep the bird quiet for a week.

                                      On the eighth day, we carried the box down to the field and opened it. The bird hopped once, then rose into the air and disappeared over the rooftops.

                                      I felt a little sad, but mostly proud.

                                      What makes it work: 'Lighter than I had expected and its heart was beating very fast' is exactly the kind of detail that earns top language marks — it shows the writer imagining the moment rather than describing a drawing. The two-word emotion at the end is honest and avoids a soppy ending.

                                      7. The Skipping Rope · Perseverance

                                      The four pictures

                                      1. A girl trips during the skipping trial while her classmates watch
                                      2. She practises alone in the corridor every evening
                                      3. She misses again and sits down, discouraged
                                      4. On Sports Day she skips without stopping and is given a certificate

                                      Model composition

                                      Last term, our teacher held a skipping trial to choose ten pupils for the Sports Day display. I wanted a place badly, but when my turn came my foot caught the rope on the fourth jump and I stumbled in front of the whole class. Two boys laughed.

                                      That evening, I took my rope down to the corridor outside our flat and practised until it was dark. I did the same the next evening, and the next. Sometimes I managed forty jumps. Sometimes I tripped on the second one and sat down on the cold floor, wanting to give up.

                                      I kept going because my grandmother said that a rope only obeys people who are stubborn.

                                      On Sports Day, I skipped for two whole minutes without a single mistake. Mrs Kaur handed me a certificate and told me she had watched me practising from her window every evening. I was proud, but not of the certificate. I was proud of all the dark evenings nobody saw.

                                      What makes it work: All four pictures are used in order, and the writer adds what the drawings cannot show: the term, the ten places, the two boys laughing, the grandmother's line about the rope. Past tense is held throughout. The ending does what a top-band P3 ending does — it names a feeling and then gives an unexpected reason for it, instead of stopping at "I was very happy".

                                      8. The Lost Little Boy · Helping others

                                      The four pictures

                                      1. At the market, a small boy stands alone and cries
                                      2. A girl kneels down and asks him what has happened
                                      3. She takes him to the information counter and an announcement is made
                                      4. His mother runs over and hugs him

                                      Model composition

                                      One Sunday morning, I was helping my father choose fish at the wet market when I heard a child crying somewhere behind the vegetable stalls. I went to look. A little boy of about four was standing alone between two crates, sobbing so hard that he could not speak.

                                      I knelt down so that I was not taller than him and asked him his name. He said it was Ryan, and that he had let go of his mother's hand to look at a tank of crabs. He did not know his mother's phone number.

                                      I took his hand and walked him to the information counter near the entrance. The uncle there made an announcement over the loudspeaker, and I stayed with Ryan and told him about my cat so that he would stop shaking.

                                      Two minutes later, a woman came running down the aisle with her slippers slapping the wet floor. She lifted Ryan up and held him tightly for a long time.

                                      She thanked me again and again. I only nodded, because my throat felt strange.

                                      What makes it work: The story is told from a clear point of view with small, believable details the pictures do not contain — the crab tank, the slapping slippers, the cat used as a distraction. Notice the kneeling detail in the second paragraph: it shows kindness through an action rather than stating "I was very kind". The last line suggests emotion without naming it, which is a step beyond the usual "I felt very happy" ending.

                                      9. The Shared Umbrella · Thoughtfulness

                                      The four pictures

                                      1. Heavy rain falls as school ends; a girl opens her umbrella
                                      2. She sees a classmate waiting at the gate with no umbrella
                                      3. The two of them walk home under one umbrella
                                      4. The next day the classmate brings her a warm drink and they sit together

                                      Model composition

                                      It rained so heavily on Tuesday afternoon that the drains outside our school were overflowing. I had brought my red umbrella, so I opened it and stepped out of the shelter feeling rather pleased with myself.

                                      Then I saw Kamala standing at the gate. She was pressed against the railing with her bag held over her head, and her shoes were already soaked. She lived in the next block to mine, but we had never once walked home together because she was quiet and I had never bothered to speak to her.

                                      I ran over and held the umbrella above both of us. It was not big enough for two, so my left shoulder was wet through by the time we reached our carpark. We talked the whole way. She was not quiet at all once somebody started.

                                      The next morning, Kamala was waiting outside my classroom with a warm Milo from the canteen. We have eaten recess together every day since.

                                      One wet shoulder, and I gained a friend I had walked past for two years.

                                      What makes it work: The writer earns the last line by admitting something unflattering in the second paragraph — that she had never bothered to speak to Kamala. That admission is what turns a kind deed into a story. The soaked shoulder appears twice, first as a cost and then in the final sentence as a bargain, which gives the composition a shape. Past tense is consistent and the vocabulary is within reach of a Primary 3 writer: overflowing, pressed, soaked, bothered.

                                      10. The Class Plant · Responsibility

                                      The four pictures

                                      1. A boy is made plant monitor and given a watering can
                                      2. During the long weekend he forgets all about it
                                      3. On Tuesday the plant is drooping and its leaves are brown
                                      4. He waters it daily and it flowers again

                                      Model composition

                                      In January, Mr Peh made me the plant monitor of Primary Four Diligence. He handed me a green watering can and told me that the chilli plant on our window ledge was now my responsibility. I promised I would look after it and I meant it.

                                      Then came the long weekend. I spent three days playing games on my father's computer and never thought about the classroom once.

                                      When I walked in on Tuesday morning, the plant had collapsed over the side of its pot. Its leaves were brown and curled, and one of them crumbled when I touched it. Nobody scolded me, which somehow made it worse. I sat at my desk and could not look at the window.

                                      After that, I watered it every single morning before the bell. I moved the pot to the sunnier end of the ledge and pulled off the dead leaves. Six weeks later there were two small white flowers on it, and by June we had four chillies.

                                      I learnt that a promise is not something you say. It is something you do every day, even on holidays.

                                      What makes it work: The second paragraph is only two sentences long, and that is deliberate — the forgetting should feel quick and careless. "Nobody scolded me, which somehow made it worse" is the kind of honest line that moves content into the top band, because it shows guilt instead of announcing it. The recovery is specific: watering, moving the pot, pulling off dead leaves, a count of flowers and chillies. The closing lesson is stated in the writer's own words rather than as a borrowed proverb.

                                      11. Grandmother's Birthday Cake · Gratitude

                                      The four pictures

                                      1. Two children count their pocket money at a table
                                      2. They bake a cake and make a card together
                                      3. The cake comes out lopsided and they look at it in dismay
                                      4. Grandmother blows out the candles and hugs them both

                                      Model composition

                                      My grandmother turned seventy in March. She had looked after my brother and me every afternoon since we were small, and we wanted to give her something she had not paid for herself.

                                      For five weeks we saved every coin we were given, hiding the tin behind the rice cooker. When we counted it on the kitchen table, we had eighteen dollars and forty cents. It was enough for flour, eggs, butter and a packet of candles.

                                      We baked the cake on Saturday while she was at the market. My brother wrote the card and I read the recipe aloud. Everything went well until we took the tin out of the oven. One side of the cake had risen and the other had not, so it leaned over like a tired old building. We stared at it in horror.

                                      We frosted it anyway and hid the worst side against the wall of the plate.

                                      When my grandmother came home and saw the candles, her eyes filled with tears. She said it was the best cake she had ever eaten, and she ate two slices to prove it.

                                      What makes it work: The composition uses all four pictures but gives the third one the most space, because the lopsided cake is where the interest lies. Two details carry the whole story: the tin hidden behind the rice cooker, and hiding the worst side of the cake against the plate. The ending is moving without being sentimental, because the writer proves the claim — she ate two slices — rather than simply asserting that everybody was happy.

                                      12. The Last Leg · Sportsmanship

                                      The four pictures

                                      1. A relay race: a girl receives the baton in second place
                                      2. The runner ahead of her trips and falls
                                      3. She stops, helps the fallen runner up, and they finish last together
                                      4. At assembly the principal gives her a special award while everyone claps

                                      Model composition

                                      I was the last runner in the Primary Four relay and my class had never won anything. When Bala slapped the baton into my hand we were second, only a few steps behind Primary Four Grace, and I thought we might finally do it.

                                      Halfway down the straight, the girl in front of me caught her foot on the edge of the track and went down hard. Her baton bounced away and she did not get up.

                                      I could have run past her. The finishing line was twenty metres away and nobody would have blamed me. Instead I stopped, pulled her up by the arm, and held on while she limped the rest of the way. Both our classes crossed the line last and second last, and the cheering stopped in a strange, sudden silence.

                                      On Monday, Mr Raj called me out at assembly and gave me a Sportsmanship Award. The whole school clapped for a very long time.

                                      I still do not have a medal for running. I have something on my wall that is harder to win.

                                      What makes it work: "I could have run past her" is the strongest sentence in the composition, because it shows the writer choosing rather than simply being nice. The sudden silence in the third paragraph is an observation, not a statement of feeling, and observations score better. The last two lines contrast what she lost with what she gained in eleven words, which is the kind of ending a Primary 4 marker remembers.

                                      A note for parents

                                      Mark one thing at a time. A Primary 3 child told to fix their tense, add more detail, vary their sentences and improve their ending will change nothing. Pick the single weakest of the two scales, say what to do about it in one sentence, and let everything else go until next week.

                                      Document 13

                                      More Grammar Practice — 14 New Sets

                                      Eleven further grammar sets covering the areas that the earlier practice book treats only briefly: articles and determiners, conjunctions, comparatives, verb patterns, conditionals, harder subject–verb agreement, punctuating speech, synthesis and transformation, spelling, editing and grammar cloze.

                                      Work one section at a time. Write your answers on paper, then mark yourself against the answer key at the end. Anything you get wrong goes on your error log and comes back in a week.

                                      GA13 · Articles & determiners · 40 items · P3

                                      Choose the correct word. Write your answer.

                                      1. Nadia found ____ (a / an / the) old coin under the sofa.

                                      2. We waited for ____ (a / an / the) hour outside the clinic.

                                      3. My uncle is ____ (a / an / the) engineer.

                                      4. She wore ____ (a / an / the) uniform to the parade.

                                      5. He has been living in Singapore for ____ (a / an / the) year.

                                      6. ____ (A / An / The) sun rose behind the flats.

                                      7. I would like ____ (a / an / the) apple, please.

                                      8. Mrs Lim is ____ (a / an / the) best teacher in our school.

                                      9. There is ____ (a / an / the) honest answer to that question.

                                      10. We go to ____ (a / the / no word) school by bus.

                                      11. My brother plays ____ (a / an / the) piano every evening.

                                      12. Rahim had ____ (a / the / no word) breakfast at half past six.

                                      13. ____ (A / The / no word) Singapore River runs past Clarke Quay.

                                      14. She is ____ (a / an / the) only pupil who brought an umbrella.

                                      15. I bought a new bag yesterday. ____ (A / An / The) bag I chose is blue.

                                      16. How ____ (much / many / a little) eggs are left in the fridge?

                                      17. There isn't ____ (much / many / few) water in the bottle.

                                      18. Only ____ (a few / a little / much) pupils handed in their forms.

                                      19. Add ____ (a few / a little / many) salt to the soup.

                                      20. I have ____ (little / few / many) money left, so I cannot buy it.

                                      21. ____ (Each / All / Both) of the boys has his own locker.

                                      22. ____ (Both / Each / Every) my parents work in Jurong.

                                      23. ____ (Every / All / Both) child received a sticker.

                                      24. We have ____ (some / any / many) time before the bell.

                                      25. Is there ____ (some / any / many) milk in the cupboard?

                                      26. She did not bring ____ (some / any / much) pencils.

                                      27. ____ (Neither / None / Both) of the two answers is correct — they contradict each other.

                                      28. ____ (Neither / None / Both) of the five boys was chosen.

                                      29. I could not decide between the two, so in the end I took ____ (either / neither / both) book.

                                      30. ____ (All / Every / Each) the children enjoyed the show.

                                      31. There were ____ (fewer / less / little) people at the bus stop than usual.

                                      32. Please use ____ (fewer / less / few) sugar in your drink.

                                      33. ____ (A / An / The) information on the poster was wrong.

                                      34. He gave me ____ (an / some / a) advice about my project.

                                      35. I need ____ (a / an / some) piece of paper.

                                      36. Hardly ____ (some / any / many) pupils were absent today.

                                      37. ____ (One / Both / All) of my shoes is missing.

                                      38. We visited ____ (a / an / the) Science Centre last term.

                                      39. My grandmother goes to ____ (a / an / the) market every morning.

                                      40. There is not ____ (much / many / few) point in arguing.

                                      GA14 · Conjunctions & simple connectors · 40 items · P3

                                      Choose the joining word that makes sense. Write your answer.

                                      1. I wanted to play outside, ____ (and / but / so) it was raining.

                                      2. It was raining, ____ (but / so / or) we stayed indoors.

                                      3. She was tired ____ (because / so / but) she had walked all day.

                                      4. Would you like rice ____ (and / or / but) noodles?

                                      5. Ravi packed his bag ____ (and / but / or) tied his shoelaces.

                                      6. ____ (Although / Because / So) it was late, we finished the project.

                                      7. We will go to the beach ____ (if / but / so) the weather is fine.

                                      8. Wait here ____ (until / because / so) I come back.

                                      9. Hafiz ate his lunch ____ (before / because / but) he went for practice.

                                      10. ____ (When / But / Or) the bell rang, everyone stood up.

                                      11. She did not go to the party ____ (because / but / and) she was unwell.

                                      12. He is only seven, ____ (yet / because / so) he can swim very well.

                                      13. Take an umbrella ____ (in case / because / so) it rains later.

                                      14. Neither my brother ____ (or / nor / and) I could find the keys.

                                      15. Both Meiling ____ (and / or / nor) Sara joined the choir.

                                      16. Either you apologise ____ (and / or / nor) you leave.

                                      17. Not only did he win, ____ (and / but / or) he also broke the record.

                                      18. I will call you ____ (as soon as / because / but) I reach home.

                                      19. The soup was too salty, ____ (but / or / because) nobody complained.

                                      20. ____ (Even though / Because / So) he practised daily, he did not make the team.

                                      21. Speak softly ____ (so that / in case / because) the baby wakes up.

                                      22. Put on your shoes ____ (so that / because / although) you can go out.

                                      23. Anita reads ____ (so / because / therefore) she writes very well.

                                      24. ____ (After / Because / So) finishing his homework, Kumar washed the dishes.

                                      25. He missed the bus ____ (as / but / or) he woke up late.

                                      26. We cannot leave ____ (until / because / so) everyone is ready.

                                      27. Jaya sings well. ____ (However / Because / And), she is shy on stage.

                                      28. It was crowded. ____ (But / Because / So) we found seats in the end.

                                      29. The road was closed. ____ (Therefore / However / Although), the bus was diverted.

                                      30. ____ (Either / Neither / Both) my sister nor my cousin can swim.

                                      31. She looked everywhere ____ (but / and / or) could not find her ruler.

                                      32. Wash your hands ____ (before / because / or) you eat, so that no dirt gets on your food.

                                      33. ____ (Once / Because / So) the film ended, we walked home.

                                      34. Hurry up, ____ (or / and / but) we will be late.

                                      35. I like durian ____ (but / because / so) my mother cannot stand it.

                                      36. The pupils cheered ____ (when / but / or) the goal was scored.

                                      37. He kept quiet ____ (since / but / or) he did not want to argue.

                                      38. ____ (Although / However / Because) she tried very hard, she could not open the jar.

                                      39. Bring a jacket ____ (as / but / or) the hall is cold.

                                      40. We had no money left, ____ (so / because / although) we walked home.

                                      GA18 · Subject–verb agreement · harder cases · P6

                                      These are the cases pupils get wrong most often at Primary 6. Choose the correct verb.

                                      1. The list of names ____ (is / are) on the noticeboard.

                                      2. A bunch of keys ____ (has / have) been left on the table.

                                      3. Neither the coach nor the players ____ (was / were) satisfied.

                                      4. Neither the players nor the coach ____ (was / were) satisfied.

                                      5. Every one of the answers ____ (is / are) wrong.

                                      6. Economics ____ (is / are) taught only in secondary school.

                                      7. The scissors ____ (is / are) in the top drawer.

                                      8. Ten dollars ____ (is / are) too much for a pencil case.

                                      9. Three quarters of the cake ____ (has / have) been eaten.

                                      10. Three quarters of the pupils ____ (has / have) arrived.

                                      11. There ____ (is / are) a pen and two rulers on the desk.

                                      12. Here ____ (is / are) the photographs you asked for.

                                      13. The number of complaints ____ (is / are) falling.

                                      14. A number of complaints ____ (has / have) been received.

                                      15. My aunt, together with her two sons, ____ (is / are) visiting us.

                                      16. Rice and curry ____ (is / are) my usual lunch.

                                      17. The bread and butter ____ (is / are) on the tray.

                                      18. Each of the twins ____ (has / have) a different bicycle.

                                      19. Both of the twins ____ (has / have) bicycles.

                                      20. One of my shoes ____ (is / are) missing.

                                      21. The committee ____ (is / are) meeting this afternoon.

                                      22. Physics and chemistry ____ (is / are) taught in the same room.

                                      23. Nobody in the class ____ (knows / know) the answer.

                                      24. Everybody ____ (has / have) their own opinion on this.

                                      25. Somebody ____ (has / have) left the tap running.

                                      26. The police ____ (is / are) still searching for the owner.

                                      27. A pair of gloves ____ (has / have) been left behind.

                                      28. The furniture in the hall ____ (is / are) very old.

                                      29. My trousers ____ (is / are) too short now.

                                      30. Either of the two answers ____ (is / are) acceptable, according to the marking scheme.

                                      31. Half of the water ____ (has / have) evaporated.

                                      32. Half of the bottles ____ (is / are) empty.

                                      33. The teacher, as well as the pupils, ____ (was / were) pleased.

                                      34. Measles ____ (is / are) a serious illness in young children.

                                      35. Twenty kilometres ____ (is / are) a long way to cycle.

                                      36. There ____ (was / were) nobody left in the hall.

                                      37. Not one of the answers ____ (was / were) correct.

                                      38. Most of the pupils ____ (has / have) handed in their forms.

                                      39. The cost of the tickets ____ (has / have) risen again.

                                      40. Neither of my parents ____ (lets / let) me go.

                                      GA15 · Comparatives & superlatives · 40 items · P4

                                      Choose the correct option.

                                      1. This bag is ____ than mine. (1) heavy (2) heavier (3) heaviest (4) more heavy

                                      2. Of all the pupils, Jun Hao is the ____. (1) tall (2) taller (3) tallest (4) most tall

                                      3. Durians are ____ expensive than mangoes. (1) much (2) more (3) most (4) very

                                      4. That was the ____ film I have ever seen. (1) bored (2) boring (3) more boring (4) most boring

                                      5. Her handwriting is ____ than her brother's. (1) neat (2) neater (3) neatest (4) more neat

                                      6. Today is ____ than yesterday. (1) hot (2) hotter (3) hottest (4) more hot

                                      7. This is the ____ book on the shelf. (1) thin (2) thinner (3) thinnest (4) most thin

                                      8. My results this term are ____ than last term's. (1) good (2) better (3) best (4) more good

                                      9. He plays the guitar ____ than I do. (1) good (2) well (3) better (4) best

                                      10. This is the ____ I have ever felt. (1) bad (2) worse (3) worst (4) badly

                                      29. Everyday speech: Until now I still don't understand. (1) Even now I still do not understand. (2) Until now I still don't understand. (3) Till now I still don't understand. (4) Until now I am still not understand.

                                      31. Everyday speech: My mother she is a nurse. (1) My mother is a nurse. (2) My mother she is a nurse. (3) My mother, she is a nurse. (4) She my mother is a nurse.

                                      32. Everyday speech: I no need help. (1) I do not need help. (2) I no need help. (3) I don't need no help. (4) I am no need help.

                                      33. Everyday speech: She go there by taking bus. (1) She goes there by bus. (2) She go there by taking bus. (3) She goes there by taking bus. (4) She go there by the bus.

                                      34. Everyday speech: Later you fall down, then you know. (1) Be careful, or you will fall. (2) Later you fall down, then you know. (3) Later you will fall down, then you know. (4) You fall down later, then you know.

                                      35. Everyday speech: Anyhow do also can. (1) It does not have to be done carefully. (2) Anyhow do also can. (3) Anyhow do is also can. (4) Doing anyhow also can.

                                      36. Everyday speech: I am staying at home the whole day already. (1) I have been at home all day. (2) I am staying at home the whole day already. (3) I stay at home whole day already. (4) I have stayed at home the whole day already.

                                      37. Everyday speech: The queue damn long. (1) The queue was extremely long. (2) The queue damn long. (3) The queue is damn long. (4) The queue very damn long.

                                      38. Everyday speech: He is the more better player. (1) He is the better player. (2) He is the more better player. (3) He is more better player. (4) He is the most better player.

                                      39. Everyday speech: Next time onwards I will remember. (1) In future I will remember. (2) Next time onwards I will remember. (3) From next time onwards I will remember. (4) Next time onward I will remember.

                                      40. Everyday speech: Discuss about the problem. (1) Discuss the problem. (2) Discuss about the problem. (3) Discuss on the problem. (4) Discuss for the problem.

                                      GA25 · Verb pairs that get confused · 40 items · P5

                                      These pairs look similar but behave differently. Write the correct verb.

                                      1. Please ____ (lend / borrow) me your ruler until recess.

                                      2. May I ____ (lend / borrow) your ruler until recess?

                                      3. My grandmother ____ (taught / learnt) me how to fold dumplings.

                                      4. I ____ (taught / learnt) how to fold dumplings from my grandmother.

                                      5. Please ____ (bring / take) these books to the library for me.

                                      6. Please ____ (bring / take) me a glass of water from the kitchen.

                                      7. The cat likes to ____ (lie / lay) on the warm windowsill.

                                      8. Please ____ (lie / lay) the tray on the table.

                                      9. The sun ____ (rises / raises) at about seven o'clock here.

                                      10. The shopkeeper ____ (rose / raised) his prices again last month.

                                      11. I could not ____ (hear / listen) what he was saying over the noise.

                                      12. Please ____ (hear / listen) carefully to the announcement.

                                      13. Did you ____ (see / watch) the man in the blue shirt?

                                      14. We sat and ____ (watched / saw) the whole match on television last night.

                                      15. The dog followed him home and would not ____ (leave / go).

                                      16. Mrs Tan asked him to ____ (check / control) his answer again.

                                      17. The noise from upstairs ____ (disturbed / troubled) my sleep all night.

                                      18. He ____ (spent / used) all his pocket money on a comic yesterday.

                                      19. Please ____ (close / near) the door behind you.

                                      20. The nurse ____ (took / made) his temperature every two hours.

                                      21. Can you ____ (tell / say) the difference between these two shades?

                                      22. What did he ____ (say / tell) when you asked him?

                                      23. He ____ (said / told) me that the shop had closed.

                                      24. I ____ (left / forgot) my wallet on the bus this morning.

                                      25. I ____ (left / forgot) her birthday completely.

                                      26. She ____ (took / made) a photograph of the whole class.

                                      27. They are going to ____ (make / do) a decision this evening.

                                      28. We must ____ (do / make) our homework before dinner.

                                      29. The heavy rain ____ (caused / made) the match to be cancelled.

                                      30. He ____ (made / caused) his sister cry by hiding her book.

                                      31. Please ____ (turn off / close) the tap; you are wasting water.

                                      32. The shop ____ (opens / opened) at nine every morning.

                                      33. Her explanation did not ____ (answer / reply) my question.

                                      34. She did not ____ (reply / answer) to my message for two days.

                                      35. He ____ (kicked / knocked) the ball hard with his right foot and it hit the fence.

                                      36. The cold weather ____ (forced / made) him to wear two jumpers.

                                      37. I must ____ (ask / question) my parents before I agree.

                                      38. Please do not ____ (touch / feel) the wet paint.

                                      39. The doctor told him to ____ (eat / take) more vegetables.

                                      40. Remember to ____ (take / eat) your medicine after dinner.

                                      GA26 · Present perfect or past simple · 35 items · P5

                                      Use the past simple for a finished time, and the present perfect when the time is not finished or not stated. Write the correct form.

                                      1. I ____ (finished / have finished) my homework already.

                                      2. I ____ (finished / have finished) my homework at six o'clock.

                                      3. She ____ (lived / has lived) in Singapore since 2019.

                                      4. She ____ (lived / has lived) in Penang for two years before she moved.

                                      5. ____ (Did / Have) you ever eaten durian?

                                      6. ____ (Did / Have) you eat durian at the party last night?

                                      7. We ____ (visited / have visited) the museum three times this year.

                                      8. We ____ (visited / have visited) the museum three times last year.

                                      9. He ____ (lost / has lost) his keys and has not found them yet.

                                      10. He ____ (lost / has lost) his keys on Tuesday but found them again.

                                      11. They ____ (just left / have just left) the building.

                                      12. The bus ____ (left / has left) ten minutes ago.

                                      13. I ____ (was / have) never been to Japan.

                                      14. My father ____ (went / has gone) to Japan in 2015.

                                      15. How long ____ (did / have) you known Priya?

                                      16. When ____ (did / have) you meet Priya?

                                      17. The rain ____ (has / did) stopped, so we can go out.

                                      18. It ____ (rained / has rained) heavily all last week.

                                      19. I ____ (saw / have seen) this film twice and I still like it.

                                      20. I ____ (saw / have seen) that film on Saturday.

                                      21. She ____ (broke / has broken) her leg and is still in plaster.

                                      22. She ____ (broke / has broken) her leg when she was nine.

                                      23. We ____ (lived / have lived) in this flat since I was born.

                                      24. ____ (Did / Has) the postman come yet?

                                      25. The postman ____ (came / has come) at eleven this morning.

                                      26. Nobody ____ (found / has found) the answer so far.

                                      27. Nobody ____ (found / has found) the answer in yesterday's lesson.

                                      28. I ____ (did not see / have not seen) him since Monday.

                                      29. I ____ (saw / have seen) him on Monday.

                                      30. Our team ____ (won / has won) every match this season.

                                      31. Our team ____ (won / has won) every match last season.

                                      32. ____ (Did / Have) you finished your lunch?

                                      33. Prices ____ (rose / have risen) a great deal since last year.

                                      34. Prices ____ (rose / have risen) sharply in 2020.

                                      35. This is the first time I ____ (tried / have tried) sushi.

                                      Answer Key

                                      GA13 · Articles & determiners · 40 items · P3

                                      • 1 an — 'Old' begins with a vowel sound, so use 'an'.
                                      • 2 an — 'Hour' begins with a vowel sound — the h is silent.
                                      • 3 an — 'Engineer' begins with a vowel sound.
                                      • 4 a — 'Uniform' begins with a 'yoo' sound, which is a consonant sound.
                                      • 5 a — 'Year' begins with a 'y' consonant sound.
                                      • 6 The — There is only one sun, so use 'the'.
                                      • 7 an — 'Apple' begins with a vowel sound.
                                      • 8 the — Superlatives take 'the'.
                                      • 9 an — The h in 'honest' is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound.
                                      • 10 no word — No article before 'school' when you mean attending lessons.
                                      • 11 the — Musical instruments take 'the' after 'play'.
                                      • 12 no word — No article before meal names.
                                      • 13 The — Rivers take 'the'.
                                      • 14 the — 'Only' points to one particular person, so use 'the'.
                                      • 15 The — Second mention of something already introduced takes 'the'.
                                      • 16 many — 'Eggs' can be counted, so use 'many'.
                                      • 17 much — 'Water' cannot be counted, so use 'much'.
                                      • 18 a few — 'Pupils' can be counted, so use 'a few'.
                                      • 19 a little — 'Salt' cannot be counted, so use 'a little'.
                                      • 20 little — 'Little' without 'a' means almost none.
                                      • 21 Each — 'Has' is singular, which matches 'each'.
                                      • 22 Both — 'Work' is plural and there are two parents.
                                      • 23 Every — 'Child' is singular, so use 'every'.
                                      • 24 some — Use 'some' in a positive statement.
                                      • 25 any — Use 'any' in questions and negatives.
                                      • 26 any — Use 'any' after a negative.
                                      • 27 Neither — 'Neither' is used for two things and takes a singular verb.
                                      • 28 None — Use 'none' for more than two.
                                      • 29 neither — 'Neither' means not one and not the other of the two.
                                      • 30 All — 'Children' is plural, so use 'all'.
                                      • 31 fewer — 'People' can be counted, so use 'fewer'.
                                      • 32 less — 'Sugar' cannot be counted, so use 'less'.
                                      • 33 The — 'Information' cannot be counted, so it never takes 'a'.
                                      • 34 some — 'Advice' cannot be counted, so it takes 'some' rather than 'a'.
                                      • 35 a — 'A piece of' makes an uncountable noun countable.
                                      • 36 any — 'Hardly' is negative in meaning, so use 'any'.
                                      • 37 One — 'Is' is singular, so use 'one'.
                                      • 38 the — 'The Science Centre' is one particular place the reader already knows, so it takes 'the'.
                                      • 39 the — 'The market' means the one she always goes to.
                                      • 40 much — 'Point' here is uncountable in meaning, so use 'much'.

                                      GA14 · Conjunctions & simple connectors · 40 items · P3

                                      • 1 but — Two ideas that disagree are joined by 'but'.
                                      • 2 so — 'So' introduces the result.
                                      • 3 because — 'Because' gives the reason.
                                      • 4 or — 'Or' offers a choice.
                                      • 5 and — Two similar actions are joined by 'and'.
                                      • 6 Although — 'Although' shows a contrast.
                                      • 7 if — 'If' introduces a condition.
                                      • 8 until — 'Until' shows up to what time.
                                      • 9 before — 'Before' shows which happened first.
                                      • 10 When — 'When' shows the time at which something happened.
                                      • 11 because — 'Because' gives the reason.
                                      • 12 yet — 'Yet' shows a surprising contrast.
                                      • 13 in case — 'In case' means as a precaution.
                                      • 14 nor — 'Neither' is always paired with 'nor'.
                                      • 15 and — 'Both' is always paired with 'and'.
                                      • 16 or — 'Either' is always paired with 'or'.
                                      • 17 but — 'Not only' is paired with 'but also'.
                                      • 18 as soon as — 'As soon as' means immediately after.
                                      • 19 but — Two main clauses in contrast are joined by 'but'.
                                      • 20 Even though — 'Even though' shows a strong contrast.
                                      • 21 in case — 'In case' warns of a possibility.
                                      • 22 so that — 'So that' shows the purpose.
                                      • 23 so — 'So' links a cause to its result in one sentence.
                                      • 24 After — 'After' plus -ing shows the earlier action.
                                      • 25 as — 'As' can mean 'because'.
                                      • 26 until — 'Until' means not before that time.
                                      • 27 However — 'However' starts a new sentence and takes a comma after it.
                                      • 28 But — 'But' shows the contrast between the two sentences.
                                      • 29 Therefore — 'Therefore' shows the result.
                                      • 30 Neither — 'Neither … nor' makes both parts negative.
                                      • 31 but — The second idea contradicts the first.
                                      • 32 before — The clause 'so that no dirt gets on your food' tells you the washing comes first.
                                      • 33 Once — 'Once' means as soon as.
                                      • 34 or — 'Or' warns of the consequence.
                                      • 35 but — 'But' joins two ideas that disagree.
                                      • 36 when — 'When' shows that the two things happened at the same moment.
                                      • 37 since — 'Since' can mean 'because'.
                                      • 38 Although — 'Although' shows a contrast and comes at the start of the clause.
                                      • 39 as — 'As' gives the reason.
                                      • 40 so — 'So' gives the result.

                                      GA18 · Subject–verb agreement · harder cases · P6

                                      • 1 is — The subject is 'list', not 'names'.
                                      • 2 has — The subject is 'bunch'.
                                      • 3 were — With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'players'.
                                      • 4 was — The nearer subject is now 'coach', which is singular.
                                      • 5 is — The subject is 'every one'.
                                      • 6 is — Subjects ending in -ics take a singular verb.
                                      • 7 are — 'Scissors' is always plural.
                                      • 8 is — An amount of money is treated as one thing.
                                      • 9 has — 'Cake' is uncountable, so the fraction is singular.
                                      • 10 have — 'Pupils' is plural, so the fraction is plural.
                                      • 11 are — With a compound subject, careful written English uses 'are'. You will also hear 'There is a pen and two rulers', which follows the nearer noun.
                                      • 12 are — The subject is 'photographs'.
                                      • 13 is — 'The number' is singular.
                                      • 14 have — 'A number of' means several, so it is plural.
                                      • 15 is — 'Together with' does not change the subject.
                                      • 16 is — 'Rice and curry' is one dish.
                                      • 17 is — 'Bread and butter' is treated as a single item.
                                      • 18 has — 'Each' is singular.
                                      • 19 have — 'Both' is plural.
                                      • 20 is — The subject is 'one'.
                                      • 21 is — A committee acting as one body takes a singular verb.
                                      • 22 are — Two separate subjects make a plural.
                                      • 23 knows — 'Nobody' is singular.
                                      • 24 has — 'Everybody' is singular.
                                      • 25 has — 'Somebody' is singular.
                                      • 26 are — 'Police' is treated as plural.
                                      • 27 has — The subject is 'pair'.
                                      • 28 is — 'Furniture' is uncountable.
                                      • 29 are — 'Trousers' is always plural.
                                      • 30 is — 'Either' means one of the two, so it is singular.
                                      • 31 has — 'Water' is uncountable.
                                      • 32 are — 'Bottles' is plural.
                                      • 33 was — 'As well as' does not change the subject.
                                      • 34 is — Illnesses ending in -es like 'measles' are singular.
                                      • 35 is — A single distance is treated as one thing.
                                      • 36 was — 'Nobody' is singular.
                                      • 37 was — 'Not one' is singular.
                                      • 38 have — 'Pupils' is plural, so the fraction word takes a plural verb.
                                      • 39 has — The subject is 'cost'.
                                      • 40 lets — 'Neither' is singular, so the verb takes -s.

                                      GA15 · Comparatives & superlatives · 40 items · P4

                                      1 (2) · 2 (3) · 3 (2) · 4 (4) · 5 (2) · 6 (2) · 7 (3) · 8 (2) · 9 (3) · 10 (3) · 11 (3) · 12 (3) · 13 (3) · 14 (2) · 15 (3) · 16 (3) · 17 (1) · 18 (1) · 19 (4) · 20 (2) · 21 (1) · 22 (2) · 23 (3) · 24 (3) · 25 (1) · 26 (2) · 27 (3) · 28 (1) · 29 (3) · 30 (2) · 31 (1) · 32 (3) · 33 (3) · 34 (2) · 35 (2) · 36 (2) · 37 (3) · 38 (3) · 39 (2) · 40 (3)

                                      • 1 heavier — One-syllable and two-syllable words ending in -y take -er.
                                      • 2 tallest — Comparing three or more takes the superlative with 'the'.
                                      • 3 more — Long adjectives take 'more' for the comparative.
                                      • 4 most boring — Comparing against all films needs the superlative.
                                      • 5 neater — 'Neat' is short, so add -er.
                                      • 6 hotter — Double the t before adding -er.
                                      • 7 thinnest — Double the n before -est.
                                      • 8 better — 'Good' becomes 'better'.
                                      • 9 better — Comparing two actions needs 'better', not 'well'.
                                      • 10 worst — 'Bad' becomes 'worse' then 'worst'.
                                      • 11 more slowly — Adverbs ending in -ly take 'more'.
                                      • 12 fastest — 'Fast' is both adjective and adverb; the superlative is 'fastest'.
                                      • 13 fewer — 'People' can be counted, so use 'fewer'.
                                      • 14 less — 'Homework' cannot be counted, so use 'less'.
                                      • 15 the narrower — With only two things, use 'the' plus the comparative.
                                      • 16 the youngest — Superlatives need 'the'.
                                      • 17 big — 'As … as' takes the plain adjective.
                                      • 18 twice as much as — The pattern is 'twice as much as'.
                                      • 19 the most — Superlative of a long adjective is 'the most'.
                                      • 20 earlier — The 'the … the' pattern uses two comparatives.
                                      • 21 worse — Comparing two things needs 'worse'.
                                      • 22 more — Adverbs in -ly take 'more'.
                                      • 23 the most — Three items need the superlative with 'the'.
                                      • 24 much — 'Much' strengthens a comparative; 'very' cannot.
                                      • 25 clearer — Two things take the comparative.
                                      • 26 almost — 'Almost as … as' works; 'more as' does not.
                                      • 27 more pleasant — 'Pleasant' is a long adjective, so use 'more'.
                                      • 28 latest — A superlative adverb normally has no 'the': 'fastest', 'latest', 'hardest'.
                                      • 29 lowest — Comparing all shops needs the superlative.
                                      • 30 faster — Comparing two takes 'faster'.
                                      • 31 good — 'As … as' takes the plain adjective 'good'.
                                      • 32 tastiest — -y becomes -iest in the superlative.
                                      • 33 quietest — Four brothers means the superlative.
                                      • 34 much — Use 'much' before a comparative.
                                      • 35 less — 'Less crowded' is the comparative of 'crowded' going downwards.
                                      • 36 farther — 'Far' becomes 'farther'.
                                      • 37 more neatly — Comparing two writers needs the comparative adverb.
                                      • 38 wisest — 'Wise' takes -est.
                                      • 39 less — 'Less comfortable' is the correct downward comparative.
                                      • 40 longest — Comparing seven days needs the superlative.

                                      GA16 · Verb patterns · gerunds & infinitives · P5

                                      • 1 singing — 'Enjoy' is always followed by -ing.
                                      • 2 to tell — 'Decide' is followed by 'to'.
                                      • 3 closing — 'Mind' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 4 to share — 'Agree' is followed by 'to'.
                                      • 5 writing — 'Finish' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 6 to see — 'Hope' is followed by 'to'.
                                      • 7 eating — 'Avoid' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 8 to be — 'Promise' is followed by 'to'.
                                      • 9 running — 'Keep' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 10 to ride — 'Teach someone' is followed by 'to'.
                                      • 11 going — 'Fancy' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 12 to tidy — 'Refuse' is followed by 'to'.
                                      • 13 hearing — 'Look forward to' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 14 to get — 'Manage' is followed by 'to'.
                                      • 15 living — 'Imagine' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 16 to carry — 'Offer' is followed by 'to'.
                                      • 17 waking — 'Be used to' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 18 to drink — 'Advise someone' is followed by 'to'.
                                      • 19 trying — A preposition such as 'of' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 20 stay — 'Would rather' is followed by the plain verb.
                                      • 21 repeat — 'Make someone' is followed by the plain verb.
                                      • 22 find — 'Let' is followed by the plain verb.
                                      • 23 to leave — 'Be allowed' is followed by 'to'.
                                      • 24 worrying — 'Cannot help' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 25 to be — 'Pretend' is followed by 'to'.
                                      • 26 complaining — 'It is no use' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 27 leave — 'Had better' is followed by the plain verb.
                                      • 28 tapping — 'Stop' plus -ing means stop that action.
                                      • 29 to buy — 'Stop to' means stop in order to do something.
                                      • 30 locking — 'Remember' plus -ing means recalling a past action.
                                      • 31 to post — 'Remember to' means do not forget to do it.
                                      • 32 postponing — 'Suggest' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 33 making — 'Busy' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 34 arriving — The preposition 'for' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 35 to do — After 'nothing left' we use 'to'.
                                      • 36 to play — 'Learn' is followed by 'to'.
                                      • 37 to have — 'Would like' is followed by 'to'.
                                      • 38 breaking — 'Deny' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 39 saying — 'Practise' is followed by -ing.
                                      • 40 to bring — 'Forget to' means do not fail to do it.

                                      GA17 · Conditionals · if-clauses · P5

                                      • 1 melts — For things always true, use the present in both halves.
                                      • 2 will cancel — Likely future: present tense in the if-clause, 'will' in the other.
                                      • 3 were — For imagining, use 'were' with 'I'.
                                      • 4 will get — A real possibility takes 'will'.
                                      • 5 would cycle — Imagining an unreal present takes 'would'.
                                      • 6 comes — A general fact takes the present tense.
                                      • 7 had left — Regret about the past takes 'had' plus the past participle.
                                      • 8 would have — The past unreal pattern is 'would have' plus the past participle.
                                      • 9 is — Do not use 'will' in the if-clause.
                                      • 10 knew — Imagining the present takes the past tense in the if-clause.
                                      • 11 will die — A likely result takes 'will'.
                                      • 12 were — Imagining takes 'were' in careful written English.
                                      • 13 would have taken — The past is unreal, so use 'would have taken'.
                                      • 14 will miss — 'Unless' means 'if not' and takes the same pattern as a likely future.
                                      • 15 had called — The if-clause about the past takes 'had called'.
                                      • 16 heat — 'You heat' is the present tense for a general truth.
                                      • 17 would build — This is imagining, so use 'would'.
                                      • 18 is — Keep 'will' out of the if-clause.
                                      • 19 had not given — The past unreal if-clause takes 'had not given'.
                                      • 20 get — A scientific fact takes the present in both halves.
                                      • 21 knew — He does not know now, so use the past tense.
                                      • 22 would have — Use 'would have' plus the past participle.
                                      • 23 bring — 'Provided' behaves like 'if' and takes the present.
                                      • 24 had not been — The past unreal takes 'had not been'.
                                      • 25 If — 'If' introduces the condition. (In very formal writing you may also see 'Should you have any problems'.)
                                      • 26 would delete — 'If I were you' is always followed by 'would'.
                                      • 27 reaches — 'Smoke' is singular, and a general truth takes the present.
                                      • 28 will be — A real plan takes 'will'.
                                      • 29 had trained — The cause is in the past, so use 'had trained'.
                                      • 30 had known — Regret about the past takes 'had known'.

                                      GA19 · Punctuating speech & dialogue · 30 items · P5
