                                      1. The soup was too hot, so Mei blew on it to make it ____. (1) cool (2) cold (3) warm up (4) boil

                                      2. Our teacher asked us to ____ in a straight line. (1) queue (2) crowd (3) gather (4) scatter

                                      3. The puppy was so ____ that it fitted into one hand. (1) tiny (2) huge (3) heavy (4) tall

                                      4. Ravi ____ the door gently so as not to wake the baby. (1) closed (2) slammed (3) banged (4) kicked

                                      5. The bag was so ____ that I had to use both hands. (1) heavy (2) light (3) empty (4) soft

                                      6. We could see the bottom of the pool because the water was very ____. (1) clear (2) deep (3) cold (4) wide

                                      7. The bread had gone ____ after three days in the tin. (1) stale (2) fresh (3) warm (4) sweet

                                      8. My father's car is ____ than my uncle's van. (1) smaller (2) small (3) smallest (4) more small

                                      9. Please put the rubbish in the ____. (1) bin (2) shelf (3) cupboard (4) drawer

                                      10. The kitten was ____ of the vacuum cleaner. (1) afraid (2) angry (3) proud (4) kind

                                      11. Nadia was ____ when she got a sticker for her work. (1) pleased (2) upset (3) bored (4) tired

                                      12. The floor was slippery, so we walked ____. (1) carefully (2) quickly (3) loudly (4) cheerfully

                                      13. He ____ his shoelaces before the race. (1) tied (2) cut (3) washed (4) dropped

                                      14. The sun was so bright that I had to ____ my eyes. (1) shade (2) open (3) wash (4) close up

                                      15. My grandmother ____ me a story every Sunday. (1) tells (2) says (3) speaks (4) talks

                                      16. We waited at the bus ____ outside our block for ten minutes, but only taxis went past. (1) stop (2) station (3) park (4) shelter

                                      17. The soup needs more salt because it tastes of ____. (1) nothing (2) everything (3) anything (4) something

                                      18. Gopal is the ____ boy in our class; he is taller than everyone. (1) tallest (2) taller (3) tall (4) most tall

                                      19. The library is ____ on Sundays, so we went on Monday. (1) closed (2) opened (3) open (4) closing

                                      20. Please ____ the window; the room is stuffy. (1) open (2) close (3) shut (4) lock

                                      21. The shirt was too small, so my mother ____ it to my cousin. (1) gave (2) took (3) brought (4) borrowed

                                      22. A ____ of birds flew over the field. (1) flock (2) herd (3) shoal (4) pack

                                      23. The ice cream began to ____ in the sun. (1) melt (2) freeze (3) burn (4) boil

                                      24. He wiped the table with a damp ____. (1) cloth (2) paper (3) broom (4) brush

                                      25. The path was very ____, so we had to climb slowly. (1) steep (2) flat (3) wide (4) smooth

                                      26. Our dog ____ loudly whenever the doorbell rings. (1) barks (2) meows (3) chirps (4) roars

                                      27. Siti ____ the flour and the eggs together in a bowl. (1) mixed (2) poured (3) cut (4) spread

                                      28. The baby is ____, so please speak softly. (1) asleep (2) awake (3) hungry (4) noisy

                                      29. I ____ my bicycle to school every day. (1) ride (2) drive (3) row (4) sail

                                      30. The floor was ____ with sand after the beach trip. (1) covered (2) cleaned (3) emptied (4) dried

                                      31. Please ____ your name at the top of the page. (1) write (2) draw (3) read (4) say

                                      32. There were ____ people on the bus, so we all got a seat. (1) few (2) many (3) lots of (4) plenty of

                                      33. The kite flew high because the wind was ____. (1) strong (2) weak (3) still (4) gentle

                                      34. He was ____ after running twice round the field. (1) tired (2) fresh (3) hungry (4) bored

                                      35. Mrs Ong ____ the register every morning. (1) takes (2) makes (3) does (4) gives

                                      36. The milk has gone ____; do not drink it. (1) sour (2) sweet (3) fresh (4) cold

                                      37. We washed our ____ before we ate. (1) hands (2) hand (3) handed (4) hanged

                                      38. The lift was ____, so we took the stairs. (1) broken (2) fixed (3) new (4) clean

                                      39. Please be ____; the baby is sleeping. (1) quiet (2) loud (3) fast (4) slow

                                      40. My sister is ____ at drawing than I am. (1) better (2) good (3) best (4) more good

                                      41. The parcel was ____ in brown paper. (1) wrapped (2) opened (3) torn (4) posted

                                      42. There is a ____ in my sock where my toe shows. (1) hole (2) whole (3) stain (4) button

                                      43. The teacher asked us to ____ our books on the shelf. (1) arrange (2) throw (3) tear (4) hide

                                      44. We ____ the bird fly away from the branch. (1) watched (2) listened (3) heard of (4) looked

                                      45. The shop sells ____ of every colour. (1) balloons (2) balloon (3) a balloon (4) the balloon

                                      46. It was so cold that we could see our ____. (1) breath (2) breathe (3) breathing (4) breathed

                                      47. Please ____ the rubbish out before dinner. (1) take (2) bring (3) send (4) carry in

                                      48. The cat sat ____ the mat and would not move. (1) on (2) in (3) at (4) of

                                      49. My uncle ____ in a hospital as a nurse. (1) works (2) work (3) working (4) worked at

                                      50. I could not find my pencil case ____. (1) anywhere (2) somewhere (3) nowhere (4) everywhere

                                      VA20 · Shades of meaning · choosing the right strength · P4

                                      All four options are close in meaning. Choose the one whose strength fits the sentence.

                                      1. The water in the kettle was ____ — it was bubbling fiercely. (1) boiling (2) warm (3) tepid (4) cool

                                      2. The afternoon was pleasantly ____, not hot at all. (1) warm (2) boiling (3) scorching (4) freezing

                                      3. It was so ____ outside that the tar on the road had softened. (1) scorching (2) warm (3) mild (4) cool

                                      4. He was ____ about losing the match but got over it by dinner. (1) disappointed (2) devastated (3) furious (4) delighted

                                      5. She was ____ when her grandmother's ring was stolen. (1) devastated (2) disappointed (3) puzzled (4) amused

                                      6. I was ____ by the noise from the flat above, though I soon got used to it. (1) annoyed (2) enraged (3) devastated (4) horrified

                                      7. The referee was ____ when the player spat at him, and sent him off at once. (1) enraged (2) annoyed (3) irritated (4) cross

                                      8. The soup was ____; we finished it, but nobody asked for more. (1) tasty (2) delicious (3) superb (4) mouth-watering

                                      9. The sound of the drill was ____ and gave me a headache. (1) deafening (2) faint (3) soft (4) gentle

                                      10. From the other room came a ____ hum I could barely hear. (1) faint (2) deafening (3) loud (4) thunderous

                                      11. The path was ____ in places, but never so sharp that we had to use our hands. (1) sloping (2) steep (3) sheer (4) vertical

                                      12. He gave the door a ____ push and it swung open without a sound. (1) gentle (2) violent (3) savage (4) furious

                                      13. She was ____ of spiders and would not enter the shed. (1) terrified (2) wary (3) curious (4) fond

                                      14. I am a little ____ of dogs I do not know. (1) wary (2) terrified (3) petrified (4) fond

                                      15. The old bridge was so ____ that two planks gave way as we crossed. (1) rickety (2) unsteady (3) wobbly (4) creaky

                                      16. He is ____ of his sister's exam results and tells everyone how hard she worked. (1) proud (2) jealous (3) envious (4) resentful

                                      17. The queue moved ____; we waited almost an hour. (1) slowly (2) quickly (3) briskly (4) rapidly

                                      18. She answered ____, before I had even finished asking. (1) instantly (2) slowly (3) eventually (4) reluctantly

                                      19. The room was ____ after the party — nothing was in its place. (1) chaotic (2) untidy (3) dusty (4) plain

                                      20. My desk is a little ____ but I know where everything is. (1) untidy (2) chaotic (3) spotless (4) ruined

                                      21. The soup was ____; I had three bowls. (1) delicious (2) edible (3) acceptable (4) bland

                                      22. The meal was ____ — not good, but we were hungry enough. (1) edible (2) delicious (3) superb (4) magnificent

                                      23. He made a ____ mistake that cost the team the match. (1) serious (2) slight (3) tiny (4) harmless

                                      24. There was a ____ difference between the two shades of blue. (1) slight (2) enormous (3) vast (4) huge

                                      25. The crowd was ____ when the goal was disallowed, but nobody left their seat. (1) annoyed (2) furious (3) enraged (4) incensed

                                      26. She looked ____ when I explained it a second time. (1) puzzled (2) furious (3) delighted (4) terrified

                                      27. After the hike we were ____ and fell asleep in the car. (1) exhausted (2) tired (3) sleepy (4) bored

                                      28. I am a bit ____ this evening but I can finish the chapter. (1) tired (2) exhausted (3) shattered (4) drained

                                      29. The rain was ____; we were soaked in ten seconds. (1) torrential (2) light (3) gentle (4) fine

                                      30. A ____ drizzle was falling, hardly enough to wet the path. (1) light (2) torrential (3) heavy (4) violent

                                      31. He gave a ____ answer and would say nothing more. (1) curt (2) detailed (3) lengthy (4) thorough

                                      32. Her explanation was ____ and covered every step. (1) thorough (2) curt (3) brief (4) vague

                                      33. The shop was ____; one customer stood at the counter and nobody else. (1) quiet (2) deserted (3) empty (4) abandoned

                                      34. The train was ____; we had to stand but there was room to turn round. (1) full (2) packed (3) crammed (4) jammed

                                      35. He was ____ about the trip and could talk of nothing else. (1) thrilled (2) interested (3) content (4) willing

                                      36. I am ____ to help if you need me. (1) willing (2) thrilled (3) desperate (4) frantic

                                      37. The old photograph had ____ a little, though the faces were still clear. (1) faded (2) vanished (3) disappeared (4) dissolved

                                      38. The glass ____ into hundreds of pieces on the tiles. (1) shattered (2) cracked (3) chipped (4) bent

                                      39. There is a small ____ in the cup but it still holds tea. (1) chip (2) shattering (3) collapse (4) explosion

                                      40. Her voice was ____ with excitement, though she was trying hard to sound calm. (1) trembling (2) steady (3) flat (4) level

                                      VA21 · Connectors for writing · 30 items · P5

                                      Choose the connector that shows the right relationship between the two ideas.

                                      1. The bus broke down. ____ (Consequently / Meanwhile / Similarly), we arrived an hour late.

                                      2. The rain had stopped. ____ (Nevertheless / Therefore / Likewise), the pitch was still unplayable.

                                      3. Wei Jie prepared the slides. ____ (Meanwhile / However / Consequently), Priya practised the speech.

                                      4. Cycling is cheap. ____ (Moreover / However / Nevertheless), it keeps you fit.

                                      5. The recipe looked simple. ____ (In fact / Therefore / Similarly), it took three hours.

                                      6. She trained every morning. ____ (As a result / However / Meanwhile), she broke her own record.

                                      7. Dogs need daily walks. ____ (Similarly / However / Instead), rabbits need daily handling.

                                      8. He did not enjoy the film. ____ (Nonetheless / Therefore / Likewise), he stayed until the end.

                                      9. We could take the train. ____ (Alternatively / Consequently / Furthermore), we could walk.

                                      10. We had planned to work in the library, but it was shut. ____ (Instead / Moreover / Therefore), we worked in the canteen.

                                      11. Plastic bottles take centuries to break down. ____ (Furthermore / However / Meanwhile), most are never recycled.

                                      12. The plan was expensive. ____ (On the other hand / As a result / Likewise), it would last twenty years.

                                      13. First we washed the tins. ____ (Next / However / Therefore), we flattened them.

                                      14. We have settled the costs and the timetable. ____ (Finally / Firstly / Meanwhile), I would like to thank the volunteers.

                                      15. The road will be resurfaced from June until August. ____ (In the meantime / Consequently / Similarly), buses will use Jalan Bahru.

                                      16. He is the youngest in the team. ____ (Even so / Therefore / Likewise), he is the captain.

                                      17. ____ (Although / Despite / However) it was raining, the match went ahead.

                                      18. ____ (Despite / Although / However) the rain, the match went ahead.

                                      19. The shop sells bread and cakes ____ (but / and / or) no longer bakes biscuits.

                                      20. ____ (Whereas / Because / Therefore) my brother likes durian, I cannot stand it.

                                      21. The experiment failed twice. ____ (Eventually / Immediately / Similarly), it worked.

                                      22. Read the whole question. ____ (Only then / Meanwhile / Likewise) should you begin to write.

                                      23. She is a careful driver. ____ (By contrast / Similarly / Furthermore), her brother is reckless.

                                      24. I have three things to tell you. ____ (To begin with / Finally / Meanwhile), let me explain why the trip was cancelled.

                                      25. The cost is high. ____ (That said / Therefore / Likewise), the results speak for themselves.

                                      26. He apologised. ____ (Even then / Therefore / Similarly), she would not speak to him.

                                      27. Wear closed shoes. ____ (Otherwise / Therefore / Meanwhile), you will not be allowed in.

                                      28. ____ (In conclusion / For instance / Meanwhile), the scheme should be continued for another term.

                                      29. Many everyday objects contain magnets — ____ (for instance / therefore / however), fridge doors and headphones.

                                      30. The bin was full. ____ (Rather than / Therefore / Similarly) leave the cup on top, he carried it downstairs.

                                      Answer Key

                                      VA11 · Similes & proverbs · 40 items · P5

                                      1 (1) · 2 (2) · 3 (1) · 4 (2) · 5 (2) · 6 (2) · 7 (1) · 8 (3) · 9 (1) · 10 (2) · 11 (1) · 12 (2) · 13 (2) · 14 (1) · 15 (1) · 16 (3) · 17 (2) · 18 (2) · 19 (2) · 20 (2) · 21 (2) · 22 (2) · 23 (2) · 24 (2) · 25 (1) · 26 (2) · 27 (1) · 28 (1) · 29 (2) · 30 (1) · 31 (1) · 32 (2) · 33 (2) · 34 (2) · 35 (2) · 36 (2) · 37 (2) · 38 (2) · 39 (1) · 40 (2)

                                      • 1 log — 'Slept like a log' means slept very deeply.
                                      • 2 peas — The simile is 'as alike as two peas in a pod'.
                                      • 3 fiddle — 'As fit as a fiddle' means in excellent health.
                                      • 4 sheet — 'As white as a sheet' describes a face pale with shock.
                                      • 5 mouse — 'As quiet as a mouse' is the set simile.
                                      • 6 ice — 'As cold as ice' is the fixed comparison.
                                      • 7 mule — 'As stubborn as a mule' means refusing to change.
                                      • 8 crystal — 'As clear as crystal' means perfectly clear.
                                      • 9 sandpaper — 'As rough as sandpaper' describes a coarse surface.
                                      • 10 chickens — The proverb warns against assuming success too early.
                                      • 11 stitch — Fixing a small problem early prevents a big one.
                                      • 12 cooks — Too many people interfering ruins the result.
                                      • 13 words — What you do matters more than what you say.
                                      • 14 cover — Appearance does not reveal worth.
                                      • 15 bird — Those who act first gain the advantage.
                                      • 16 perfect — Repeated effort leads to mastery.
                                      • 17 way — Determination finds a solution.
                                      • 18 wrongs — Returning bad behaviour does not justify it.
                                      • 19 leap — Think carefully before acting.
                                      • 20 spots — People rarely change their basic nature.
                                      • 21 day — Great things take time.
                                      • 22 iron — Act while the opportunity lasts.
                                      • 23 cloud — Every difficulty has something good in it.
                                      • 24 dogs — Do not stir up an old problem.
                                      • 25 feather — Similar people keep company.
                                      • 26 pen — Writing has more power than force.
                                      • 27 policy — Telling the truth is always wisest.
                                      • 28 choosers — Those in need must accept what is offered.
                                      • 29 hay — Use a good opportunity while it lasts.
                                      • 30 bee — 'As busy as a bee' means working hard.
                                      • 31 eel — 'As slippery as an eel' is the set simile.
                                      • 32 horse — 'Eats like a horse' means eats a great deal.
                                      • 33 bat — 'As blind as a bat' is the fixed comparison.
                                      • 34 nose — 'As plain as the nose on your face' means obvious.
                                      • 35 jack — Someone who does everything does nothing excellently.
                                      • 36 eggs — Do not risk everything on one plan.
                                      • 37 milk — There is no point regretting what cannot be undone.
                                      • 38 feather — 'As light as a feather' is the set simile.
                                      • 39 sore — 'Like a sore thumb' means very noticeable.
                                      • 40 never — Arriving late is better than not arriving.

                                      VA12 · Homophones · words that sound the same · P4

                                      • 1 blew — 'Blew' is the past of 'blow'; 'blue' is the colour.
                                      • 2 there — 'There is' points out that something exists.
                                      • 3 Their — 'Their' shows possession.
                                      • 4 They're — 'They're' means 'they are'.
                                      • 5 too — 'Too' means excessively.
                                      • 6 to — 'To' shows direction.
                                      • 7 two — 'Two' is the number.
                                      • 8 its — Possessive 'its' has no apostrophe.
                                      • 9 It's — 'It's' means 'it is'.
                                      • 10 Your — 'Your' shows possession.
                                      • 11 You're — 'You're' means 'you are'.
                                      • 12 piece — A 'piece' is a part of something.
                                      • 13 peace — 'Peace' means calm or the end of conflict.
                                      • 14 whole — 'Whole' means entire.
                                      • 15 hole — A 'hole' is an opening.
                                      • 16 fair — 'Fair' means just; a 'fare' is the money you pay for a journey.
                                      • 17 fare — A 'fare' is the cost of a journey.
                                      • 18 plain — A 'plain' is flat land; a 'plane' flies.
                                      • 19 peek — A 'peek' is a quick look; a 'peak' is the top of a mountain.
                                      • 20 weather — 'Weather' means conditions outside.
                                      • 21 whether — 'Whether' introduces a choice.
                                      • 22 flour — 'Flour' is used in baking.
                                      • 23 flower — A 'flower' grows on a plant.
                                      • 24 allowed — 'Allowed' means permitted.
                                      • 25 aloud — 'Aloud' means out loud.
                                      • 26 principal — The 'principal' is the head of a school.
                                      • 27 principal — 'Principal' can also mean main or chief.
                                      • 28 waist — The 'waist' is part of the body.
                                      • 29 waste — 'Waste' means to use carelessly.
                                      • 30 rose — 'Rose' is the past of 'rise'.
                                      • 31 rows — 'Rows' are lines of seats.
                                      • 32 passed — 'Passed' is the past of 'pass'.
                                      • 33 past — 'Past' means beyond.
                                      • 34 won — 'Won' is the past of 'win'; 'one' is the number.
                                      • 35 weak — 'Weak' means lacking strength.
                                      • 36 week — A 'week' is seven days.
                                      • 37 threw — 'Threw' is the past of 'throw'.
                                      • 38 through — 'Through' means from one side to the other.
                                      • 39 stationary — 'Stationary' means not moving.
                                      • 40 stationery — 'Stationery' means writing materials.

                                      VA13 · Compound words · 30 items · P4

                                      • 1 park — 'Car park' is written as two words in British English but functions as one idea.
                                      • 2 tooth — 'Toothbrush' is one word.
                                      • 3 bath — 'Bathroom' is one word.
                                      • 4 sun — 'Sunlight' is one word.
                                      • 5 cloth — 'Dishcloth' is written as one word.
                                      • 6 sun — 'Sunset' is one word.
                                      • 7 goal — 'Goalkeeper' is one word.
                                      • 8 note — 'Notebook' is one word.
                                      • 9 foot — 'Footpath' is one word.
                                      • 10 thunder — 'Thunderstorm' is one word.
                                      • 11 noon — 'Afternoon' is one word: after + noon.
                                      • 12 note — 'Notepaper' is one word.
                                      • 13 back — 'Backyard' is one word.
                                      • 14 cake — 'Teacake' is one word.
                                      • 15 fighter — 'Firefighter' is one word.
                                      • 16 work — 'Homework' is one word.
                                      • 17 pack — 'Backpack' is one word.
                                      • 18 board — 'Blackboard' is one word.
                                      • 19 pour — 'Downpour' is one word.
                                      • 20 cut — 'Paper cut' is written as two words.
                                      • 21 fall — 'Rainfall' is one word.
                                      • 22 time — 'Lunchtime' is one word.
                                      • 23 box — 'Lunchbox' is one word.
                                      • 24 coat — 'Raincoat' is one word.
                                      • 25 bridge — 'Footbridge' is one word.
                                      • 26 roads — A 'crossroads' is one word and always ends in s.
                                      • 27 shop — 'Bicycle shop' is written as two words.
                                      • 28 worm — A 'bookworm' loves reading.
                                      • 29 overs — 'Leftovers' is one word and is always plural.
                                      • 30 sill — 'Windowsill' is one word.

                                      VA14 · Describing feelings & character · 50 words for composition · P5

                                      1 (1) · 2 (2) · 3 (1) · 4 (1) · 5 (1) · 6 (1) · 7 (1) · 8 (1) · 9 (2) · 10 (1) · 11 (1) · 12 (1) · 13 (1) · 14 (1) · 15 (1) · 16 (1) · 17 (1) · 18 (1) · 19 (1) · 20 (1) · 21 (1) · 22 (1) · 23 (1) · 24 (1) · 25 (1) · 26 (1) · 27 (1) · 28 (1) · 29 (1) · 30 (1) · 31 (1) · 32 (1) · 33 (1) · 34 (1) · 35 (1) · 36 (1) · 37 (1) · 38 (1) · 39 (1) · 40 (1) · 41 (1) · 42 (1) · 43 (1) · 44 (1) · 45 (1) · 46 (1) · 47 (1) · 48 (1) · 49 (1) · 50 (1)

                                      • 1 elated — 'Elated' means extremely joyful — stronger than 'happy'.
                                      • 2 indifferent — 'Indifferent' means showing no interest either way.
                                      • 3 dejected — 'Dejected' means low in spirits after a disappointment.
                                      • 4 seething — 'Seething' means boiling with anger held in.
                                      • 5 sheepish — 'Sheepish' means embarrassed at one's own mistake.
                                      • 6 overawed — 'Overawed' means made to feel small by something impressive.
                                      • 7 wistfully — 'Wistful' means sadly longing for something past. Because 'looked at' here means 'gazed at', the adverb 'wistfully' is needed.
                                      • 8 stern — 'Stern' means serious and severe.
                                      • 9 boastful — 'Boastful' means speaking too proudly about oneself.
                                      • 10 modest — 'Modest' means not boasting.
                                      • 11 timid — 'Timid' means easily frightened.
                                      • 12 foolhardy — 'Foolhardy' means brave without thinking of the danger.
                                      • 13 diligent — 'Diligent' means hard-working and careful.
                                      • 14 curt — 'Curt' means rudely short.
                                      • 15 genial — 'Genial' means friendly and cheerful.
                                      • 16 composed — 'Composed' means calm and in control.
                                      • 17 dumbfounded — 'Dumbfounded' means so astonished that one cannot speak.
                                      • 18 restless — 'Restless' means unable to keep still through impatience.
                                      • 19 unruly — 'Unruly' means badly behaved and hard to control.
                                      • 20 suspicious — 'Suspicious' means believing something is wrong.
                                      • 21 overjoyed — 'Overjoyed' means extremely happy.
                                      • 22 solemn — 'Solemn' means serious and grave.
                                      • 23 resentful — 'Resentful' means bitter about unfair treatment.
                                      • 24 reassuring — 'Reassuring' means making somebody feel safe.
                                      • 25 reluctant — 'Reluctant' means unwilling.
                                      • 26 frenzied — 'Frenzied' means wildly excited and uncontrolled.
                                      • 27 frail — 'Frail' means weak and delicate.
                                      • 28 perceptive — 'Perceptive' means showing sharp understanding.
                                      • 29 indignant — 'Indignant' means angry at something unjust.
                                      • 30 considerate — 'Considerate' means thinking of others' feelings.
                                      • 31 nagging — 'Nagging' means persistent and impossible to ignore.
                                      • 32 infectious — 'Infectious' laughter spreads to other people.
                                      • 33 stunned — 'Stunned' means shocked into stillness.
                                      • 34 fanatical — 'Fanatical' means extremely enthusiastic.
                                      • 35 grudging — 'Grudging' means given unwillingly.
                                      • 36 obstinate — 'Obstinate' means stubbornly refusing to change.
                                      • 37 beaming — 'Beaming' means shining with happiness.
                                      • 38 mortified — 'Mortified' means deeply embarrassed.
                                      • 39 demoralised — 'Demoralised' means having lost confidence and hope.
                                      • 40 observant — 'Observant' means quick to notice things.
                                      • 41 wary — 'Wary' means cautious because of possible danger.
                                      • 42 half-hearted — 'Half-hearted' means done without real feeling.
                                      • 43 weak — 'Weak with relief' describes the body going limp when a fear passes.
                                      • 44 obliging — 'Obliging' means willing to help.
                                      • 45 humbled — 'Humbled' means made to feel modest by somebody's goodness.
                                      • 46 tactless — 'Tactless' means careless of other people's feelings.
                                      • 47 conscientious — 'Conscientious' means taking care to do things properly.
                                      • 48 uneasy — 'Uneasy' means troubled and uncomfortable.
                                      • 49 unwavering — 'Unwavering' means steady and never moving away.
                                      • 50 thankful — 'Thankful' means grateful and relieved.

                                      VA15 · Vivid verbs · show, don't tell · P5

                                      1 (1) · 2 (1) · 3 (1) · 4 (1) · 5 (1) · 6 (1) · 7 (1) · 8 (1) · 9 (1) · 10 (1) · 11 (1) · 12 (1) · 13 (1) · 14 (1) · 15 (1) · 16 (1) · 17 (1) · 18 (1) · 19 (1) · 20 (1) · 21 (1) · 22 (1) · 23 (1) · 24 (1) · 25 (1) · 26 (1) · 27 (1) · 28 (1) · 29 (1) · 30 (1) · 31 (1) · 32 (1) · 33 (1) · 34 (1) · 35 (1) · 36 (1) · 37 (1) · 38 (1) · 39 (1) · 40 (1)

                                      • 1 hobbled — 'Hobbled' shows both slowness and pain in one word.
                                      • 2 strode — 'Strode' suggests long, confident steps.
                                      • 3 tiptoed — 'Tiptoed' shows the care taken to be silent.
                                      • 4 trudged — 'Trudged' carries the weight of exhaustion.
                                      • 5 barked — 'Barked' shows short, sharp anger.
                                      • 6 breathed — 'Breathed' suggests words barely spoken aloud.
                                      • 7 choked out — 'Choked out' shows tears interrupting the words.
                                      • 8 whined — 'Whined' carries the complaining tone.
                                      • 9 stared — 'Stared' means a long, fixed look.
                                      • 10 glanced — 'Glanced' means a very brief look.
                                      • 11 glared — 'Glared' is an angry stare.
                                      • 12 peered — 'Peered' suggests straining to see.

                                      Document 15

                                      Continuous Writing — Eight Full Model Compositions

                                      Paper 1 Part 2 is worth 40 marks: 20 for content and 20 for language. This is the single largest block of marks in the whole examination.

                                      Use these the hard way. Set a timer for 46 minutes — six to plan, forty to write — and write the whole composition before you read the model. Reading the model first is comfortable and teaches you nothing.

                                      The marking bands

                                      Content — 20 Language — 20
                                      17–20 · Fully relevant, a clear and interesting plot, well-developed characters and feelings 18 17–20 · Varied sentences, accurate tenses, precise vocabulary, almost no errors 18
                                      13–16 · Relevant with a clear plot; some development of feelings 14 13–16 · Generally accurate; some variety; a few errors that do not obscure meaning 14
                                      9–12 · Mostly relevant; the plot is thin or rushed in places 10 9–12 · Simple sentences, repeated structures, several errors 10
                                      5–8 · Partly relevant; events listed rather than told 6 5–8 · Frequent errors; meaning sometimes unclear 6
                                      0–4 · Largely irrelevant to the theme or the pictures 2 0–4 · Meaning often lost 2

                                      A word of warning about these models. They are deliberately plain. They work by structure, specific detail and honest feeling rather than by rich description. A Singapore marking scheme also rewards vivid vocabulary, varied sentence openings and figurative language, so do not read these as permission to write flatly. Take the shape from them, and bring your own colour to it.

                                      1. Honesty

                                      The task

                                      Write a composition about a time when someone owned up to something.

                                      Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: a broken window • a spilt drink on a desk • a queue at a school office.

                                      About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.

                                      A plan that would work: Setting: school office, Thursday recess. Characters: narrator, Mrs Halim. Problem: cracked a window and walked away. Climax: the assembly announcement about the science club. Resolution: owns up, is punished anyway, feels lighter.

                                      Model composition (253 words)

                                      I had been in the school office twice before, both times to collect something. The third time was different.

                                      It began with a football and a window that cracked, rather than smashed, so quietly that nobody came running. I stood with the ball in my hands and waited for somebody to shout. Nobody did. After about ten seconds I walked away.

                                      I got through the whole of Tuesday. I was almost through Wednesday when Mrs Halim announced at assembly that a window had been damaged, that the school would not be replacing it this term, and that the science club would therefore have to move.

                                      It was the science club that did it. Not guilt exactly — something smaller and more annoying, like a stone in a shoe.

                                      At recess on Thursday I joined the queue outside the general office. There were four people ahead of me and I thought about leaving at least twice. When my turn came I said it in one breath, before I could stop myself: "I broke the window in the science corridor on Tuesday."

                                      Mrs Halim put down her pen and looked at me for a long moment.

                                      "Thank you," she said. "That will have been difficult."

                                      I had to help the cleaner for four Fridays, and my father was not pleased, and the science club still had to move. None of that was the part I remember. What I remember is walking out of that office feeling about five kilograms lighter than when I went in.

                                      Why it scores: The composition does not start with the crime; it starts with the office, which is where it will end. The delay between Tuesday and Thursday is where the real story lives, and the writer gives it most of the space. "Like a stone in a shoe" does more work than a paragraph about feeling guilty would. Note that the confession is not rewarded — the punishment still happens — which is what stops the ending from being childish.

                                      2. A difficult decision

                                      The task

                                      Write a composition about a difficult decision.

                                      Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: two friends arguing • a mobile phone showing a message • an empty seat on a bus.

                                      About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.

                                      A plan that would work: Setting: school, then eleven days. Characters: narrator, Aishah. Problem: asked to cover a lie. Climax: says no and loses the friendship for eleven days. Resolution: Aishah returns, almost apologises.

                                      Model composition (251 words)

                                      Aishah and I had been friends since Primary 1. On the Tuesday of the second week of term, she asked me to lie for her.

                                      It was not a big lie. Her mother had told her to come straight home; she wanted to go to the mall with two girls from the other class. All she needed was for me to say she had been at my flat doing the Social Studies project.

                                      She held out her phone with the message already typed. All I had to do was press send from my own.

                                      "It's one message," she said. "Just say yes."

                                      I have thought since about how easy it would have been. I could have typed four words and gone back to my dinner.

                                      What stopped me was not honesty, which I would like to claim. It was that I could picture Aunty Zaleha at our door the following week, thanking my mother for having Aishah over, and my mother's face while she worked out what was happening.

                                      I said no. Aishah said, "Fine," in the way that means the opposite, and did not walk home with me for eleven days. I counted.

                                      On the twelfth day she sat down next to me at recess, opened her lunchbox, and said, "My mother found out anyway. Someone posted a photograph." Then she said, quietly, "You would have been in trouble too."

                                      That was as close to thank you as I was going to get, and I found that it was enough.

                                      Why it scores: The decision is small, which makes it believable. The writer refuses to claim a noble motive — "not honesty, which I would like to claim" — and that honesty about dishonesty is what lifts the content mark. The eleven days are counted, which shows the cost. The ending gives no apology and no hug, only a sentence that means one, and the narrator accepting it.

                                      3. Perseverance

                                      The task

                                      Write a composition about not giving up.

                                      Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: a swimming pool • a musical instrument • a flight of stairs.

                                      About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.

                                      A plan that would work: Setting: a third-floor flat, January to March. Characters: grandmother, narrator, father. Problem: she cannot manage the stairs. Climax: found practising alone on the second landing. Resolution: reaches the ground floor in five weeks and goes to the market alone.

                                      Model composition (219 words)

                                      My grandmother moved in with us in January, four months after her fall, and she could not manage the stairs.

                                      We live on the third floor of a block with no lift. For the first three weeks she did not leave the flat at all. She sat by the window in the afternoons and watched the void deck, and said she was perfectly happy, which was a lie we all agreed to believe.

                                      Then one Saturday my father found her on the second landing, holding the rail with both hands, quite out of breath.

                                      "I am practising," she said.

                                      After that we practised together. Four steps on the first day. Six on the second. We went down in the morning when the stairwell was cool and back up before lunch, and at every landing she stopped and told me something — about the kampung, about my grandfather, about a teacher she had disliked in 1958 — and I understood that the stories were how she rested without admitting that she was resting.

                                      It took five weeks to get to the ground floor and back without stopping.

                                      She goes to the market by herself now, on Tuesdays and Fridays, and comes home with more than she can comfortably carry. Nobody has told her to take less. We tried that once.

                                      Why it scores: The perseverance belongs to somebody else, which is a harder and more interesting choice than writing about yourself. The numbers do the work: three weeks, four steps, six steps, five weeks. The observation about the stories being disguised rest is the single best line and shows genuine inference. The last three sentences are funny and affectionate, and end the piece without a moral. One caution: this works because the prompt does not say "you". Check the wording of your own prompt first — if it asks about you, you must be at the centre of the story.

                                      4. A kind act

                                      The task

                                      Write a composition about an act of kindness.

                                      Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: a coin • a hawker centre • an umbrella.

                                      About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.

                                      A plan that would work: Setting: a hawker centre, last November. Characters: narrator, Mdm Chong. Problem: sixty cents short. Climax: she leaves her stall to pay. Resolution: repayment refused, so he becomes a daily customer.

                                      Model composition (216 words)

                                      The drinks auntie at our hawker centre is called Mdm Chong and she has never once got my order wrong in four years.

                                      Last November I went down for lunch on the day my mother's wallet had been stolen. I had exactly two dollars and forty cents, which I had counted three times on the way, and I ordered chicken rice at the stall on the end.

                                      It was three dollars.

                                      I have thought since about how long I stood there. Probably four seconds. It felt considerably longer, and I could hear the queue behind me.

                                      Then a hand came past my shoulder and put a coin on the counter, and Mdm Chong said something in Teochew to the chicken rice uncle that I did not understand, and he laughed, and the plate came.

                                      She had left her own stall unattended to do it.

                                      I tried to pay her back the next day. She refused, twice, and the second time she was annoyed, so I stopped trying. What I do instead is go to her stall for my drink every single day, even when the queue is long and the other stall is empty, and I have done that for ten months now.

                                      I do not think she has noticed. That is not really the point.

                                      Why it scores: The act is tiny — sixty cents — and the writer knows it, which is why the piece spends its length on the four seconds beforehand and the ten months afterwards rather than on the coin. Leaving her own stall unattended is the detail that shows the kindness cost something. The refusal to be repaid, and the narrator's stubborn daily reply, make the ending earned rather than sentimental.

                                      The same story at Primary 5 length (158 words)

                                      The drinks auntie at our hawker centre is Mdm Chong, and she has never got my order wrong in four years.

                                      Last November I went down for lunch on the day my mother's wallet had been stolen. I had two dollars and forty cents. The chicken rice was three dollars.

                                      I stood there for about four seconds. It felt much longer, and I could hear the queue behind me.

                                      Then a hand came past my shoulder and put a coin on the counter. Mdm Chong had left her own stall to do it.

                                      I tried to pay her back the next day. She refused twice, and the second time she was annoyed, so I stopped trying.

                                      What I do instead is buy my drink from her every single day, even when her queue is the longer one. I have done that for ten months. I do not think she has noticed, and that is not really the point.

                                      5. An unexpected discovery

                                      The task

                                      Write a composition about an unexpected discovery.

                                      Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: an old box • a locked cupboard • a photograph.

                                      About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.

                                      A plan that would work: Setting: the spare room. Characters: narrator, father (in the past). Problem: finds his father's old reports. Climax: reads the Primary 4 comment. Resolution: says nothing, but understands his father differently.

                                      Model composition (219 words)

                                      The box was under the bed in the spare room and it was full of school reports, which I did not expect to be interesting.

                                      They were my father's. Primary 1 to Secondary 4, in order, held together with a rubber band that snapped when I touched it.

                                      My father is an engineer. He checks his work twice. He has told me, more than once and in some detail, that carelessness is a choice.

                                      In Primary 4 he was ranked thirty-first out of thirty-eight.

                                      I read the whole of that report sitting on the floor of the spare room with dust on my knees. His teacher, a Mrs Pereira, had written: Kumar is a bright boy who has decided that he is not. I would like to change his mind before he leaves this school.

                                      Underneath, in different ink, somebody had written the date 1987 and the words she did.

                                      I put everything back exactly as I found it, including the broken rubber band, and I have never mentioned it.

                                      But when he tells me off about carelessness now, I listen differently. He is not describing a rule he has always kept. He is describing something that happened to him in 1987, and he is trying to pass it on, and he is not very good at saying so.

                                      Why it scores: The discovery is not treasure or a secret — it is a rank on an old report, which is far more interesting. The teacher's comment is quoted in full because it is the hinge of the whole piece, and the two words in different ink do more than any amount of explanation. The final paragraph re-reads the father's behaviour in the light of the discovery, which is exactly the kind of inference a top band rewards.

                                      The same story at Primary 5 length (145 words)

                                      The box was under the bed in the spare room, and it was full of old school reports.

                                      They were my father's, from Primary 1 to Secondary 4, held together with a rubber band that snapped when I touched it.

                                      My father is an engineer. He checks his work twice. He has told me more than once that carelessness is a choice.

                                      In Primary 4 he was ranked thirty-first out of thirty-eight.

                                      His teacher had written: Kumar is a bright boy who has decided that he is not.

                                      Underneath, in different ink, somebody had added the date 1987 and the words she did.

                                      I put everything back exactly as I had found it and have never mentioned it. But when he tells me off about carelessness now, I listen differently. He is not repeating a rule. He is passing on something that happened to him.

                                      6. Facing a fear

                                      The task

                                      Write a composition about facing a fear.

                                      Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: a stage • a dog • deep water.

                                      About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.

                                      A plan that would work: Setting: school, nine days before the play. Characters: narrator, Mrs Fong, Vanessa. Problem: cast in a speaking part after two years of silence. Climax: the performance. Resolution: gets through it; the fear remains but is no longer total.

                                      Model composition (242 words)

                                      I was cast as the narrator in the Primary 6 play, which has more lines than any other part, because Mrs Fong did not know that I had stopped speaking in class two years earlier.

                                      It was not shyness, exactly. I answered questions. I simply did not speak unless a reply was required, and after a while people stop asking, and after another while it becomes the thing everyone knows about you.

                                      I told her I could not do it. She said, "All right," and gave the part to Vanessa, and I was relieved for about four days.

                                      Then Vanessa got chickenpox.

                                      There were nine days left. Mrs Fong did not ask me again. She left the script on my desk at the end of a lesson, face down, without saying anything at all, and walked out of the room, and that was somehow much harder to refuse than a question would have been.

                                      I learnt it in five days. I was sick twice on the afternoon of the performance. My hands shook so badly during the first paragraph that the pages made a noise the microphone picked up.

                                      And then, somewhere in the second scene, I forgot to be frightened. Not bravely — I was simply too busy.

                                      I still do not enjoy speaking in front of people. But I know now that the fear does not last the whole way through, and that is a genuinely useful thing to know.

                                      Why it scores: The fear is specific and has a history, which makes it real. The script left face down is the best moment in the piece precisely because nothing is said. Note the honesty of "not bravely — I was simply too busy", and the refusal of a triumphant ending: the fear is not cured, only better understood. Examiners reward that far more than "I was no longer afraid of anything".

                                      7. Responsibility

                                      The task

                                      Write a composition about being trusted with something important.

                                      Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: a set of keys • a younger child • a pet.

                                      About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.

                                      A plan that would work: Setting: home, six afternoons in June. Characters: narrator, brother, mother. Problem: brother gets out of the flat. Climax: finds him on the landing below. Resolution: tells his mother; is trusted again.

                                      Model composition (232 words)

                                      For six days in June I was in charge of my brother, who is four, from two o'clock until my mother came home at five.

                                      The first two days went perfectly, which is the dangerous part.

                                      On Wednesday I let him watch a video while I finished a chapter, and when I looked up the flat was quiet in a way that is never good. The front door was open. Not wide — about a hand's width, the way it is when somebody small has pulled it and not been able to pull it far.

                                      I have never moved faster in my life. I found him on the landing one floor down, sitting on the steps, entirely calm, waiting for the cat from 04-12 that he had apparently been visiting for three days.

                                      I did not scold him. I sat down on the step beside him and waited until my hands stopped shaking, which took a while, and then we went back upstairs and I locked the door and put the key on top of the fridge.

                                      I told my mother that evening. All of it.

                                      She was quiet for a moment, and then she said the thing I did not expect: "Thank you for telling me. You will be looking after him again on Monday."

                                      I have never once opened a book in that flat since without first checking the door.

                                      Why it scores: The structure is excellent: two days that only looked easy — note that he had already been visiting the cat for three days — then the slip, then the consequence, then a resolution that is a further responsibility rather than a punishment. "Quiet in a way that is never good" and the hand's width of open door are the details that make the fear land. Not scolding the brother shows character. The mother's line is the best sentence in the piece because it is both forgiveness and a test.

                                      8. Something I regret

                                      The task

                                      Write a composition about something you regret.

                                      Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: a birthday cake • an unanswered telephone • a hospital corridor.

                                      About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.

                                      A plan that would work: Setting: Sunday evenings across a year, then a hospital in November. Characters: narrator, great-aunt. Problem: avoids her weekly calls. Climax: the hospital visit, when he realises how much she had remembered. Resolution: she dies; he now answers the telephone first.

                                      Model composition (224 words)

                                      My great-aunt telephoned our flat every Sunday evening at about seven, and for most of 2024 I did not pick up.

                                      It was not unkindness. The calls were long and slow and largely about people I had never met, and I was twelve, and there was always something else. My mother would call out that it was Ah Yee, and I would say I was doing homework, which was occasionally true.

                                      In November she went into hospital, and we visited on a Saturday, and she was smaller than I remembered and very pleased to see us.

                                      She asked me about my school, and about the recorder, which I had stopped playing in Primary 4, and about a friend called Danial whose name I had apparently mentioned to her once, years before, and forgotten I had mentioned.

                                      She had remembered all of it.

                                      I have thought about that a great deal since. She was not telephoning every Sunday to talk. She was telephoning to listen, and the reason the calls were slow was that she was giving me room, week after week, to say something — and for the better part of a year I did not.

                                      She died in February.

                                      The telephone still rings on Sunday evenings sometimes, for other reasons, and I am now the first person in our flat to reach it.

                                      Why it scores: The regret is not dramatic and there is no dying apology, which is exactly why it works. The turn comes at "She had remembered all of it" — one short paragraph that re-reads the whole year. The insight that the slow calls were room being made for him is the sort of realisation that earns a top content band. The final image shows the change instead of announcing it, and the phrase "for other reasons" quietly carries the loss.

                                      Booklet B · Comprehension · 18 marks

                                      Read the passage and answer the questions. Note the marks for each question.

                                      The Mango Tree

                                      There is a mango tree behind our block. It is older than my father.

                                      Every year, in April, it makes far more mangoes than one family could eat. Most of them fall onto the grass and spoil, because nobody can reach the high branches.

                                      Last April, my grandfather had an idea. He tied an old plastic bottle to the end of a long bamboo pole. He cut the bottom off the bottle first, so that a mango would drop straight into it.

                                      It worked. In one afternoon we picked forty-one mangoes.

                                      That was far too many for us. My grandfather washed them, put them into paper bags, and wrote a number on each bag. Then he gave one bag to every flat on our floor. There are eight flats, so each bag had five mangoes in it, and one was left over for him.

                                      The next morning, somebody had left a tin of biscuits outside our door. There was no note.

                                      A week later, Mrs Rahim from the flat at the end knocked and gave us a jar of mango chutney she had made from her bag. She said she had not spoken to anybody on our floor for two years.

                                      The tree is still there. My grandfather still has the bamboo pole behind the door, and he keeps the bottle on it all year, even in the months when there is nothing at all to pick.

                                      1. Where is the mango tree? (1m)

                                      2. Why did most of the mangoes spoil before the grandfather's idea? (2m)

                                      3. Describe the tool the grandfather made. (2m)

                                      4. How many mangoes did they pick in one afternoon? (1m)

                                      5. How do we know the grandfather wanted to be fair to the neighbours? (2m)

                                      6. Who do you think left the tin of biscuits, and why is the writer not certain? (2m)

                                      7. What did Mrs Rahim do with her mangoes, and what did she tell the family when she came? (2m)

                                      8. How do we know the neighbours were grateful? Give one piece of evidence. (1m)

                                      9. Which word in the passage means 'go bad'? (1m)

                                      10. What does the grandfather hope will happen next April, and how do we know? (2m)

                                      11. Why do you think the grandfather wrote a number on each paper bag? (2m)

                                      Booklet B · Comprehension

                                      • 1 It is behind their block of flats.
                                      • 2 They fell onto the grass and were wasted, because nobody could reach the high branches to pick them.
                                      • 3 He tied an old plastic bottle to the end of a long bamboo pole, and cut the bottom off the bottle so that a mango would drop straight into it.
                                      • 4 Forty-one.
                                      • 5 He gave a bag to every flat on the floor, put the same number of mangoes in each bag, and kept only the one that was left over for himself.
                                      • 6 It was probably one of the neighbours who had been given a bag of mangoes. The writer cannot be certain because there was no note with the tin.
                                      • 7 She made mango chutney from them and brought a jar of it to the family. She told them she had not spoken to anybody on their floor for two years.
                                      • 8 Either: somebody left a tin of biscuits outside their door the next morning; or Mrs Rahim brought them a jar of mango chutney a week later.
                                      • 9 'Spoil'.
                                      • 10 He hopes there will be another crop of mangoes to pick and share. We know because he keeps the bottle on the bamboo pole all year round, ready, even in the months when there is nothing to pick.
                                      • 11 So that he could make sure every bag held the same number of mangoes and every flat got a fair share. It shows he had counted them and wanted to divide them evenly.

                                      5. A pupil hands in her form on 10 November for an over-subscribed activity. Will being early help her? (1) No, because places are decided by ballot (2) Yes, because forms are taken in order (3) Yes, because she is a P4 pupil (4) No, because the form is late

                                      6. Which activity would cost a family money? (1) Robotics (2) Choir (3) Art Club (4) Gardening

                                      7. Why does the notice say in bold that you may not join two activities? (1) To make clear that only one choice is allowed (2) Because two activities cost more (3) Because the hall is too small (4) Because some activities clash

                                      8. A pupil checks the noticeboard on 16 November for her result. Why will she not find it? (1) The results are not posted until 22 November (2) Results are sent by post (3) She must ask her form teacher (4) The ballot has been cancelled

                                      Booklet B · Grammar Cloze · 10 marks

                                      The Lost Shoe

                                      On the first day of the holidays, my cousin Farid lost one shoe in the sea at Changi.

                                      He (1)__ standing in the water up to his knees when a wave knocked him over. By the time he stood up again, the left shoe (2)_ gone. We searched for almost an hour, walking up and down the shallow water, (3)___ we never found it.

                                      Farid had to walk back to the car park with one shoe (4)__ and one shoe off, which his sister found far funnier (5)____ he did.

                                      That evening his mother said she (6)__ not going to buy a new pair until September, because the old ones (7)____ almost too small anyway.

                                      Farid spent the rest of the holidays in his school shoes. He (8)__ complained at all. But on the last Sunday, (9)_ we went back to the same beach, he left both shoes in the car and walked to the water barefoot, (10)___ a person who has learnt something.

                                      There is one spelling or grammar error in each numbered line. Write the correction — one word only.

                                      1. Our class has been collecting old newspaper since April. (1m)

                                      2. Each pupil bring a bundle from home every Monday. (1m)

                                      3. We tie them with string and stack them neatly in the coridor. (1m)

                                      4. The bundles are then wieghed on a scale borrowed from the canteen. (1m)

                                      5. Last month we collected more paper then any other class. (1m)

                                      6. Mrs Ong was very pleased of the result. (1m)

                                      7. The money from the paper are used to buy books for the library. (1m)

                                      8. So far we have bought eleven new books, including three atlas. (1m)

                                      9. My favourite is a book about heros who explored the Arctic. (1m)

                                      10. I have read it three times allready. (1m)

                                      11. Next term we will started collecting bottles as well. (1m)

                                      12. Mrs Ong says that bottles are worth more then paper. (1m)

                                      Booklet B · Comprehension · 16 marks

                                      Read the passage and answer the questions. Note the marks for each question.

                                      The Quiet Shop

                                      There is a bookshop near my aunt's flat that has a sign on the door reading NO TALKING, PLEASE. It is not a library. It is a shop, and things in it are for sale.

                                      The owner, Mr Pillai, is not unfriendly. He nods when you come in and nods when you leave. If you need to ask him something, you write it on one of the small yellow squares of paper beside the till, and he writes back underneath.

                                      My aunt says he has run the shop that way for eleven years, and that when he first put the sign up, customers stopped coming. For six months the shop was nearly empty.

                                      Then something changed. People who wanted to be left alone began to travel there on purpose — from other estates, and then from other parts of the island. A newspaper wrote about it. Now the shop is busier on a Saturday than any bookshop in the mall, and it is completely silent.

                                      The first time my aunt took me, I found it uncomfortable. I kept wanting to say something about a book I had found, and there was nobody to say it to. I bought nothing and was glad to leave.

                                      The second time, I stayed for two hours.

                                      What changed was a girl of about six at the shelf by the window. She had found a book about sharks and was holding it open with both arms because it was too big for her hands. She did not say anything. She simply turned it round and showed it to me, and I nodded, and she went back to reading. The whole exchange took four seconds and I have remembered it for three years.

                                      I do not think the sign is really about noise. I think Mr Pillai worked out that most of us have nowhere at all to go where nothing is expected of us, and that this is worth more than conversation.

                                      I have written him two notes in three years. He has answered both. I still do not know what his voice sounds like.

                                      1. What is unusual about the sign on the door of the shop? (2m)

                                      2. How does Mr Pillai answer a customer's question? (2m)

                                      3. What happened to the shop in the first six months after the sign went up? (1m)

                                      4. Give two ways in which we know the shop later became successful. (2m)

                                      5. Why did the narrator find the first visit uncomfortable? (2m)

                                      6. How do we know the narrator's opinion of the shop changed? (2m)

                                      7. Which two-word phrase in the passage means 'deliberately'? (1m)

                                      8. In your own words, explain what the narrator thinks the sign is really for. (2m)

                                      9. What does the last sentence tell us about how the narrator and Mr Pillai know each other? (2m)

                                      1 (2) · 2 (3) · 3 (2) · 4 (3) · 5 (2) · 6 (2) · 7 (3) · 8 (1) · 9 (2) · 10 (3)

                                      Booklet A · Vocabulary

                                      1 (1) · 2 (1) · 3 (1) · 4 (1) · 5 (1) · 6 (1) · 7 (1) · 8 (1)

                                      Booklet A · Vocabulary Cloze

                                      1 (1) · 2 (1) · 3 (1) · 4 (1) · 5 (1)

                                      Booklet A · Visual Text

                                      1 (1) · 2 (1) · 3 (1) · 4 (1) · 5 (1) · 6 (1) · 7 (1) · 8 (1)

                                      • 2 brings

                                      Booklet B · Synthesis and Transformation

                                      • 1 The box was too heavy for Farid to lift
                                      • 2 Priya said that she was bringing the tickets
                                      • 3 The rain was so heavy that we stayed indoors

                                      Booklet B · Comprehension

                                      • 1 It says NO TALKING, PLEASE, which is what you would expect in a library rather than in a shop where things are for sale.
                                      • 2 The customer writes the question on a small yellow square of paper beside the till, and Mr Pillai writes his reply underneath it.
                                      • 3 Customers stopped coming and the shop was nearly empty.
                                      • 4 Any two of: people travelled there on purpose from other estates and other parts of the island; a newspaper wrote about it; it is now busier on a Saturday than any bookshop in the mall.
                                      • 5 He kept wanting to say something about a book he had found, and there was nobody he was allowed to say it to.
                                      • 6 On the first visit he bought nothing and was glad to leave, but on the second visit he stayed for two hours.
                                      • 7 'On purpose'.
                                      • 8 He thinks it is not about noise at all. He believes Mr Pillai realised that most people have nowhere to go where nothing at all is expected of them, and that having such a place matters more than being able to talk.
                                      • 9 They have exchanged two written notes over three years, but the narrator has never heard Mr Pillai speak. It shows that they have got to know each other without a single spoken word.
